payload.message:
This one settled the tree-sitter-python vs. Ruff question decisively, and caught a real bug in the spec while it was at it:

- **Ruff's Rust-native parser crates are a dead end for this**: `ruff_python_ast`/`ruff_python_parser` are explicitly disclaimed by Ruff itself as unstable internal implementation details ("frequent breaking changes," still v0.0.x) — tempting since they're Rust-native, but not a publishable dependency contract. Stick with tree-sitter-python.
- **tree-sitter-python's open issues cluster around bleeding-edge type-hint syntax** (PEP 604/695), not the parts monokl actually needs — decorators, classes, `__all__` are stable ground.
- **Pyright resolves `__all__` and re-exports at the binder phase, before type inference** — genuinely cheap syntax-level work. That's direct support for hitting `Structural` precision on two of the spec's six open Python questions without needing a real type checker.
- **Telling data point**: Sourcegraph's own precision-focused Python tool, `scip-python`, is a *fork of pyright* — not a lighter structural analyzer they built themselves. Even a well-resourced team reached for the full type checker rather than approximate it. That's good validation that targeting `Structural` (not `Exact`) precision for v1.1 is the pragmatic, well-precedented choice, not corner-cutting.
- **Monokl's tokenizer needs zero changes for Python** — snake_case already segments correctly on the existing `_` delimiter rule. The `@` decorator handling is a symbol-*schema* problem (needs a `decorator` field, which the spec already floats), not a tokenizer problem.
- **Caught a real spec bug**: line 8182 references `CapabilityPrecision::Approximate`, which isn't an actual variant of the real enum (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact`). Should be `Heuristic`. Concrete fix, not just a recommendation.

Bottom line: keep tree-sitter-python as planned, target `Structural` for re-export attribution/`__all__`/decorator tagging, `Structural`-but-heuristic for Protocol matching, `Heuristic` for annotation resolution.

Still waiting on the Rust throughput/tokenization thread.

<result># Research Findings: ra_ap_syntax vs syn, Salsa, and Rust Tokenization

## A. Bounding `ra_ap_syntax` parse-only throughput

No published number exists — confirmed harder. Checked directly: rust-analyzer's `crates/syntax` has no `benches/` directory at all ([GitHub API listing](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/tree/master/crates/syntax) — only `Cargo.toml`, `fuzz/`, `rust.ungram`, `src/`, `test_data/`). The historic ["Parsing seems slow" issue #1643](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/issues/1643) diagnosed redundant `Parser::nth` lookahead and Arc-drop overhead but published no throughput figure. The 2024 [issue #17491 "A Plan for Making Rust Analyzer Faster"](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/issues/17491) contains the "twice as slow as syntree" claim verbatim (contributor davidbarsky, benchmarking *tree construction only*, explicitly caveated as unfair since rowan's structural sharing serves incremental editing that syntree doesn't do) plus the "lack of mechanical sympathy" critique (heap-allocated Arcs, overused hashing, underused indexing, no identifier interning). `rowan`'s own repo/docs publish no benchmarks.

Two adjacent anchors help bound it. [tree-sitter-rust](https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter/discussions/3429) — also a lossless, error-recovering CST parser — is reported ~3x slower than rustc's hand-written parser. [`syn`](https://fasterthanli.me/articles/the-virtue-of-unsynn), an AST-only parser assuming valid input, is anecdotally reported parsing ~11,000 lines in ~100ms in a warm-build context — not a rigorous MB/s figure, but a real data point (order of ~100K+ lines/sec). No apples-to-apples benchmark of `ra_ap_syntax`/`rowan` against `syn` or tree-sitter-rust exists anywhere I could find.

**Best-bounded estimate:** lossless CST construction (trivia preservation, green/red tree, structural sharing) is inherently more work per token than `syn`'s AST-only parse of already-valid tokens. Combined with the 2x rowan-vs-syntree gap and tree-sitter's ~3x-vs-rustc gap, expect `ra_ap_syntax` to land in the same broad order of magnitude as tree-sitter-rust — plausibly 3–10x slower than `syn` per byte — likely low tens of MB/s on modern hardware rather than the ~100+ MB/s a bare AST parser could hit. For per-invocation CLI use over typical repo sizes (thousands of files, not gigabytes), this is probably still acceptable latency, but it is not free.

## B. `syn` as the structural-tier alternative

`syn` gives up exactly what the spec's questions predicted: no lossless trivia (comments/whitespace aren't first-class tree nodes the way ra_ap_syntax's CST preserves them for verbatim block-text reproduction), and no incremental reparse (moot here since monokl's Rust tier is cold per-invocation anyway). The sharper, *practical* concern is error recovery. `syn::File::parse` fails fast: [`syn::parse::Error`](https://docs.rs/syn/latest/syn/parse/struct.Error.html) documents returning `Err` at the first bad token, with the recommended pattern being to emit `compile_error!` and stop — there is no "give me what parsed and mark the rest broken" mode. `ra_ap_syntax` is IDE-designed specifically to always produce a tree, tagging error nodes rather than aborting. For monokl, which searches real working trees — WIP branches, merge-conflict markers, mid-edit files — a single syntax error anywhere in a `.rs` file would make `syn` yield zero symbols for that entire file, while `ra_ap_syntax` keeps extracting symbols around the error. That is a real regression, not a theoretical one.

## C. Salsa as monokl's own cache, independent of `ra_ap_hir`

Salsa is a generic, IR-agnostic memoized-query engine, not coupled to rust-analyzer's data model. Two concrete precedents of standalone use: Astral's **ty** (formerly red-knot) Python type checker built its own Salsa-based incremental system from scratch, independent of rust-analyzer's queries ([talkpython.fm](https://talkpython.fm/episodes/show/506/ty-astrals-new-type-checker-formerly-red-knot), [DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/astral-sh/ruff/6-red-knot-type-checker)); and **Biome**, a JS/TS linter/formatter toolchain in a domain adjacent to monokl's, uses Salsa in its workspace/analyzer layer (evidenced by a recent [salsa-setter deadlock fix](https://github.com/biomejs/biome/commit/6450276764ee4794a0fcb46c139f95b68d892427)). Monokl could define its own queries (symbols-for-file, postings-for-term) memoized on content hash, without touching `cargo metadata`/crate-graph machinery — a materially lighter proposition than embedding `ra_ap_hir`. Caveat: Salsa's API has undergone significant breaking rewrites; pin a version deliberately.

## D. Tokenizer, grounded in `tokens.rs` (monokl-spec.md:866-937)

Traced each construct against the actual code. `vec!`/`println!` → `!` is a pure separator, base identifier survives as "vec"/"println" (fine). Turbofish `::<Vec<u8>>` → `::`/`<`/`>` are separators, inner identifiers tokenize normally, single-letter generics (`T`) correctly dropped by the len≥2 filter. `#[derive(Debug, Clone)]` → tokens "derive", "debug", "clone" — meaningfully indexed, contrary to worry. Confirmed gap: `'a` is dropped as noise (apostrophe separates, "a" is len-1). Longer lifetimes (`'ctx`, `'static`) survive but collide indistinguishably with plain identifiers — minor precision loss. A real, cheap-to-fix gap: `STOP_WORDS` includes `mod`/`impl`/`pub`/`type` etc. but omits `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe` — these will appear as high-frequency near-universal tokens across any Rust corpus (BM25's IDF partially compensates, but it's free precision left on the table). Edge case: raw identifiers (`r#type`) vanish entirely since the escaped keyword is itself a stopword.

## Recommendation

Keep `ra_ap_syntax` for the structural tier. Its error recovery on malformed/in-progress code is a load-bearing feature for a search tool scanning real working trees, not a nice-to-have — `syn`'s fail-fast model would silently blank out symbol extraction for any file with a syntax error, which is worse than the unquantified throughput cost of the CST. Investigate Salsa separately and independently of the `ra_ap_hir` question — it has real standalone precedent (ty, Biome) and would give monokl warm-daemon-style incremental recomputation for its own queries without a crate-graph load. For the tokenizer, add `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe` to `STOP_WORDS` as a low-cost precision improvement; no other change is warranted.</result>

payload.message:
Two different questions are bundled in "what other languages" — and they have different answers:

**Is the current roadmap (TS/JS → Rust/Python → C#) right?** Probably yes, and not by guesswork — the spec's own references (an ADR for `proto-dotnet`/`orbit`, `Broadway.Marketplace` fixtures) point to C# reflecting a real internal codebase at the company, not a speculative market-coverage pick. That's the right kind of signal to expand on.

**Should monokl add languages beyond those four?** Here's the more interesting strategic finding from everything we just learned about codegraph: monokl commits to a fully-native parser per language (OXC, ra-ap-syntax) — precise, but each new language is a real engineering project, not a config file. codegraph gets to 30+ languages cheaply because it's one generic tree-sitter-walking engine with thin per-language config objects bolted on. Java's back, and it settled cleanly:

- **No viable native Rust Java parser exists** — checked `oak-java` and `java-lang` specifically (both single-maintainer, pre-1.0, near-zero organic adoption). Even codegraph's own hand-optimized "native, no-WASM" performance kernel still compiles `tree-sitter-java` natively via FFI rather than replacing the grammar — decisive confirmation tree-sitter-java is simply the right tool here.
- **Semantic analysis is strictly bimodal for Java** — full JDT/javac classpath resolution (daemon-only, with real documented pain: 20s cold completion on huge projects, OOM crashes on 3000+-file imports) or pure syntax. Unlike Rust/TS, there's no established lightweight middle tier.
- **Explicit FQN imports cut both ways**: non-wildcard imports give an unambiguous textual mapping (easier than Go/TS), but idiomatic Java leans much more heavily on JAR-only external symbols (JDK, Spring, Guava, Lombok) with no local source than comparable Rust/Python code does — a structurally harder version of a gap monokl already has elsewhere.
- **codegraph's real Java extractor is 334 lines — more hand-tuned than even its Rust extractor** — but ~150 of those lines are just Lombok-generated-member synthesis (`@Getter`/`@Data`/`@Builder` → synthetic getters/setters/`equals`/`hashCode`), because Lombok codegen would otherwise silently break call-chain resolution. It also has a dedicated Spring resolver, but notably **no Maven/Gradle multi-module resolver** — a real gap even in a mature tool.
- **Same stop-word gap pattern, again**: `public`, `private`, `static`, `final`, `void`, `new`, `implements`, `package`, `throws`, `super`, `null` all missing from the current TS/Rust-tuned list.
- **Recommendation**: hand-tuned `Structural`-tier analyzer on tree-sitter-java (not generic fallback), matching Rust's current tier — Lombok synthesis is worth the investment, Maven/Gradle multi-module resolution can stay `Heuristic` for now, and `Exact` is off the table (daemon-only).

Still waiting on Go before I do the consolidated update to both the artifact and the spec's language-roadmap section.

<result># Go as monokl's 4th Language — Research Findings

## A. Native Rust Go-parser landscape

**gosyn** ([chikaku/gosyn](https://github.com/chikaku/gosyn)) is real and viable, contrary to expectations for a niche parser: 152,004 downloads, 17 published versions since Feb 2022, last crates.io publish 2026-07-14 (days old), commits weekly, MIT-licensed, 33 stars/7 forks, 3 real downstream dependents. Source confirms Go 1.18+ generics support — `parse_type_parameters()`, `type_parameters()`, and tests for generic instantiation/generic pointer types all exist. This is the strongest native-parser candidate found across all four languages evaluated this session.

By contrast: **go-parser/go-types** (Goscript project) explicitly excludes generics ("pre-1.18... excluding generics") and the whole project is now unmaintained, superseded by Volang. **golang-parser** (bk-rs/golang-rs) is a struct-tag-to-Rust-struct converter, not a general parser (13 stars). **gofmt** (zjykzk) is a brand-new (Oct 2025, 594 downloads) formatter, unproven. **gomod-rs/gomod-parser** only parse `go.mod`, not source. No "goast" Rust crate exists.

## B. Semantic-analysis cost model

`go/packages.Load` scales with package count, not embeddable in a cold CLI call: on a 20k-package monorepo (77,688 files), `InitialWorkspaceLoadDuration` was **3m26s** cold, with `go list` alone taking 1m6s ([golang/go#69523](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/69523)). Even a *warm* gopls daemon serving a new client on a 2,047-package repo took 10+ seconds before becoming usable ([golang/go#48829](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/48829)). This confirms daemon-only architecture, same conclusion as Rust's `ra_ap_hir`.

A lighter, syntax-only path is exactly monokl's existing Rust pattern (parse + structural extraction, no resolution) — directly portable via gosyn, since Go's own `go/parser`/`go/ast` are Go-only and using them at all means cgo/FFI, which monokl wants to avoid.

Import resolution *is* easier than Rust's for the common case — codegraph's own `resolveGoCrossPackageReference` proves it out today: read `go.mod`'s module directive, strip the prefix from an import path to get a project-relative directory, look up the exported symbol. No macros, no monomorphization. # Paper Summary: Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases

## Domain & Authors
This paper addresses **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for software engineering**, specifically repository-level code analysis. The author is Manideep Reddy Chinthareddy, a Software Engineer from Centerville, USA.

## Problem Addressed
The paper tackles a critical limitation in code-based RAG systems: "vector similarity often introduces context flattening" and "fails on multi-hop architectural reasoning." Traditional vector-only retrieval cannot reliably capture structural dependencies like inheritance chains, dependency injection patterns, and interface-driven wiring that are essential for answering complex code questions.

## Methodology
The research compares three retrieval approaches on Java codebases (Shopizer, ThingsBoard, OpenMRS Core):

1. **No-Graph**: Standard vector similarity search over code chunks
2. **LLM-KB**: LLM-generated dependency graphs built during indexing
3. **DKB (Proposed)**: Deterministic AST-derived graphs using Tree-sitter parsing with bidirectional traversal and interface-aware expansion

All approaches use identical 15-question benchmark suites per repository and shared hyperparameters (chunk_size=1000, top-k=10).

## Key Findings

**Indexing Performance:**
- DKB builds graphs in seconds (2.81s on Shopizer; 13.77s on ThingsBoard; 5.60s on OpenMRS)
- LLM-KB requires substantially longer (200.14s, 883.74s, 222.17s respectively)

**Indexing Reliability (Critical Finding):**
- LLM-KB exhibits probabilistic incompleteness: on Shopizer, 377 files were "SKIPPED/MISSED by LLM"
- File success rate: 0.688 (833/1210 files processed)
- Chunk coverage: LLM-KB at 0.641 vs. DKB at 0.902 compared to baseline
- Graph nodes: LLM-KB produced 842 nodes vs. DKB's 1158 nodes

**Cost Analysis:**
- Shopizer end-to-end costs: $0.04 (No-Graph), $0.09 (DKB), $0.79 (LLM-KB)
- Normalized multipliers: ~2.25× for DKB, ~19.75× for LLM-KB
- Larger workloads amplify the difference: on combined OpenMRS+ThingsBoard, LLM-KB reached 45.64× multiplier

**Query Latency:**
- No-Graph: 9.52±2.98s (Shopizer); 10.92±1.43s (ThingsBoard); 11.82±2.79s (OpenMRS)
- DKB: 10.51±4.17s; 11.17±1.97s; 12.21±6.96s
- LLM-KB: 13.36±7.87s; 15.29±4.94s; 11.94±4.88s (higher variance and outliers)

**Answer Correctness (Shopizer 15-question suite):**
- DKB: 15/15 correct (perfect)
- LLM-KB: 13/15 correct (2 partial)
- No-Graph: 6/15 correct (highest hallucination risk)

Across all 45 questions (three repositories): DKB achieved 43/45 correct, LLM-KB 38/45, No-Graph 31/45.

## Main Conclusions

1. **Deterministic advantage**: DKB provides "more reliable grounding than probabilistic extraction, particularly for multi-hop and upstream discovery queries"

2. **Indexing completeness matters**: LLM-KB's file-level extraction omissions create "unpredictable blind spots" that reduce both corpus coverage and graph effectiveness

3. **Cost-effectiveness**: DKB offers a "low-overhead, deterministic structural signal" without LLM-mediated inflation, making it practical for production systems

4. **Trade-offs exist**: While DKB excels on architectural questions requiring multi-hop traversal, vector-only performs competitively on localized questions and some repository types

5. **Architectural grounding**: DKB's bidirectional traversal and interface-consumer expansion particularly improve "upstream discovery" scenarios where controllers/services must be identified through interface implementations

## Recommendations
The authors recommend DKB for "correctness-sensitive tasks (impact analysis, controller discovery, transaction boundary inference)" and emphasize that enterprises should prioritize deterministic structure for stable corpus coverage in repository-level code analysis.
[/external_agent_tool_result]

payload.message:
This is genuinely strong, independent validation of monokl's core architectural bet — and it comes from a completely different angle than anything we've researched so far.

**The paper**: "Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases" (Chinthareddy, Jan 2026) compares three retrieval strategies for code RAG on real Java codebases (Shopizer, ThingsBoard, OpenMRS): pure vector similarity ("No-Graph"), LLM-generated dependency graphs ("LLM-KB"), and **deterministic AST-derived graphs via Tree-sitter** ("DKB") — which is architecturally almost exactly what monokl's `WorkspaceIndex` (ImportGraph + SymbolIndex, built from real parser output) already is.

The results land squarely in monokl's favor:

- **LLM-generated graphs are unreliable at the indexing step itself**: on Shopizer, the LLM silently skipped/missed 377 of 1210 files (68.8% success rate) — a completeness failure that compounds into every downstream query.
- **Deterministic AST graphs are dramatically cheaper to build**: 2.81–13.77s vs. 200–884s for LLM-generated graphs — 70–150× faster indexing, and only ~2.25× the cost of no-graph-at-all vs. LLM-KB's 20–45× cost multiplier.
- **Answer correctness favors the deterministic graph decisively**: across all 45 benchmark questions, DKB scored 43/45, LLM-KB 38/45, pure vector similarity only 31/45 — and the gap is largest specifically on multi-hop architectural questions (impact analysis, interface-driven controller/service discovery) — exactly the query shape monokl's `dependents`/`refs`/`definition`/`explain`/`data-flow` commands target.

This directly reinforces the "reject embedding-based rerank" call from thread 03, but from a different, stronger angle: it's not just "no evidence embeddings help," it's "deterministic structural graphs measurably beat both vector-only *and* LLM-extracted graphs on the exact kind of question monokl is built to answer." It's also a nice independent precedent for the eval-harness thread — a real methodology (fixed benchmark questions per repo, indexing time/cost/coverage/correctness as named metrics) monokl's own harness could borrow from.

Let me add this as a citation to the spec.

payload.message:
Four concrete contributions, distinct from the paper's own summary:

1. **The first apples-to-apples benchmark for monokl's exact retrieval paradigm.** Everything else in this research (Aider's PageRank, codegraph's own eval) was either unvalidated or measuring something adjacent. This is a real controlled comparison of deterministic-structural-graph retrieval vs. vector-only vs. LLM-extracted-graph, on real codebases, with a fixed question set — and monokl's `WorkspaceIndex` (ImportGraph + SymbolIndex) is architecturally the "DKB" condition, not a rough analogy.

2. **It closed off a design path nobody had flagged as a risk**: using an LLM to extract the dependency graph at indexing time instead of parsing it deterministically. Monokl was never going to do this, but now there's a cited, numeric reason not to reconsider it later if it comes up as "the smarter option" — LLM-extraction was 70–150× slower *and* silently dropped 32% of files on one repo.

3. **Corroboration from an independent source and method** that vector-only retrieval underperforms structural signals specifically on multi-hop code questions — the same conclusion thread 03 reached from tool-survey evidence, now backed by a controlled experiment instead of absence-of-counter-evidence.

4. **A reusable eval-harness template**: fixed per-repo question suites, indexing time/cost/coverage/correctness as named metrics — a concrete precedent to borrow from when thread 05's proposed harness actually gets built.

It didn't change any decision already made — it made three existing ones (reject embeddings, keep deterministic AST parsing, build a real eval harness) better-evidenced than before.

2. **It closed off a design path nobody had flagged as a risk**: using an LLM to extract the dependency graph at indexing time instead of parsing it deterministically. Monokl was never going to do this, but now there's a cited, numeric reason not to reconsider it later if it comes up as "the smarter option" — LLM-extraction was 70–150× slower *and* silently dropped 32% of files on one repo.

3. **Corroboration from an independent source and method** that vector-only retrieval underperforms structural signals specifically on multi-hop code questions — the same conclusion thread 03 reached from tool-survey evidence, now backed by a controlled experiment instead of absence-of-counter-evidence.

4. **A reusable eval-harness template**: fixed per-repo question suites, indexing time/cost/coverage/correctness as named metrics — a concrete precedent to borrow from when thread 05's proposed harness actually gets built.

It didn't change any decision already made — it made three existing ones (reject embeddings, keep deterministic AST parsing, build a real eval harness) better-evidenced than before.

<result># Vetting Report: arXiv:2601.08773 ("Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases")

## 1. Author/Venue Credibility — weak
Manideep Reddy Chinthareddy lists himself only as "Software Engineer, Centerville, USA" — no institutional affiliation. His Google Scholar profile ([scholar.google.com/citations?user=zC16CcwAAAAJ](https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=zC16CcwAAAAJ)) shows a **verified email at `fanniemae.com`** (Fannie Mae, a US mortgage-finance company), i.e. he appears to be a working engineer unaffiliated with any RAG/PL/static-analysis research group. Total citations: **4**, h-index: **1**. His only other output is three more solo arXiv preprints, all in unrelated domains and all submitted within roughly the same two-month window (Dec 2025–Jan 2026): "Stateless Snowflake" (distributed ID generation, [arXiv:2512.11643](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11643)), a NoSQL chunked-storage pattern ([arXiv:2512.06852](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.06852v1)), and "Enterprise Identity Integration for AI-Assisted Developer Services." This pattern — rapid, single-author white papers spanning distributed systems, storage, identity, and now RAG — reads as a prolific solo-practitioner habit, not domain specialization in code intelligence or IR. No GitHub work beyond this study's artifact, no clearly-matching LinkedIn with RAG/static-analysis focus was found (search returned several different unrelated "Manideep Reddy" profiles). arXiv classification is **cs.SE (primary), cs.AI (secondary)**; no endorsement details are publicly shown (arXiv doesn't disclose endorsers), and the Comments field is just "46 pages, 2 figures" — no journal-ref, no DOI, no evidence of peer review or conference submission. The only "discussion" found (themoonlight.io, aimodels.fyi, papers.cool) consists of automated LLM-generated paper-summary aggregators that cover nearly every new arXiv paper — not human critical commentary. No Hacker News/Reddit/X threads found.

## 2. Reproducibility — real but minimal
A public repo exists: [github.com/Manideep-Reddy-Chinthareddy/graph-based-rag-ast-vs-llm](https://github.com/Manideep-Reddy-Chinthareddy/graph-based-rag-ast-vs-llm), containing `nograph_gemini.py`, `llmkb_gemini.py`, `dkb_gemini_v2.py`, JSON outputs, cost/log folders, plus a pinned fork of Shopizer. This is a genuine, seemingly-runnable artifact (real NetworkX/Tree-sitter/Gemini code), not a sham — but it has **0 stars, 0 forks, 4 commits, no README, no license, no tests/CI**, i.e. it's unreviewed personal research code. No standalone benchmark dataset or human-verified answer key was found; how correctness was scored (self-graded vs. independent judge) is unclear from available extraction.

## 3. DKB Algorithm — concrete, but simpler than the terminology implies
Construction: two Tree-sitter passes over Java — Pass 1 registers class/interface/enum/record/annotation declarations as nodes; Pass 2 adds typed edges (`injects` from field/constructor-parameter type references, `extends`/`implements` via `child_by_field_name("superclass"/"interfaces")`), stored as a **NetworkX DiGraph** with edge attribute `relation`. Critically, per the actual source, **"bidirectional traversal" is a single 1-hop expansion**, not a depth-parameterized BFS: at query time it takes `graph.successors(node)` (what the class depends on) and `graph.predecessors(node)` (what depends on it) — no recursion or depth loop exists despite the paper's Algorithm-1 prose implying a depth variable *d*. "Interface-aware expansion" = if a successor edge has `relation=="implements"`, the code additionally fetches `predecessors()` of that interface node (other implementers/consumers wired to it) and merges them in — computed on-the-fly by walking the same graph twice, not a precomputed implementor index. For a Rust port: petgraph DiGraph, nodes = types, edges = enum{Injects,Extends,Implements} from tree-sitter-java queries on `field_declaration`/formal params/`superclass`/`super_interfaces`; at query time gather seed's direct successors+predecessors, then for any Implements successor, also gather that interface's predecessors, dedupe, emit.

## 4. Related Work / Novelty — re-confirms known practice
Cites Lewis et al. RAG, Microsoft GraphRAG, RepoGraph, cAST, SWE-bench/RepoBench/RepoEval. **Does not cite CodeQL, Sourcegraph SCIP, or CodeRAG-Bench.** The core claim — deterministic structural graphs beat embeddings for multi-hop code questions — is well-established in code intelligence (CodeQL, LSIF/SCIP have relied on exact AST/compiler graphs for a decade); this paper's contribution is narrowly quantifying that inside an LLM-RAG-QA harness on three mid-size repos, not a new insight.

## 5. Verdict
The numbers are **directionally consistent with, but not rigorous confirmation of, monokl's design** — single author, no peer review, zero independent citations, unclear scoring methodology, n=45 questions across 3 repos, and a graph algorithm considerably simpler (1-hop) than "bidirectional traversal" suggests. Cite it as one data point ("early evidence, consistent with established static-analysis practice") rather than load-bearing proof. Strong evidence would require: independent replication, a documented/human-audited answer key, larger and more diverse codebases, and peer review or third-party citation.</result>

<result># Research: Reverse Trait-Implementation Index for Monokl

## 1. How real Rust tooling builds "who implements this trait"

rust-analyzer builds this as a **per-crate Salsa-memoized full pass**, not a lazy per-query scan. The `hir-ty` crate's `trait_impls_in_crate_query` walks every module in a crate's `DefMap`, and for each `impl` block records the impl id keyed by (trait id, self-type fingerprint) into a `TraitImpls` struct wrapped in `Arc` ([method_resolution.rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/e131bfc747df1b21ae6ea04eb9c55001e06b7bf0/crates/hir_ty/src/method_resolution.rs)). That's a genuine reverse index (trait → impls), built once per crate and reused by both method resolution and IDE features, then invalidated/rebuilt incrementally by Salsa when the crate changes. The IDE-facing "Go to Implementation" feature ([goto_implementation.rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/blob/master/crates/ide/src/goto_implementation.rs)) doesn't reimplement this — it classifies the token under the cursor and delegates to `Impl::all_for_trait(sema.db, trait_)` (traits), `Impl::all_for_type` (ADTs/inherent impls), or `impls_for_trait_item` (trait methods/consts, walking back to the owning trait), all bottoming out in that same per-crate index.

rustdoc does the analogous thing for HTML output: while rendering, it accumulates a global implementors list per trait across the whole crate graph (impls can live in other crates) and emits it as a static `implementors/.../trait.TraitName.js` file the trait's doc page loads at view time ([rustc-dev-guide](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/rustdoc.html); [rust-lang/rust#43893](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/43893)). It's a build-time global pass, not a per-page-view computation.

cargo-modules embeds `ra_ap_hir`/`ra_ap_ide` (confirmed in its [Cargo.toml](https://github.com/regexident/cargo-modules/blob/main/Cargo.toml)) and inherits trait-impl awareness from rust-analyzer's own index rather than building a second one.

**Takeaway**: the standard approach is exactly monokl's existing enricher shape — a dedicated reverse-index structure built during a full pass. rust-analyzer differs only by adding Salsa incremental caching, which monokl deliberately forgoes.

## 2. Would petgraph be a better fit?

No compelling case. First, `SymbolIndex` and the proposed trait-impl index aren't graphs — they're `name -> Vec<(FileIdx, usize)>` dictionaries, out of petgraph's scope regardless. Second, for `ImportGraph`: petgraph's `Graph`/`DiGraph` ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/petgraph/latest/petgraph/graph/struct.Graph.html)) is a `u32`-backed-`NodeIndex` adjacency list — near-identical to monokl's hand-rolled `FileIdx` design. Its one real win, `neighbors_directed(idx, Incoming)` ([petgraph::visit](https://docs.rs/petgraph/latest/petgraph/visit/index.html)), replaces what monokl already gets from explicit forward/reverse `FxHashMap`s — arguably more transparent for a two-enricher system than an opaque `NodeIndex`. Adopting it would also either leak petgraph's `NodeIndex` as the public handle (undermining the "`FileIdx` is not `Serialize`" compile-time guard) or require wrapping it anyway, gaining nothing. petgraph also pulls in `fixedbitset`, `hashbrown`, `indexmap` ([crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/petgraph/dependencies)) for algorithms (SCC, Dijkstra) monokl doesn't need. **Verdict**: keep the hand-rolled `FxHashMap` approach.

## 3. Idiomatic bounded BFS in Rust

`VecDeque<(FileIdx, u32 /*depth*/)>` frontier, `FxHashSet<FileIdx>` visited-set checked **at enqueue time** (not just dequeue — mirrors codegraph's separate `enqueued` set), a `depth_limit` compared before pushing, and a `result_cap` checked at every `results.push()` site, not just the loop head. For cap-signaling: rather than a bare `Vec<T>` that silently stops growing, extend michi's existing single `thiserror` enum with a non-fatal variant `TraversalCapExceeded { visited: usize, cap: usize }`, surfaced via `Result<TraversalReport, MonoklError>` where `TraversalReport { sites: Vec<_>, truncated: bool }` — making a cap-hit a first-class, matchable outcome.

## 4. Sketch: `TraitImplEnricher` / `TraitImplIndex`

This mirrors `SymbolIndexEnricher`, not a new graph. `TraitImplIndex` is `FxHashMap<String, Vec<(FileIdx, usize)>>` keyed by trait name, pointing at impl-block sites — inverting `RustStructEntry.trait_impls: Vec<String>` across the corpus. `update()` iterates each file's struct entries, pushing `(file_idx, decl_offset)` per trait name; `finalize()` sorts each `Vec` by `(FileIdx, offset)` for determinism. The map stays `FxHashMap` (never serialized) — only final CLI result lists need stable order, so no `BTreeMap` swap applies here. For "upstream discovery": trait `T` → `TraitImplIndex` gives implementor sites → cross-reference each struct in `SymbolIndex` for usage sites → expand via `ImportGraph` reverse edges under the §3 bounded-BFS rules — composing all three indices without a fourth graph structure.

## Recommendation

Add `TraitImplEnricher` + `TraitImplIndex` following the `SymbolIndexEnricher` pattern exactly; skip petgraph entirely; implement interface→implementor "upstream discovery" as a capped BFS composing `TraitImplIndex` → `SymbolIndex` → `ImportGraph` reverse edges, with enqueue-time `FxHashSet` visited tracking and an explicit `TraversalReport{truncated}` return.

Both are now in the spec (Part 5 §2).

This closes out the thread that started from the Graph-RAG paper — even though the paper itself turned out to be weak evidence, it pointed at a real, well-motivated gap that's now a concrete, buildable spec addition grounded in actual Rust tooling precedent.

Here's the consolidated language-support picture, pulled from everything that's already landed (all of this is applied in the spec's Part 5 §6):

**TypeScript/JavaScript** (existing) — `oxc_semantic` identified as a clear add for real scope-aware reference resolution (same arena, same version lockstep as the rest of OXC). Query grammar validated against real agent tool-call patterns. Ranking: adopt over-fetch-then-rerank staging, reject embedding-based rerank.

**Rust** (existing, refined) — `ra_ap_syntax` confirmed correct over `syn` (syn's fail-fast parsing would blank out symbols on any file with a syntax error — a real regression for a tool scanning working trees). `ra_ap_hir` is real but daemon-only (~5s/100 crates just for project load) — deferred, coupled to a future persistent-session decision. Salsa flagged as an independent, lighter-weight caching option worth its own spike. Tokenizer stop-words fixed (`crate`/`self`/`super`/`dyn`/`async`/`await`/`unsafe` added). Plus the newest addition: a `TraitImplEnricher`/`TraitImplIndex` design for "who implements this trait" reverse lookups, modeled on rust-analyzer's own `trait_impls_in_crate_query` and rustdoc's implementors-list pattern.

**Python** (new in v1.1) — tree-sitter-python confirmed correct (Ruff's tempting Rust-native crates are self-disclaimed as unstable). Target `Structural` precision, validated by Sourcegraph's own `scip-python` being a pyright *fork* rather than a lighter analyzer built in-house — confirms `Structural` is the pragmatic target, not corner-cutting. Tokenizer needs zero changes. Caught and fixed a real spec bug (`CapabilityPrecision::Approximate` → `Heuristic`).

**Go** (new, language #4) — the standout result: **`gosyn` is a real, actively-maintained native Rust parser** (152k+ downloads, confirmed Go 1.18+ generics support) — unlike every other language evaluated, Go didn't need to fall back to tree-sitter at all. Semantic analysis is daemon-only (3m26s cold load on a 20k-package monorepo), but heuristic `go.mod`-based import resolution is genuinely easier than Rust's (no macros/monomorphization). `go.work` and `//go:build` tags explicitly scoped out of v1. Target `Structural` precision.

**Java** (new, language #5) — no viable native Rust parser exists; tree-sitter-java confirmed correct (even codegraph's own optimized native kernel still uses it via FFI rather than replacing the grammar). Semantic analysis is strictly bimodal — no lightweight middle tier like Rust/Go have — and JAR-only external symbols (no local source) bite harder here than anywhere else. Worth hand-tuning investment specifically for Lombok-member synthesis, mirroring what codegraph found necessary. `Structural` for same-module resolution, `Heuristic` for cross-JAR/multi-module, `Exact` off the table entirely.

**C#** — dropped per your explicit call.

Meanwhile, the four Rust-best-practices audit agents (error handling, generics/traits, lifetimes/iterators/closures, concurrency) are still running against the full spec — I'll report those as they land.

<result># Concurrency Audit — monokl-spec.md

## 1. `persist.rs` `CacheState`/`lock_state()` poisoning (lines 1425–1441)

**Design:** `lock_state()` = `cache_state().lock().unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner)` — silently recovers from a poisoned `Mutex<CacheState>`.

**Real concern, not just style.** Trace the actual mutation sequence in `flush()` (lines 1532–1560): it calls `state.write_queue.drain(..)` into a local `cache` clone *before* doing anything that could panic (`serde_json::to_string_pretty`, `evict_lru`). If a panic occurs after the drain but before `state.cache_file = Some(cache)` is assigned (e.g. inside `evict_lru`'s serialization loop), the mutex poisons with `write_queue` already emptied but the merged result never committed — silently discarding queued writes. The next `lock_state()` call recovers silently, and callers have no signal that data vanished. This is exactly the "structurally valid but logically corrupt" scenario the audit asked about — not a hypothetical.

Compounding this: `analyze()`'s Tier 1–4 path (lines 1686, 1698–1699) calls into `persist::lookup`/`lookup_by_hash`/`refresh_mtime`/`queue_write` from *inside* Phase 1's `par_iter()` closure, so the lock is being acquired/released at high frequency from many rayon workers concurrently — more surface area for a mid-critical-section panic than a single-threaded caller would have.

**Also note an inconsistency**: `pipeline/session.rs`'s `standard_index()` (line 6059) uses `.lock().map_err(|_| {...})?` — treating poisoning as a *propagated error*, the opposite policy from `persist.rs`. The spec applies two different poisoning philosophies to structurally similar `Mutex`-guarded state without acknowledging the discrepancy.

**Recommendation:** Pick one policy. Given the corruption risk shown above, treat poisoning as fatal (mirror `session.rs`'s approach) rather than recovering silently — a poisoned `CacheState` means an unknown subset of `write_queue` may have been lost. `parking_lot::Mutex` (no poisoning) is not a fix; it just hides the same problem structurally instead of solving it. If silent recovery is truly desired for availability, at minimum log at `error!` level, not swallow.

## 2. Phase 2's sequential enricher fold (lines 2091–2125, 2945–2948)

**Design:** Phase 2 is a sequential `for analysis in &analyses { for enricher in &mut enrichers { enricher.update(...) } }`.

**Correctly sequential *per enricher*, but there's a real, correctly-typed opportunity being left unused.** `WorkspaceEnricher: Send` only (line 1880) — not `Send + Sync` — which is exactly the bound needed to move each `Box<dyn WorkspaceEnricher>` onto its own thread (not share one across threads). Since each enricher independently folds over the same read-only `&[Arc<FileAnalysis>]` (both `ImportGraphEnricher` and `SymbolIndexEnricher` only push into private `Vec`s, order-independent for correctness), running the two enrichers concurrently against the shared sorted `analyses` slice is sound and type-correct today.

That said, it's a low-value win: only two enrichers exist, so the ceiling is ~2x on a phase that's pure `Vec::push` bookkeeping versus Phase 1's actual OXC parsing — rayon scope/join overhead could easily eat the gain at typical enricher counts. Verdict: **real opportunity, correctly reasoned as not worth the complexity** given current enricher count and cost profile. Worth revisiting only if the enricher list grows substantially.

## 3. `DashMap<String, Arc<FileAnalysis>>` key type (lines 1365, 1372–1377, 5804)

`cache().get(path.as_str())` **is correct, not an oversight.** `DashMap<K,V>::get<Q>` requires `K: Borrow<Q>`; `String: Borrow<str>` is a standard-library impl, and `String`'s `Hash`/`Eq` are defined to delegate to `str`, so hash/eq consistency holds — this is the same idiom that makes `HashMap<String,_>::get("foo")` work everywhere in Rust. No bug.

On the performance framing: there's no allocation at *lookup* either way (`.as_str()` is a free borrow); the only allocation is at `insert()` (`path.to_string()`), and an `Utf8PathBuf`-keyed map would pay an equivalent clone on insert. So String-vs-`Utf8PathBuf` keying is a wash performance-wise. The spec doesn't state a rationale for String over `Utf8PathBuf`; a plausible one (unstated) is NAPI-boundary parity (paths arrive as JS strings via `@orin-axi/monokl`). Recommendation: harmless either way; if changed, prefer `Utf8PathBuf` purely for stronger typing, not performance.

## 4. `Send + Sync` on `LanguageAnalyzer` implementors (lines 1260, 1612–1614, 5119–5122)

`RustAnalyzer { workspace_root: Option<Utf8PathBuf>, package_roots: FxHashMap<String, Utf8PathBuf> }` is trivially `Send + Sync` — no `Rc`/`RefCell`/raw pointers anywhere, and `FxHashMap<K,V>` (a `HashMap` with `FxBuildHasher`, itself a ZST) is `Send`/`Sync` whenever `K,V` are, which they are here.

`TsAnalyzer { resolver: Resolver }` depends on `oxc_resolver::Resolver` being `Send + Sync`; this holds in practice (its internal resolution cache is built for concurrent use), but **the spec never demonstrates this** — no `static_assertions::assert_impl_all!(TsAnalyzer: Send, Sync)` anywhere, despite this bound being load-bearing (`Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>` shared across rayon workers, line 5108). Since this is an external-crate assumption baked silently into a trait bound the whole design depends on, it's the kind of thing that should be pinned with an explicit compile-time assertion rather than left to "it happens to compile." **Recommendation:** add `assert_impl_all!` tests for both analyzer structs.

## 5. Data races between concurrent `analyze()` calls (lines 2091–2101, 1680–1708)

**Provably safe within Phase 1**: `walk_entries` comes from a single-threaded `ignore::WalkBuilder` walk, so each path is unique; `par_iter()` therefore never has two threads calling `cache::insert()`/`persist::queue_write()` for the *same* key concurrently inside one `WorkspaceIndex::build`. No race there.

**A real, if narrow, cross-call race exists**: `pipeline/search.rs` Stage 8 (line 5930) also runs `analyzer.analyze()` under `into_par_iter()`, and `WorkspaceSession` (§6027) caches one `AnalyzerRegistry` + `DashMap` across repeated calls in a long-lived process. Two independent top-level calls (e.g. a `search()` and a `dependents()`-triggered `standard_index()` build) sharing one session could legitimately call `analyze()` on the same path concurrently. `DashMap::insert`'s last-write-wins is safe here only in the "eventually consistent" sense — both writers compute from an actual disk read at call time, so neither value is *stale* relative to its own read, but the two reads could observe genuinely different file states if the file is edited mid-race. That's an inherent TOCTOU property of any filesystem-backed cache, not a monokl-specific flaw, and the tiered mtime/hash design already treats this as "eventually corrected on next stat" rather than promising linearizability. Not a bug; worth a one-line note in the doc that this is accepted, not proven-impossible.

## 6. `fs2` advisory locks vs. atomic tempfile+rename (lines 1552–1558, 4963, 5019, 5829–5834)

These solve **different problems, not redundant ones**: tempfile+rename (already in `flush()`) guarantees no reader ever sees a torn/partial `cache.json`; it does *not* prevent a lost-update race where two concurrent processes each read-merge-write and the second `rename()` silently discards the first process's queued entries. `fs2` advisory locking around the read-merge-write critical section is what prevents that lost update, and is a reasonable, standard choice given the closed world (only monokl processes touch `.monokl/cache.json`).

**Gap**: the spec asserts fs2 is used (twice, in prose only) but never shows the actual lock-acquisition code or states where in the `flush()`/`init()` sequence the lock is taken/released, nor whether it's shared or exclusive, nor stale-lock handling after a killed process. For a "reconstruction-grade" spec this is an under-specified mechanism. **Recommendation:** add the missing code snippet (open/create a `.monokl/cache.lock` sibling file, exclusive-lock around the read-merge-write-rename span in `flush()`, shared-lock or no-lock for pure reads) so the two mechanisms' division of labor is unambiguous.</result>

<result># Generics & Traits Audit — `docs/monokl-spec.md`

## 1. Core traits: `LanguageAnalyzer`, `WorkspaceEnricher`, registry additions

**Well-designed and correct:**
- `pub trait LanguageAnalyzer: Send + Sync` (line 1260) — the bound is exactly right: `Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>` is shared read-only across `rayon::par_iter()` workers (line 2091, 5930), so both `Send` and `Sync` are required and present.
- `pub(crate) trait WorkspaceEnricher: Send` (line 1880) — only `Send`, not `Sync`, and that's *correct*, not a bug: enrichers are moved into a single-threaded loop (lines 2110-2118) and mutated exclusively via `&mut self` after the parallel analyze phase finishes; they're never shared concurrently, so `Sync` would be an over-constraint. `finalize(self: Box<Self>, …)` (line 1882) is a legal object-safe receiver.
- `capabilities(&self) -> AnalyzerCapabilities` (line 5151) aggregates 4 `CapabilityPrecision` fields + 2 bools into one struct return — the right way to avoid 6 separate trait methods (`refs_precision()`, `definition_precision()`, …). Good factoring, not bloat.

**Real bug — trait definition is incomplete relative to its own usage.** `AnalyzerRegistry`/`query_support.rs` call `analyzer.language_id()`, `analyzer.capabilities()`, `analyzer.analyze_with_profile(...)` through `&dyn LanguageAnalyzer` / `Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>` (lines 5147-5165, 6568-6624, 6598). For dyn dispatch to resolve these, they **must** be trait methods. But the canonical trait block (1260-1263) only ever declares `supports`/`analyze`, and `impl LanguageAnalyzer for TsAnalyzer` (1674-1709) is never restated with the three new methods. As literally specified, `AnalyzerRegistry::from_workspace_opts` pushing `Arc::new(TsAnalyzer::…)` into `Vec<Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>>` (line 5064) would not type-check. This is the single highest-risk gap for verbatim reconstruction. Fix — restate the trait and give `analyze` a default in terms of `analyze_with_profile` (also resolves §5):
```rust
pub trait LanguageAnalyzer: Send + Sync {
    fn language_id(&self) -> LanguageId;
    fn supports(&self, path: &Utf8Path) -> bool;
    fn capabilities(&self) -> AnalyzerCapabilities;
    fn analyze_with_profile(&self, path: &Utf8Path,
        source: Box<dyn FnOnce() -> Result<String>>, profile: AnalysisProfile)
        -> Result<Arc<FileAnalysis>>;
    fn analyze(&self, path: &Utf8Path, source: Box<dyn FnOnce() -> Result<String>>)
        -> Result<Arc<FileAnalysis>> {
        self.analyze_with_profile(path, source, AnalysisProfile::Full)
    }
}
```
and add the matching methods to `TsAnalyzer`'s impl block. Adjacent gap: `AnalyzerCapabilities` and `CapabilityPrecision` are used ~22 times (constructed, compared with `<` at 6614/6670) but their type definitions (derives for `Copy`/`PartialOrd`/`Ord`) never appear anywhere in the doc — can't verify they support the comparisons the spec relies on.

## 2. Generic functions

`rank_blocks<S: std::hash::BuildHasher>` / `score<S: BuildHasher>` (lines 1040, 1086) accepting `&HashMap<String, usize, S>` is the idiomatic, std-blessed way to accept both `HashMap` and `FxHashMap` without `rank/` depending on `rustc_hash` — zero-cost via monomorphization, correctly used in `pipeline.rs` where `df: FxHashMap<String, usize>` is passed straight in (line 8 of `grep1` context). Minor refinement: only `.get()` is used (line 1098), so an even narrower/cleaner idiom is `df: impl Fn(&str) -> usize` — decouples the function from "must be a `HashMap`" entirely (works for a sorted `Vec`, an FST, etc.) at the same zero cost. Not urgent; current form is defensible. Other generics are all appropriately chosen: `impl Into<Utf8PathBuf>` constructors (585, 2830-2836, 7544) are correct ergonomic argument-position `impl Trait`; `render_json<T: Serialize>` (2278-2292) is correctly generic since `Serialize` isn't dyn-friendly in a useful way and instantiation count is small. No misuse found.

## 3. Trait object catalog

- `Box<dyn FnOnce() -> Result<String>>` (1262, 1680, 5177, 6567) — **necessary**, not merely acceptable: making the source-loader generic (`F: FnOnce() -> Result<String>`) would make `analyze` generic and break object safety, which would break every `Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>`/`&dyn LanguageAnalyzer` call site in the registry and query_support. Correct trade-off.
- `Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>` (5053-5108) and `Vec<Box<dyn WorkspaceEnricher>>` (2072, 2143, 6063) — correct use of dynamic dispatch: the registry is heterogeneous and feature-gated (TS/Rust/future Python/C#); per-file dispatch cost is negligible next to actual parsing, and monomorphizing over N analyzer types would need an enum-of-analyzers with no real benefit. Keep as-is.
- **Minor bug**: `fn panic_payload_to_napi_error(payload: &Box<dyn Any + Send>)` (line 2778) — classic "reference to a boxed trait object" anti-pattern (`clippy::borrowed_box`). Should be `&(dyn Any + Send)`.
- `Option<Box<InspectEntry>>` inside `RustData` (line 7176) is a deliberate, correct use of `Box` for enum-size normalization ("without inflating non-Rust language data," line 7180) — unrelated to dynamic dispatch, good design.

## 4. Tagged enums (`InspectEntry`, `LangData`, `DependencyTarget`)

The serde-tagged enum is the right idiom here over trait+`Box<dyn Trait>`: these types need `Deserialize` (trait objects can't deserialize without an external registry/`typetag`, not in the crate's dependency surface), and `schema.rs`'s `full_union_schema()` (~3921-3928) needs an exhaustive, closed variant set to emit `oneOf` — trivial with `match`, awkward with type-erased objects. Keep the enum shape.

**Inconsistency found**: `LangData` (376, 7187) is `#[non_exhaustive]`, but `InspectEntry` (3232, 7306), `DependencyTarget` (319, 7219), and `RustPathAnchor` (340, 7206) are not — despite the doc's own roadmap already growing these (`RustPath` variant added to `DependencyTarget`; Python variants explicitly planned for `InspectEntry`, line 4710). Recommend `#[non_exhaustive]` on all three to match `LangData`'s treatment and avoid a semver break on the next language phase the spec itself promises.

## 5. Blanket impls / default methods

Biggest missed opportunity: `TsAnalyzer::analyze` (1680-1708) and `RustAnalyzer::analyze_cached_or_parse` (5174-5236) duplicate the same stat→`persist::lookup`→content-hash→`persist::lookup_by_hash`→parse→`cache::insert` skeleton almost verbatim, differing only in the parse step and one profile-validity check (5206-5207). The default-`analyze` fix in §1 removes one layer of duplication; the remaining tier-lookup skeleton should become a shared helper (e.g. `cache_tiers::lookup_or_parse(path, source, parse_fn, is_valid_fn)` taking closures) so each analyzer supplies only its parse step.

## 6. Lifetimes / arena principle

Only one `pub struct` with an explicit lifetime in the entire ~8400-line spec: `Lexer<'a>` (line 633), a short-lived query-DSL tokenizer over `&str` — never touches OXC's `Allocator`/`AstNode`, never stored in `FileAnalysis`. `line_ranges_for_file<'a>` (6323) is a free function, not a struct, borrowing from an already-owned `ScopeSelection` (elision requires the explicit `'a` since there are two reference args). No `AstNode<'a>` or arena type appears in any public struct — ADR 0002's principle (line 2929) is upheld everywhere checked. No violations.</result>

<result># Error-Handling Audit: monokl Spec (`docs/monokl-spec.md`)

## 1. Panics / policy violations in non-test code

**Real violations found:**
- **Line 6308** (`git_scope.rs`, `scope_files_with_index`): `crate::types::QueryScope::FullRepo => unreachable!("handled above"),` — a genuine panic path in production code. It's redundant: `FullRepo` is already handled by an early return two lines above, so the match never needs to re-list it. **Fix**: restructure so the early-return arm is folded into the same match, eliminating the impossible arm entirely:
  ```rust
  match scope.mode {
      QueryScope::FullRepo => Ok(full_repo_selection(files)),
      QueryScope::ChangedFiles => { let p = prepare_scope_inputs(files, root, scope)?; Ok(changed_files_selection(p)) }
      QueryScope::ChangedLines => { let p = prepare_scope_inputs(files, root, scope)?; Ok(changed_lines_selection(p)) }
      QueryScope::ImpactedNeighbors => { let p = prepare_scope_inputs(files, root, scope)?; Ok(impacted_neighbors_selection(p, index)) }
  }
  ```
- **Policy gap**: the workspace lint table (lines 2866–2882) denies `clippy::panic` and `clippy::todo` but **not** `clippy::unreachable` or `clippy::unimplemented`. That's why line 6308 slips past the stated policy undetected — the deny list should add both.
- **Lines 4831/4833/4834** (`tests/integration_new_commands.rs` helper `run_ok_json`): `.expect("failed to spawn monokl binary")`, `.expect("stdout is UTF-8")`, `panic!(...)`. These are fine *behaviorally* (test helper), but the lint-exemption mechanism shown (line 153, `#![cfg_attr(test, allow(...))]` in `lib.rs`) only covers the `monokl` lib crate — it does **not** propagate to files under `tests/`, which compile as separate crate roots. As specified, none of the six integration test files carry their own `#![allow(clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::expect_used, clippy::panic)]`, so under a package-wide `[lints]` table these targets would fail to build under `deny`. **Fix**: add the allow attribute at the top of each integration test file.
- **`dedup.rs` line 1183**: `(a.line_end - a.line_start + 1).min(b.line_end - b.line_start + 1)` — unguarded `usize` subtraction that assumes `line_end >= line_start` on every `CodeBlock`. Nothing enforces that invariant at the type level; a future producer that violates it panics on underflow. **Fix**: use `line_end.saturating_sub(line_start) + 1`, matching the `saturating_sub` pattern the spec itself uses correctly elsewhere (`git_scope.rs` line 6274).
- **Line 5775**: `rust_inspection.rs` gains a *module-wide* `#![allow(clippy::expect_used)]` to justify `.expect()` in `LazyLock::new(|| Regex::new(...))`. This is broader than needed — it silently permits any other `.expect()` added later in that file. **Fix**: scope the allow to just the regex statics, e.g. `#[allow(clippy::expect_used)] static RE_X: LazyLock<Regex> = ...`.

**Done well**: `tokens.rs`'s char-array indexing (`chars[idx-1]`/`chars[idx+1]`) is always guard-checked before use; `WorkspaceIndex`, `ImportGraph`, `SymbolIndex` consistently use `.get()`/`.map_or(&[], ...)` instead of raw indexing; `napi/boundary.rs` correctly uses `catch_unwind` + graceful payload conversion (no `.unwrap()`) at the one place panics are legitimately expected to cross an FFI boundary.

<result>## Lifetime Audit — `docs/monokl-spec.md`

### Findings

**1. `parse_full` (lines 1715–1779) — correctly contained, and it shows.** Every arena-borrowed value (`Statement<'_>`, spans, `&str` slices) is converted to `String`/`usize`/owned enums before being pushed into `symbols`/`dependencies`/`exports`/`jsx_elements`/`blocks`. The explicit `drop(parsed); drop(allocator);` (line 1745–1746) before building `FileAnalysis` is redundant under NLL (nothing borrowed survives the loop anyway) but is a deliberate, valuable piece of self-documentation of ADR 0002 — leave it, don't "clean it up."

**2. Helper functions (`module_export_name_to_string` 1826–1832, `byte_offset_to_line` 1842–1845, `first_line_signature` 1859–1863, `find_tsconfig_from_root` 1847–1857) all correctly take arena/borrowed input and return owned output**, with elision doing all the work — no explicit lifetime parameters are needed or given, and none should be added.

**3. `resolve_import` (1658–1664) and `looks_like_workspace_alias`** — elision is fully sufficient (`&self`, `&Utf8Path`, `&str` in; owned `Option<Utf8PathBuf>` out). Nothing to change.

**4. Same pattern holds on the Rust side.** `extract_item_block` (5404–5445) and Part 4's `extract_symbols`/`ast_symbol` (7938–7970) immediately do `.name().map(|n| n.text().to_string())` on every `ra-ap-syntax` node — never storing a `SyntaxNode`/token. `wrapped_function_body_start`/`variable_function_signature` (8043–8087) go further: they return raw `u32` byte offsets rather than borrowed spans, which is an even cleaner way to avoid lifetime entanglement than returning `Option<&Expression<'_>>` would have been.

**5. Minor style nit, not a bug:** `module_export_name_to_string`'s `id.name.as_str().to_string()` (1828–1830) could be `id.name.to_string()` directly if oxc's `Atom` implements `Display` (it does) — the `.as_str()` hop is unnecessary but harmless.

**6. No genuine `Cow<'_, str>` opportunities found.** Candidates like `first_line_signature`, `rust_binding` (5546–5572), and `expand_use_clause` (5528–5544) already do all their work on `&str` and convert to `String` exactly once, at the return boundary — introducing `Cow` there would add enum-matching overhead for no benefit. The one place duplication of an owned `String` occurs (`ImportDefaultSpecifier` binding: `imported: local.clone(), local, ...`, prose ~1783) needs the clone regardless of `Cow`, since two struct fields must each independently own the value.

## Iterator Audit

**Correctly left as loops (do not convert):**
- `tokenize`/`tokenize_source` (879–940) — lookahead/lookbehind over `chars[idx±1]` and a stateful `current_word`/`current_fragment` accumulator with a post-loop flush. No iterator adapter expresses this more clearly.
- `apply_budget` (1210–1247) — three interdependent mutable accumulators (`results`, `total_bytes`, `total_tokens`) plus early-`break` truncation logic. A `.scan()`/`.take_while()` rewrite would be harder to read, not easier.
- `WorkspaceIndex::build`'s `files`/`file_index` population loop (2103–2109) — builds two independently-owned collections from one pass; the two `.clone()` calls on `analysis.source_path` are structurally required (Vec element + HashMap key can't share ownership without `Rc`/`Arc`), so this is correctly a loop, not a chain-vs-loop defect.

**Genuine improvement — `dedup_blocks` (1162–1176):**
```rust
'outer: for block in blocks {
    for kept in &result {
        if kept.block.file == block.block.file && overlaps_significantly(&kept.block, &block.block) {
            continue 'outer;
        }
    }
    result.push(block);
}
```
The labeled loop can drop entirely in favor of `.any()`:
```rust
for block in blocks {
    let is_dup = result.iter()
        .any(|kept| kept.block.file == block.block.file && overlaps_significantly(&kept.block, &block.block));
    if !is_dup { result.push(block); }
}
```
Same O(n²) cost, no label, reads as "keep unless it duplicates something already kept."

**Genuine improvement — the two `WorkspaceEnricher::update` impls (1918–1924, 1955–1959):**
```rust
fn update(&mut self, idx: FileIdx, analysis: &FileAnalysis) {
    for dep in &analysis.dependencies {
        if let Some(resolved) = target_resolved(dep) { self.deferred.push((idx, resolved.clone())); }
    }
}
```
No branching beyond a single filter — textbook `filter_map`+`extend`:
```rust
self.deferred.extend(analysis.dependencies.iter()
    .filter_map(|dep| target_resolved(dep).map(|r| (idx, r.clone()))));
```
`SymbolIndexEnricher::update` (unconditional push) is the even simpler `self.entries.extend(analysis.symbols.iter().map(|s| (idx, s.name.clone(), s.line)));`

**`.clone()` usage in iterator chains is already well-judged, not `.cloned()`-able:** `evict_lru`'s `.map(|(p, e)| (p.clone(), e.last_accessed_ns)).collect()` (line 1564) deliberately clones only the path, not the whole (expensive) `PersistedFileAnalysis` — using `.cloned()` there would be a regression, not an improvement. `full.blocks.iter().filter(...).cloned().collect()` (6018) already correctly uses `.cloned()` over `.map(|b| b.clone())`.

**No double-collect-then-iterate found** in any of the given code (`query/plan.rs`'s three separate `terms.iter().enumerate().filter().map().collect()` passes for required/excluded/scored are each single-pass and, at the 64-term cap, not worth merging into one fold — merging would trade clarity for a sub-microsecond win).

## Closure Audit

**`Box<dyn FnOnce() -> Result<String>>` is the correct idiom, not a needless allocation.** `LanguageAnalyzer` (1260–1263) is used as a trait object throughout — `Vec<Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>>` in `AnalyzerRegistry` (5053), `&dyn LanguageAnalyzer` in `WorkspaceIndex::build` (2071) and `query_support.rs` (6568, 6583, 6608...). A generic `impl FnOnce() -> Result<String>` parameter would make `analyze` generic, which is not object-safe and would break every one of these call sites. Boxing is required by the design, not a mistake — leave as-is.

**Real bug: unnecessary clone in `WorkspaceIndex::build`'s hot loop (lines 2091–2101):**
```rust
let mut analyses: Vec<Arc<FileAnalysis>> = walk_entries.par_iter().filter_map(|path| {
    let path = path.clone();
    let path_for_closure = path.clone();
    match analyzer.analyze(&path, Box::new(move || { ... &path_for_closure ... })) { ... }
}).collect();
```
`path: &Utf8PathBuf` from `par_iter()` already derefs to `&Utf8Path` for `analyzer.analyze(path, ...)` and implements `Display` for the `tracing::warn!("...{path}...")` call — the first `let path = path.clone();` clones a `Utf8PathBuf` on every file in a parallel hot path for no reason. Fix:
```rust
walk_entries.par_iter().filter_map(|path| {
    let path_for_closure = path.clone();
    match analyzer.analyze(path, Box::new(move || { ... &path_for_closure ... })) { ... }
}).collect();
```
One clone removed per file, no behavior change.

**Everywhere else the "clone-into-a-`move`-closure" pattern is minimal and correct**: `pipeline/inspecting.rs::extract`'s `file_for_closure = req.file.clone()` (6002), `query_support.rs::analyze_with_profile`'s `owned = file.to_owned()` (6572), and `extract_dependencies`'s `move |leaf| { ... path, workspace_root, package_roots ... }` (5463) all capture exactly what's needed — in the last case the "moved" captures are `Copy` references, not deep clones, and `move` is required only because the closure escapes the enclosing `flat_map` closure's stack frame. None of these should change.</result>

Helper functions (`module_export_name_to_string` 1826–1832, `byte_offset_to_line` 1842–1845, `first_line_signature` 1859–1863, `find_tsconfig_from_root` 1847–1857) all correctly take arena/borrowed input and return owned output**, with elision doing all the work — no explicit lifetime parameters are needed or given, and none should be added.

**3. `resolve_import` (1658–1664) and `looks_like_workspace_alias`** — elision is fully sufficient (`&self`, `&Utf8Path`, `&str` in; owned `Option<Utf8PathBuf>` out). Nothing to change.

**4. Same pattern holds on the Rust side.** `extract_item_block` (5404–5445) and Part 4's `extract_symbols`/`ast_symbol` (7938–7970) immediately do `.name().map(|n| n.text().to_string())` on every `ra-ap-syntax` node — never storing a `SyntaxNode`/token. `wrapped_function_body_start`/`variable_function_signature` (8043–8087) go further: they return raw `u32` byte offsets rather than borrowed spans, which is an even cleaner way to avoid lifetime entanglement than returning `Option<&Expression<'_>>` would have been.

**5. Minor style nit, not a bug:** `module_export_name_to_string`'s `id.name.as_str().to_string()` (1828–1830) could be `id.name.to_string()` directly if oxc's `Atom` implements `Display` (it does) — the `.as_str()` hop is unnecessary but harmless.

**6. No genuine `Cow<'_, str>` opportunities found.** Candidates like `first_line_signature`, `rust_binding` (5546–5572), and `expand_use_clause` (5528–5544) already do all their work on `&str` and convert to `String` exactly once, at the return boundary — introducing `Cow` there would add enum-matching overhead for no benefit. The one place duplication of an owned `String` occurs (`ImportDefaultSpecifier` binding: `imported: local.clone(), local, ...`, prose ~1783) needs the clone regardless of `Cow`, since two struct fields must each independently own the value.

## Iterator Audit

**Correctly left as loops (do not convert):**
- `tokenize`/`tokenize_source` (879–940) — lookahead/lookbehind over `chars[idx±1]` and a stateful `current_word`/`current_fragment` accumulator with a post-loop flush. No iterator adapter expresses this more clearly.
- `apply_budget` (1210–1247) — three interdependent mutable accumulators (`results`, `total_bytes`, `total_tokens`) plus early-`break` truncation logic. A `.scan()`/`.take_while()` rewrite would be harder to read, not easier.
- `WorkspaceIndex::build`'s `files`/`file_index` population loop (2103–2109) — builds two independently-owned collections from one pass; the two `.clone()` calls on `analysis.source_path` are structurally required (Vec element + HashMap key can't share ownership without `Rc`/`Arc`), so this is correctly a loop, not a chain-vs-loop defect.

**Genuine improvement — `dedup_blocks` (1162–1176):**
```rust
'outer: for block in blocks {
    for kept in &result {
        if kept.block.file == block.block.file && overlaps_significantly(&kept.block, &block.block) {
            continue 'outer;
        }
    }
    result.push(block);
}
```
The labeled loop can drop entirely in favor of `.any()`:
```rust
for block in blocks {
    let is_dup = result.iter()
        .any(|kept| kept.block.file == block.block.file && overlaps_significantly(&kept.block, &block.block));
    if !is_dup { result.push(block); }
}
```
Same O(n²) cost, no label, reads as "keep unless it duplicates something already kept."

**Genuine improvement — the two `WorkspaceEnricher::update` impls (1918–1924, 1955–1959):**
```rust
fn update(&mut self, idx: FileIdx, analysis: &FileAnalysis) {
    for dep in &analysis.dependencies {
        if let Some(resolved) = target_resolved(dep) { self.deferred.push((idx, resolved.clone())); }
    }
}
```
No branching beyond a single filter — textbook `filter_map`+`extend`:
```rust
self.deferred.extend(analysis.dependencies.iter()
    .filter_map(|dep| target_resolved(dep).map(|r| (idx, r.clone()))));
```
`SymbolIndexEnricher::update` (unconditional push) is the even simpler `self.entries.extend(analysis.symbols.iter().map(|s| (idx, s.name.clone(), s.line)));`

**`.clone()` usage in iterator chains is already well-judged, not `.cloned()`-able:** `evict_lru`'s `.map(|(p, e)| (p.clone(), e.last_accessed_ns)).collect()` (line 1564) deliberately clones only the path, not the whole (expensive) `PersistedFileAnalysis` — using `.cloned()` there would be a regression, not an improvement. `full.blocks.iter().filter(...).cloned().collect()` (6018) already correctly uses `.cloned()` over `.map(|b| b.clone())`.

**No double-collect-then-iterate found** in any of the given code (`query/plan.rs`'s three separate `terms.iter().enumerate().filter().map().collect()` passes for required/excluded/scored are each single-pass and, at the 64-term cap, not worth merging into one fold — merging would trade clarity for a sub-microsecond win).

## Closure Audit

**`Box<dyn FnOnce() -> Result<String>>` is the correct idiom, not a needless allocation.** `LanguageAnalyzer` (1260–1263) is used as a trait object throughout — `Vec<Arc<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>>` in `AnalyzerRegistry` (5053), `&dyn LanguageAnalyzer` in `WorkspaceIndex::build` (2071) and `query_support.rs` (6568, 6583, 6608...). A generic `impl FnOnce() -> Result<String>` parameter would make `analyze` generic, which is not object-safe and would break every one of these call sites. Boxing is required by the design, not a mistake — leave as-is.

**Real bug: unnecessary clone in `WorkspaceIndex::build`'s hot loop (lines 2091–2101):**
```rust
let mut analyses: Vec<Arc<FileAnalysis>> = walk_entries.par_iter().filter_map(|path| {
    let path = path.clone();
    let path_for_closure = path.clone();
    match analyzer.analyze(&path, Box::new(move || { ... &path_for_closure ... })) { ... }
}).collect();
```
`path: &Utf8PathBuf` from `par_iter()` already derefs to `&Utf8Path` for `analyzer.analyze(path, ...)` and implements `Display` for the `tracing::warn!("...{path}...")` call — the first `let path = path.clone();` clones a `Utf8PathBuf` on every file in a parallel hot path for no reason. Fix:
```rust
walk_entries.par_iter().filter_map(|path| {
    let path_for_closure = path.clone();
    match analyzer.analyze(path, Box::new(move || { ... &path_for_closure ... })) { ... }
}).collect();
```
One clone removed per file, no behavior change.

**Everywhere else the "clone-into-a-`move`-closure" pattern is minimal and correct**: `pipeline/inspecting.rs::extract`'s `file_for_closure = req.file.clone()` (6002), `query_support.rs::analyze_with_profile`'s `owned = file.to_owned()` (6572), and `extract_dependencies`'s `move |leaf| { ... path, workspace_root, package_roots ... }` (5463) all capture exactly what's needed — in the last case the "moved" captures are `Copy` references, not deep clones, and `move` is required only because the closure escapes the enclosing `flat_map` closure's stack frame. None of these should change.</result>

Yes — a few genuinely unexplored pieces of prior art that are closer analogs to monokl than anything researched so far:

- **GitHub's [`stack-graphs`](https://github.com/github/stack-graphs) + `tree-sitter-graph`** — a Rust library purpose-built for scope-based name resolution across languages, without a full type-checker. This directly targets the exact problem that kept coming up (TS reference resolution, Rust's heuristic module-path walker, Python/Go/Java all lacking a cheap-but-real resolution tier) — worth checking whether it's a better general answer than solving it per-language.
- **[`ast-grep`](https://ast-grep.github.io/)** — Rust-native, tree-sitter-based structural search with its own query DSL. This is architecturally the closest sibling to monokl of anything examined yet (closer than codegraph, which is TypeScript). Worth studying its query-language design and how it handles less-invested languages.
- **[`difftastic`](https://difftast.icl/)** — Rust-native, tree-sitter-based structural diff, same author has written good engineering material on tree-sitter performance tradeoffs in Rust. Directly relevant since monokl already specs a `diff` command.
- **The call-graph/points-to analysis literature (CHA, RTA, k-CFA)** — I flagged this as high-value two turns ago when you asked about backing the work with established science, but we got pulled into the Rust-idiom audit and doc reorg before actually researching it. Still open.

Lower priority but worth a mention: **CodeQL, SCIP/LSIF, Kythe, Glean** — decade-old production code-intelligence schemas, only ever cited in passing as "established practice." Actually studying how they structure queries/indices would be good grounding, even if monokl doesn't adopt their schema.

Want me to run research on the top four now?

payload.message:
Good instinct — and yes, `oxc`/`vscode`/`typescript-go` are all sharp picks for reasons beyond "big and popular":

- **`typescript-go`** (microsoft/typescript-go) is an unusually good choice: it's a Go port of a codebase (the TS compiler) whose original TypeScript version is one of the densest, most self-referential TS codebases that exists — meaning it stress-tests monokl's *planned* Go analyzer against real idiomatic Go, while conceptually mirroring a TS corpus you'd also want to test against.
- **`oxc`** is meta in the best way — it's the actual parser monokl depends on for TS/JS. Testing monokl's Rust analyzer against the crate that *is* monokl's TS/JS dependency closes a nice loop, and it's a multi-crate Rust workspace with real trait-heavy design.
- **`vscode`** — huge, real, enterprise-scale TS with an extension-host architecture; good for stress-testing scale and interface-heavy patterns, distinct from a compiler's density.

Rounding out the other languages with the same logic — pick codebases that stress the exact resolution patterns the research already flagged as hard, not just "popular":

- **Rust**: `rust-analyzer` itself (we've drawn heavily on its patterns already — testing against it is a nice closed loop) and `ripgrep`/`tokio` for contrast (macro-heavy async vs. rust-analyzer's own trait-heavy IDE code).
- **Python**: Django or FastAPI — monokl's spec already anticipates Django/FastAPI-aware resolvers, so these directly validate that.
- **Go**: Kubernetes — heavy interface usage, which is exactly what the `TraitImplIndex`-equivalent "who implements this" resolution needs to prove itself against, alongside `typescript-go`.
- **Java**: a Spring Boot app with Lombok — codegraph's own Java extractor sank most of its hand-tuning into exactly that combination, so it's the right stress test if monokl follows the same path.

Before I lock this in as the eval-harness corpus (this maps directly onto the "≥10 repos spanning language/size" requirement from the eval-harness research), want me to verify actual scale on each — file counts, LOC, whether they're realistically clonable/parseable sizes — and write the finalized list into `05-research-and-decisions.md`?

payload.message:
Yes, and it's worth more than a mention — SCIP could genuinely touch monokl's output schema design, not just be a "nice to know" reference. Let me actually research it properly rather than going on my own possibly-stale recollection, since a few things could be architecturally significant if true:

- SCIP's symbol-naming scheme (a standardized way to globally identify a symbol across packages) vs. monokl's current ad-hoc `(FileIdx, line)`/name-based identity
- Its `Relationship` model (implementation, type_definition, override) — this maps directly onto the `TraitImplIndex` work from a few turns ago; if SCIP already has a standard shape for "who implements this," that's worth knowing before finalizing monokl's own
- Whether monokl could *emit* SCIP as an alternate output mode, making its analysis consumable by any SCIP-aware tool, not just agents calling it directly
- Whether monokl could *ingest* an existing SCIP index (from `scip-java`, `scip-python`, etc.) as a supplementary precision source for languages where monokl's own resolution is weaker — a capability tier sourced externally rather than built in-house

Both good adds, and for the same reason — they fill idiom gaps the current list doesn't cover:

- **Apollo Router** (Rust) — a production network service: query planning, federation protocol handling, heavily async (tokio). That's a genuinely different texture from what's already picked — rust-analyzer is IDE/incremental-computation code, ripgrep is a CLI text-processing tool, Apollo Router is a long-running async service. Good stress test for the async/await and trait-object-heavy patterns a network gateway leans on.
- **DGS** (Netflix's GraphQL framework for Java/Spring) — one nuance worth deciding before locking it in: do you want to analyze **DGS's own framework source** (`netflix/dgs-framework` — annotation-processing and reflection-heavy internals), or **an app built with DGS** (real `@DgsComponent`/`@DgsQuery`/`@DgsData`-annotated resolver code)? Given the Java research found codegraph's own extractor sank most of its hand-tuning into resolving Spring+Lombok annotation patterns in *consuming* code, an example app is probably the more directly relevant pick — the framework's own internals test something closer to "how well does monokl handle heavy reflection/codegen," a different question.

Updated candidate list, unless you want changes: TS/JS → `typescript-go`(Go port)/`oxc`/`vscode`; Rust → `rust-analyzer`/`ripgrep`/`tokio`/**Apollo Router**; Python → Django or FastAPI; Go → Kubernetes/`typescript-go`; Java → Spring Boot+Lombok app or **a DGS-based app**.

Still waiting on the SCIP research to land — I'll fold both threads together once it's back, then verify actual scale on the full list before writing it into the spec.
