This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is designing "monokl" — a Rust crate providing AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents (part of the "orin-axi" GitHub org/suite alongside Firkin, Lumen, Pulse, all meant to depend on a shared crate `michi`). Across this very long session, the user's explicit requests, in order, were:
   - Read and understand the reconstruction-grade spec doc for monokl.
   - Research and consider "our michin-axi work" (michi) and best practices from oxc-react-docgen.
   - Research and fully understand competitor "codegraph" (colbymchenry/codegraph), both its docs site and codebase, and compare monokl's design against it — explicitly demanding genuine deep research (not a shallow pass) and genuine deep code reading (not shallow grep-based review).
   - Decide what further research to run to "enhance our spec," considering "result quality and performance" — user picked specific sub-topics via AskUserQuestion.
   - Confirm whether Rust and Python language support had been adequately researched (they hadn't) — commissioned follow-up research to close that gap.
   - Confirm the language roadmap: explicitly dropped C# ("No C#, let's ignore that"), confirmed Go/Java should be the next languages, prioritized for "general market reach" rather than internal company needs.
   - Requested "make sure there are no references to stubhub in our docs or anywhere in git history — clean it up" (full company de-identification), and separately confirmed via answer to a clarifying question that the repo will be hosted under the real "orin-axi" GitHub org and that naming should reflect that.
   - Shared an arXiv paper URL for consideration ("FYI https://arxiv.org/html/2601.08773v1"), later asked "What did the paper give us?", then asked to research the paper further in context of the rest of the work AND "consider our rust best practices" (this specific phrasing launched the trait-impl/Rust-ecosystem research).
   - Asked whether more academic papers should be sought to back the work "by state-of-the-art science and computer science" — this specific literature search (CHA/RTA/points-to analysis) was recommended by me but has NOT yet been executed; still open/pending.
   - Requested a full Rust-best-practices audit of the entire spec covering "error handling, generics, traits, lifetimes, iterators, closures, concurrency."
   - Mid-turn, pivoted to a much larger request: "Lets take a stab at cleanin gup the docs for AI context... outline the architecture... appropriate README, ARCHITECTURE, CONTRIBUTING, PRINCIPLES, etc docs... include agents.md and claude.md... setup our repo for the project at hand following out bet practices... docs to be readable, scannable, friendly, eng focused, succint and free of AI slop, word salad and filler words." This is the biggest single directive and reshaped the whole task from "patch one giant file" to "properly scaffold the repo's documentation."
   - After I reported the restructuring, explicitly said "Fold those in now" — referring to three specific still-open minor audit findings I had listed (non_exhaustive uniformity, duplicated cache-tier helper, missing fs2 code).
   - Asked the open-ended "What's next?" — exploratory, seeking my recommendation for the actual next phase of the project.
   - Asked "Any other projects, research we should consider for inspiration?" — wanting additional real-world prior-art tools/papers.
   - Proposed selecting "great codebases that are representative of what we should be able to process" as test/eval targets, specifically naming "TS's go implementation. oxc, vscode, etc." as examples — wants a concrete list finalized, feeding the eval-harness corpus requirement.
   - Asked to confirm "We want to consider scip right?" (Sourcegraph Code Intelligence Protocol) as another piece of prior art/potential design influence — I launched a background research agent on this, still pending.
   - **Most recent, not yet substantively answered**: "For java should we consider DGS? apollo router for rust on top of the existin gones?" — asking whether Netflix DGS (a Java GraphQL framework) should be added as another representative Java codebase, and Apollo Router (a Rust-based GraphQL router) as another representative Rust codebase, in addition to (not replacing) the already-proposed candidates (Spring Boot+Lombok for Java; rust-analyzer/ripgrep/tokio for Rust).

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Two-level architecture: `LanguageAnalyzer` (per-file, produces owned `FileAnalysis`) + `WorkspaceEnricher` (folds per-file analyses into `WorkspaceIndex`, containing `ImportGraph` + `SymbolIndex`).
   - Arena lifetime containment (ADR 0002): no OXC `Allocator`-borrowed data may escape a per-file `analyze()` call; everything in `FileAnalysis` must be owned.
   - `CapabilityPrecision` model: `Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact` — lets different language analyzers report different resolution quality per operation, with `Skipped`/`Warning` diagnostics instead of silent failure/crash.
   - `AnalyzerRegistry` — dispatches files to the first matching `LanguageAnalyzer`; composite `config_hash` for cache invalidation.
   - Two-tier cache: mtime/size fast-path → blake3 `ContentHash` fallback; two storage layers (in-memory `DashMap`, disk-persisted `.monokl/cache.json` version+config-hash gated).
   - 8-stage `search` pipeline: query parse → canonicalize → text prefilter (`grep-searcher`) → boolean eval → block retrieval → BM25 rank (K1=1.5, B=0.5) + node-type/coverage boosts → dedup (>50% line overlap) → token budget (tiktoken o200k_base, 2MB hard cap).
   - `TraitImplEnricher`/`TraitImplIndex` — new design (added to spec) for a reverse "who implements this trait" index, modeled on rust-analyzer's `trait_impls_in_crate_query` and rustdoc's implementors-list generation; composes with `SymbolIndex`/`ImportGraph` via a hardened, capped BFS (enqueue-time `FxHashSet` visited-set, explicit depth limit, cap checked at every push site, `TraversalCapExceeded`/`TraversalReport` instead of silent truncation).
   - `cache_tiers::lookup_or_parse` — newly extracted shared helper (parameterized over `from_persisted`/`cached_is_valid`/`parse` closures) unifying `TsAnalyzer`/`RustAnalyzer`'s previously-duplicated 4-tier cache skeleton.
   - `MonoklError` (thiserror-based, `#[non_exhaustive]`) — variants: `Io`, `Walk`, `RegexBuild`, `NonUtf8Path`, `TooManyTerms`, `TokenizerInit`, `Json`, `PathOutsideRoot`, `StaleDiskCache`, `InvalidGitRef`, `Git`, `SymlinkRejected`, `FileTooLarge`, `LockPoisoned` (all now correctly declared after fixes; `Parse`/`Query` removed as dead code).
   - `LanguageAnalyzer` trait (now complete): `language_id() -> LanguageId`, `supports()`, `capabilities() -> AnalyzerCapabilities`, `analyze_with_profile()`, with `analyze()` as a default method delegating to `analyze_with_profile(..., AnalysisProfile::Full)`.
   - `LanguageId` enum: `TypeScript, Rust, Python, Go, Java` (no CSharp — dropped per roadmap decision).
   - `LangData` enum (`#[non_exhaustive]`, serde tag="language"/content="data"): `Ts, Rust, Python, Go, Java` (CSharp variant removed/replaced).

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Two-level architecture: `LanguageAnalyzer` (per-file, produces owned `FileAnalysis`) + `WorkspaceEnricher` (folds per-file analyses into `WorkspaceIndex`, containing `ImportGraph` + `SymbolIndex`).
   - Arena lifetime containment (ADR 0002): no OXC `Allocator`-borrowed data may escape a per-file `analyze()` call; everything in `FileAnalysis` must be owned.
   - `CapabilityPrecision` model: `Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact` — lets different language analyzers report different resolution quality per operation, with `Skipped`/`Warning` diagnostics instead of silent failure/crash.
   - `AnalyzerRegistry` — dispatches files to the first matching `LanguageAnalyzer`; composite `config_hash` for cache invalidation.
   - Two-tier cache: mtime/size fast-path → blake3 `ContentHash` fallback; two storage layers (in-memory `DashMap`, disk-persisted `.monokl/cache.json` version+config-hash gated).
   - 8-stage `search` pipeline: query parse → canonicalize → text prefilter (`grep-searcher`) → boolean eval → block retrieval → BM25 rank (K1=1.5, B=0.5) + node-type/coverage boosts → dedup (>50% line overlap) → token budget (tiktoken o200k_base, 2MB hard cap).
   - `TraitImplEnricher`/`TraitImplIndex` — new design (added to spec) for a reverse "who implements this trait" index, modeled on rust-analyzer's `trait_impls_in_crate_query` and rustdoc's implementors-list generation; composes with `SymbolIndex`/`ImportGraph` via a hardened, capped BFS (enqueue-time `FxHashSet` visited-set, explicit depth limit, cap checked at every push site, `TraversalCapExceeded`/`TraversalReport` instead of silent truncation).
   - `cache_tiers::lookup_or_parse` — newly extracted shared helper (parameterized over `from_persisted`/`cached_is_valid`/`parse` closures) unifying `TsAnalyzer`/`RustAnalyzer`'s previously-duplicated 4-tier cache skeleton.
   - `MonoklError` (thiserror-based, `#[non_exhaustive]`) — variants: `Io`, `Walk`, `RegexBuild`, `NonUtf8Path`, `TooManyTerms`, `TokenizerInit`, `Json`, `PathOutsideRoot`, `StaleDiskCache`, `InvalidGitRef`, `Git`, `SymlinkRejected`, `FileTooLarge`, `LockPoisoned` (all now correctly declared after fixes; `Parse`/`Query` removed as dead code).
   - `LanguageAnalyzer` trait (now complete): `language_id() -> LanguageId`, `supports()`, `capabilities() -> AnalyzerCapabilities`, `analyze_with_profile()`, with `analyze()` as a default method delegating to `analyze_with_profile(..., AnalysisProfile::Full)`.
   - `LanguageId` enum: `TypeScript, Rust, Python, Go, Java` (no CSharp — dropped per roadmap decision).
   - `LangData` enum (`#[non_exhaustive]`, serde tag="language"/content="data"): `Ts, Rust, Python, Go, Java` (CSharp variant removed/replaced).
   - `AnalysisProfile` enum: `Dependencies, Structural, Full`.
   - BM25 tuning (K1=1.5, B=0.5), rounding to 6 decimals for cross-platform determinism.
   - Non-goals (documented in PRINCIPLES.md): no persistent search index, no full Salsa (yet — open track), no embedding-based retrieval by default, no stemming, no in-memory trigram index (rejected: measured 600MB-1.2GB), no tree-sitter for TS/JS (OXC instead), no running agent loop.
   - Native parser landscape per language: TS/JS = OXC (native Rust, adopted); Rust = `ra_ap_syntax` (kept over `syn` — syn's fail-fast parsing is a real regression for scanning WIP/broken code); Python = tree-sitter-python (Ruff's Rust-native crates rejected as unstable); Go = `gosyn` (real, viable native Rust parser — the standout finding); Java = tree-sitter-java (no viable native Rust parser exists).
   - `oxc_semantic` — recommended addition for TS/JS scope-aware reference resolution (lockstep-versioned, same arena discipline as existing OXC deps).
   - `ra_ap_hir` / Salsa — real Rust semantic resolution capability, but daemon-only cost model; Salsa flagged as an independent, lighter investigation track (real precedent: Astral's `ty`/red-knot, Biome) decoupled from the `ra_ap_hir`-needs-a-daemon question.
   - SCIP (Sourcegraph Code Intelligence Protocol) — currently under active research (background agent still running) for potential relevance to monokl's symbol identity/relationship modeling and possible output-format or ingestion strategy.
   - Eval harness design (recommended, not yet built): two-layer — deterministic retrieval eval (RepoBench-R/CodeSearchNet-style recall@k/MRR) + agent A/B (model/effort pinned, ≥5 runs/condition median+IQR, ≥10 repos frozen task list, report token AND dollar cost separately, broken out by cache-read vs fresh-input mix).
   - Rust workspace clippy lint policy: deny `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic`, `unreachable`, `unimplemented`, `dbg_macro`, `todo` in lib code (allowed only in `#[cfg(test)]`); `unsafe_code = "deny"`.
   - `camino::Utf8Path`/`Utf8PathBuf` used everywhere instead of `std::path::Path`; `rustc-hash::FxHashMap`/`FxHashSet` for hot-path maps; `BTreeMap` for anything serialized to JSON (deterministic key order).
   - RTK (Rust Token Killer) — user's global bash-command proxy (per their global CLAUDE.md) that summarizes/truncates verbose bash output for token savings; occasionally produces misleading summarized output (e.g. "[N more lines]" instead of real `head` output) requiring the Read tool for precision instead.

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-stack-graphs" color="blue" summary="stack-graphs research complete: verdict is skip/defer">
## How it works

Stack graphs extend the *scope graphs* framework from Eelco Visser's group at TU Delft (Visser et al.'s work on modular name resolution) with a stack mechanism. The core paper is Creager, "Stack graphs: Name resolution at scale" (arXiv:2211.01224 / DROPS OASIcs EVCS 2023.8). Name binding info is encoded as a graph where paths = valid bindings; resolving a reference is path-finding. The novel bit over plain scope graphs: compound references (`A.foo`) require *pausing* resolution of one name to resolve another — a natural stack operation, hence "stack graphs." Crucially, graph construction is **file-isolated** — each file's subgraph is built with zero visibility into other files — and cross-file resolution happens later via *partial-path stitching* (`stack-graphs` crate's `partial`/`stitching` modules). This is what gives it incrementality: unchanged files are never reanalyzed. (docs.rs/stack-graphs, arXiv:2211.01224)

## Cost to adopt

Real, published crates: `stack-graphs` (0.14.1, published 2021-05 through 2024-12-13) and `tree-sitter-graph` (0.12.0, the generic tree-sitter→graph DSL engine, still published under github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-graph — NOT archived, last release Dec 2024). Defining a language means writing a `.tsg` file: pattern-match tree-sitter node types, emit graph nodes/edges/attrs (`push_symbol`, `pop_symbol`, scope edges), with `if`/`if none` guards for context sensitivity. I pulled the actual TypeScript definition (`languages/tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript/src/stack-graphs.tsg`) — **it's 6,297 lines**. That is substantially more code than a hand-rolled heuristic resolver would typically require, and it's write-only-once-you-learn-a-bespoke-DSL effort, not reusable Rust.

## Per-language maturity — the critical gap for monokl

Only **four** language definitions were ever built in github/stack-graphs: **Java, JavaScript, Python, TypeScript**. There is no Rust and no Go definition anywhere in the repo or its ecosystem. So for monokl's five languages, stack-graphs offers real prior art for exactly the ones where you're least stuck (TS) and nothing for Rust or Go, where the pain is worst.

Production usage is real, not vaporware: GitHub's Precise Code Navigation shipped on Python in Dec 2021 (github.blog/2021-12-09) and TypeScript in Mar 2024 (github.blog/changelog/2024-03-14), both explicitly "powered by stack graphs."

**However: github/stack-graphs was archived by GitHub on 2025-09-09** — read-only, "no longer supported or updated," with an explicit "if you wish to continue development, fork it." Last release was tree-sitter-stack-graphs v0.10.0, Dec 13, 2024. So GitHub built it, shipped it in production for 4 years, then stopped investing in the open-source side — no announced successor. (The generic `tree-sitter-graph` DSL engine lives on separately under the `tree-sitter` org and isn't archived, but the name-resolution-specific layer and all per-language definitions are frozen.)

## Precision model fit

No confidence/precision tiers exist anywhere in the docs or paper — resolution is a binary path-exists/doesn't-exist search. The one exploitable signal: ambiguous references naturally produce *multiple* candidate paths (unresolved overloads, dynamic dispatch), while unambiguous ones produce exactly one. Monokl could map "exactly one path" → `Exact` and "N>1 candidate paths" → `Structural`, but that mapping is something monokl would have to build itself — it isn't a first-class concept in the library.

## Verdict: skip, don't adopt

This is honestly still "per-language work," just relocated into an unfamiliar declarative DSL rather than Rust you already control — and the TypeScript definition suggests it's *more* total code than a heuristic resolver, not less. Combined with: (a) zero existing coverage for Rust or Go, monokl's hardest gaps; (b) the repo being archived with no successor, meaning any new `.tsg` work for Go/Rust would be unsupported from day one with no upstream to file issues against; (c) binary resolution requiring monokl to invent its own precision-tier mapping anyway — there's no case here for adoption over the current path.

The one place I'd flag as worth a second look, not a full adopt: monokl could fork/vendor the existing **Python and TypeScript** `.tsg` definitions as a reference implementation or even reused artifact for those two languages specifically (proven, production-tested rulesets, permissively licensed MIT/Apache-2.0) — but that's "borrow a finished asset for 2 of 5 languages," not "adopt stack-graphs as the resolution architecture." Given monokl's daemon-free CLI constraint is already satisfied by stack-graphs' file-incremental design, this narrow option is at least architecturally compatible if ever revisited — but I wouldn't spend cycles on it now.

Sources: github.com/github/stack-graphs (README, archival notice), docs.rs/stack-graphs, arXiv:2211.01224, github.blog/open-source/introducing-stack-graphs, github.blog/2021-12-09-precise-code-navigation-python..., github.blog/changelog/2024-03-14-precise-code-navigation-for-typescript-projects, crates.io API for stack-graphs/tree-sitter-graph, github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-graph, github.com/github/stack-graphs/languages/tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript/src/stack-graphs.tsg.
</teammate-message>

## difftastic research findings

**1. Core algorithm** — Confirmed from Wilfred Hughes's primary source ["Difftastic, the Fantastic Diff"](https://www.wilfred.me.uk/blog/2022/09/06/difftastic-the-fantastic-diff/): after parsing, difftastic converts each tree-sitter tree to a uniform s-expression (`List{open, children, close}` / `Atom{position, content, kind}`, in `src/parse/syntax.rs`). Diffing is framed as **shortest path on a DAG**: a vertex = `(left_position, right_position, parent-exit-stack)`; edges cost less for "unchanged" matches, more for novel/added/removed atoms; **Dijkstra's algorithm** finds the min-cost route = "most unchanged edges." This is fundamentally a **sequential positional alignment** (walking both flattened token streams in lockstep, tracking nested-list entry/exit), not a general tree-edit-distance over subtree identity.

Graph size is O(L·R) (quadratic in token counts) but vertex parent-stacks made it naively O(2^N) in nesting depth — fixed by lazily constructing vertices and capping to "at most two graph vertices per position pair." Biggest bottleneck is vertex construction itself (millions of vertices on large diffs). Mitigations: aggressive prefix/suffix trimming of unchanged regions, and a **fallback to plain line-diff when the graph would be too big**. A* was tried as an alternative router — "didn't see much improvement" over Dijkstra.

A follow-up optimization write-up, ["How do I boost difftastic by 4x"](https://blog.quarticcat.com/posts/optimize-difftastic/), shows the real-world perf work was almost entirely **shrinking the `Vertex` struct** (nested enums → bitmap → pointer-tagged pointer+counters, −8 bytes/vertex), pruning zero-weight-edge chains (15-25% search-space cut), reusing neighbor-vector allocations, and switching allocators (mimalloc→jemalloc, trading ~20% runtime for fewer pathological-case blowups) — net 4x speedup, 23% of original memory. <teammate-message teammate_id="research-ast-grep" color="green" summary="ast-grep deep-dive: engine, langs, ranking, perf">
Cloned github.com/ast-grep/ast-grep and read the core matcher, config/rule DSL, language registration, and CLI worker end to end (not just README/grep). Findings below.

**1. Query language / matching engine.** A pattern string is parsed by the *target language's own parser* (tree-sitter) then converted into a `PatternNode` tree — `Terminal`/`Internal`/`MetaVar` — via `convert_node_to_pattern` (crates/core/src/matcher/pattern.rs:223-245). So "compiling a pattern" is really "parse it as normal code, then walk the resulting CST." Matching walks goal vs. candidate nodes with `match_node_impl` (crates/core/src/match_tree/match_node.rs:8-55), using a generic `Aggregator` trait (match_tree/mod.rs:18-27) implemented once for the real `MetaVarEnv` and once for a cheap `ComputeEnd` counter — nice zero-cost reuse of one recursive algorithm for both "does it match" and "where does the match end." Ellipsis (`$$$`) handling is genuinely subtle: it clones the aggregator to *probe* the next goal node against each candidate before committing, specifically to stop failed metavar probes from leaking bindings into the real env (match_node.rs:153-182, with a regression test at pattern.rs:346-362 citing PR #2670). A `MatchStrictness` enum — `Cst/Smart/Ast/Relaxed/Signature/Template` (match_tree/strictness.rs:9-16) — is a tunable spectrum from "match everything including whitespace/comments" down to "match text only, ignore node kind entirely." This strictness knob is exposed per-pattern in the YAML rule (`pattern: {context, selector, strictness}`, crates/config/src/rule/mod.rs:199-211).

The YAML rule DSL (crates/config/src/rule/mod.rs) has three tiers: atomic (`pattern`, `kind`, `regex`, `nthChild`, `range`), relational (`inside`/`has`/`precedes`/`follows`, crates/config/src/rule/relational_rule.rs), composite (`all`/`any`/`not`/`matches`→ReferentRule for named+parameterized reusable utility rules, with cycle detection via `check_cyclic`). Relational rules take a `stopBy` (Neighbor/End/until-a-rule-matches) and an optional `field` that resolves to a tree-sitter field ID (`child_by_field_id`) for precise structural targeting, e.g. matching only inside a for-loop's `condition` field (relational_rule.rs:708-717 test). Rules pre-compute a `BitSet` of possible node-kind ids (`potential_kinds`, ops.rs:31-40, rule_core.rs:124-133) as an O(1) filter before running the real matcher on every node — this is ast-grep's only "index," and it's purely a kind-id bitset, nothing text-based.

**2. Multi-language architecture.** Adding a language is genuinely just: pick an expando char (to dodge `$` not being a valid identifier char in that grammar) and point a macro at a tree-sitter crate — `impl_lang!`/`impl_lang_expando!` (crates/language/src/lib.rs:64-148). There is no node-kind mapping layer, no per-language metavariable-extraction config beyond the single char choice. Consequence: rules are **not portable across languages** — `kind: function_declaration` only works for grammars that literally name that node that way, and ast-grep doesn't try to unify this. Quality gap between "flagship" and long-tail languages is real but narrow: Rust (crates/language/src/rust.rs) and Haskell (haskell.rs) have nearly identical, thin test suites (~5-10 pattern tests each) — the language's "quality" in ast-grep is really just whatever the upstream tree-sitter grammar's correctness is. There are explicit workarounds for known upstream grammar bugs, e.g. tree-sitter-typescript's wrong span for unnamed nodes (match_tree/strictness.rs:68-70, citing ast-grep#1419 and tree-sitter-typescript#306) — so grammar immaturity leaks directly into matcher correctness, which is exactly the class of pain monokl's OXC-for-TS decision was presumably trying to avoid.

**3. Ranking.** There is none. I grepped the whole repo for score/rank/bm25/relevance outside of the `transform` module (string-case transforms, unrelated) and found nothing — matches are pure boolean structural hits returned in file/scan order. No relevance sort, no dedup, no token budgeting.

**4. Performance.** Parallelism is `ignore::WalkParallel` (the ripgrep crate) with a classic multi-producer/single-consumer `mpsc` channel (crates/cli/src/utils/worker.rs:118-158) — not rayon (grepped, zero hits). Every invocation fully parses every file that survives the gitignore/glob filter (crates/cli/src/utils/mod.rs:143-144, `lang.ast_grep(file_content)`) — there is no persistent cache (mtime, content-hash, or otherwise) across runs; it's a stateless one-shot CLI. The only pre-match optimization is `Pattern::fixed_string()` (matcher/pattern.rs:188-205: recursively extracts the single longest literal-text child of a pattern) checked via plain substring `file_content.contains(...)` in crates/cli/src/utils/mod.rs:169-172 — but this runs **after** the whole file is already parsed into a tree; it only skips the rule-matching walk, not the parse itself. This is a materially weaker prefilter than monokl's grep-searcher-before-parse stage, and ast-grep has nothing analogous to a two-tier mtime/blake3 cache at all.

**Recommendations for monokl:**

1. **query/ module** — adopt a `MatchStrictness`-style tunable spectrum for the structural side of a query (at minimum a "signature" mode: match node kind, ignore literal text/comments). Monokl's BM25 text layer already handles fuzzy/ranked matching; a strictness knob would let the AST-evaluation stage relax without falling all the way back to pure text search.
2. **patterns/schema command family** — borrow the `inside`/`has`/`follows`/`precedes` relational vocabulary with `stopBy` (immediate neighbor vs. until-end vs. until-a-rule) and field-targeted matching (child-by-field-id). This is a clean, proven primitive for "structural pattern within structural context" that's more composable than kind+text alone, and maps well onto whatever OXC/ra_ap_syntax/tree-sitter field APIs each analyzer already exposes.
3. **query/ module (ellipsis/dedup correctness)** — if monokl's pattern matching ever supports multi-node capture (`$$$`-equivalent), copy the probe-before-commit technique (clone env, test, only commit on success) to avoid metavar binding leaks on failed backtracking — this was a real bug class in ast-grep (PR #2670) worth avoiding preemptively rather than discovering later.
4. **Not a design flaw, a validation** — ast-grep's `AnalyzerRegistry`-equivalent is cheap (macro + tree-sitter crate + one char) specifically because it only does structural match/no-match with no cross-language kind normalization and no relevance ranking. Monokl's heavier per-language cost (InspectEntry classifiers, BM25 boosts) is inherent to attempting semantic/ranked search rather than a gap to close — ast-grep offers no prior art for BM25 boosts, dedup, or token budgeting since it doesn't attempt any of that.
</teammate-message>

Literature review done, all citations verified via search (not recalled from memory) — authors/venues/pages cross-checked against dblp/ACM DL/arXiv. Ready to paste into 05-research-and-decisions.md as a new §7 (903 words):

---

## 7. Literature grounding: CHA/RTA/k-CFA and points-to analysis vs. `CapabilityPrecision`

Call-graph and points-to analysis is a mature subfield with a clean precision/cost ladder that
maps onto `CapabilityPrecision` (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact`) better than
expected, with one real gap the literature exposes.

**Class Hierarchy Analysis (CHA)** — Dean, Grove, Chambers, "Optimization of Object-Oriented
Programs Using Static Class Hierarchy Analysis," ECOOP 1995, pp. 77-101. CHA resolves a virtual
call from the declared class/interface hierarchy alone: any subtype of the static receiver type is
a possible target, full stop — no dataflow, no reachability, no instantiation check. Fast, purely
syntactic, known-unsound (ignores reflection, dynamic loading, generics-driven dispatch). This is
`TraitImplIndex`'s (§2) shape exactly: it indexes every `impl Trait for Type` from the AST with no
check on whether `Type` is ever constructed — a declared-hierarchy fact, not a program-behavior
fact. `Structural` is a correct label for this.

**Rapid Type Analysis (RTA)** — Bacon & Sweeney, "Fast Static Analysis of C++ Virtual Function
Calls," OOPSLA 1996, pp. 324-341. RTA refines CHA with one extra static pass: track which classes
are actually instantiated (`new`) anywhere in the reachable program and prune CHA's target set to
those. On their benchmarks (7 C++ programs, 5-20 KLOC) this resolved 71% of virtual calls
statically, vs. CHA's much larger over-approximation. Critically, RTA is still single-pass,
non-iterative, and needs no aliasing or points-to information — it costs the same order as CHA,
not the order of a real type checker. That means RTA is not a stand-in for `Exact`; it is a
finer-grained rung *inside* what monokl currently collapses into one `Structural` tier. Concretely:
CHA-shaped = "declared hierarchy says `Type` could implement `Trait`"; RTA-shaped = "...and `Type`
is actually constructed somewhere in this corpus." An RTA-style filter over `TraitImplIndex` —
cross-referencing implementor types against observed struct-literal/constructor sites, already
information monokl's `SymbolIndex` pass collects — is a legitimate, still-`Structural`-cost
enhancement worth recording, not a new precision tier.

**k-CFA** — Shivers, "Control-Flow Analysis of Higher-Order Languages, or Taming Lambda," PhD
thesis, CMU-CS-91-145, May 1991 (formalizing the earlier "Control-Flow Analysis in Scheme," PLDI
1988, pp. 164-174). k-CFA answers a different question than CHA/RTA: not "which subtype could this
be" but "which closure could this call site invoke," by abstracting environments to
k-deep call-string contexts. It is EXPTIME-hard for any static k>0 — Van Horn & Mairson, "Deciding
kCFA is complete for EXPTIME," ICFP 2008, pp. 275-282 — and the blow-up is fundamental, not an
implementation artifact (companion result: Might, Smaragdakis, Van Horn, "Resolving and Exploiting
the k-CFA Paradox," PLDI 2010, showing even k=1 degenerates badly on OO-flavored code specifically
because class-based dispatch, monokl's actual target, isn't what k-CFA's context-sensitivity is
built to disambiguate). k-CFA is the wrong shape and the wrong cost class for monokl: it targets
first-class-closure flow in dynamically-typed/functional code, not "what implements this
interface" or "what does this import resolve to." Tellingly, even IDE-scale JS tooling built for
monokl's actual problem class explicitly avoids it — Feldthaus, Schäfer, Sridharan, Dolby, Tip,
"Efficient Construction of Approximate Call Graphs for JavaScript IDE Services," ICSE 2013, use a
cheaper field-based approximate analysis instead of full k-CFA specifically to hit interactive
latency. Verdict: k-CFA is correctly out of scope; no part of this spec should be revised toward it.

**Points-to analysis** — the two foundational styles: Andersen, "Program Analysis and
Specialization for the C Programming Language," PhD thesis, DIKU, University of Copenhagen, 1994
(inclusion-based/subset-constraint, more precise, worse complexity); Steensgaard, "Points-to
Analysis in Almost Linear Time," POPL 1996, pp. 32-41 (equality-based/union-find, "almost linear,"
less precise). Bravenboer & Smaragdakis, "Strictly Declarative Specification of Sophisticated
Points-to Analyses," OOPSLA 2009 (the Doop framework), show Andersen-style points-to specified in
Datalog scales across a dial of context-sensitivity (context-insensitive up to k-object-sensitive)
rather than being one fixed cost point — the literature's actual answer for what a non-`ra_ap_hir`
path toward `Exact` looks like, relevant to the open Salsa/persistent-daemon track (§4) as a second
candidate design, not just `ra_ap_hir`.

**Recent IDE-scale precedent.** PyCG (Salis, Sotiropoulos, Louridas, Spinellis, Mitropoulos, ICSE
2021, arXiv:2103.00587) — dependency-free static call-graph generation for Python — reports 99.2%
precision but only 69.9% recall, concrete quantified evidence that even careful assignment-based
static analysis without type inference has a real recall ceiling for a dynamic language, directly
backing this doc's own admission (§04-analysis-fidelity.md, problem 5) that Python forward-reference
resolution without pyright is `Heuristic`, not `Structural`. SootUp (Karakaya, Schott, Klauke,
Bodden et al., TACAS 2024) modernizes Soot's engineering (lazy class loading, fail-early
validation) but not its cost model — full points-to/call-graph construction there is still a
batch, whole-classpath operation, reinforcing rather than challenging monokl's daemon/non-daemon
split. No CodeQL/Semmle paper describing an explicit graded-precision model comparable to
`CapabilityPrecision` was found — de Moor et al., "Keynote Address: .QL for Source Code Analysis,"
SCAM 2007, pp. 3-16, describes the Datalog query engine, and CodeQL's public Java/Kotlin call-graph
docs describe one virtual-dispatch-aware resolution strategy with no published notion of graded
confidence tiers. Worth stating plainly rather than implying false precedent.

**Verdict:** no new tier needed, and no change to k-CFA's exclusion. One concrete, low-cost
documentation fix: `Structural`'s definition in §11 should note it currently spans both a
CHA-shaped fact (declared-hierarchy membership) and would span an RTA-shaped fact
(hierarchy-membership-plus-instantiation) if the `TraitImplIndex` instantiation filter above is
ever built — both are real, distinct precision levels in the literature that this spec currently
collapses into one label. That collapse is defensible as shipped (same cost order, same
soundness caveats), but should be named rather than left implicit.

---

Notes on verification: I independently confirmed every paper via web search (title/authors/venue/pages), not from memory — e.g. corrected my own assumption that SootUp was FASE 2022 (it's actually TACAS 2024). I could NOT find any CodeQL/Semmle paper with an explicit precision-tiering methodology — said so plainly rather than forcing a citation that doesn't exist. </teammate-message>

8	that were constructed but never declared) are fixed directly in
9	[01-core-architecture.md](./01-core-architecture.md) and
10	[03-multi-language-platform.md](./03-multi-language-platform.md) — this log records why.
11	
12	Part of the [monokl spec](./README.md).
13	
14	---
15	
16	# Part 5: Pre-implementation research amendments
17	
18	> Added before any of Parts 1-4 have been built. A competitive deep-dive against
19	> colbymchenry/codegraph (a mature, production multi-language code-intelligence tool) plus
20	> targeted follow-on research were used to stress-test this spec's assumptions before they
21	> calcify into code. Two categories below: fixes already applied directly to the sections
22	> above, and decisions/open tracks that change what future PRs should do.
23	
24	## 1. Fixes applied in this document
25	
26	- **§Python fidelity, problem 5** (type annotation resolution): `CapabilityPrecision::Approximate`
27	  was not a real variant of the enum defined in §11 (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural <
28	  Exact`). Corrected to `CapabilityPrecision::Heuristic`.
29	- **§Section 6, `STOP_WORDS`**: added `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe`
30	  — near-universal Rust tokens the original TS/Rust-tuned list omitted, found by tracing the
31	  tokenizer's actual splitting rules against real Rust source rather than assuming coverage.
32	
33	## 2. Adopted, not yet implemented
34	
35	- **Add `oxc_semantic` to the `lang-ts` feature's dependency set**, versioned in lockstep with
36	  `oxc_parser`/`oxc_ast`/`oxc_span`/`oxc_allocator` (same version string — no separate
37	  compatibility matrix). `SemanticBuilder::build(&program)` runs against the same per-file
38	  `Allocator` arena the parser already uses and produces a `Semantic` result (scope tree +
39	  symbol table: `SymbolId`/`ScopeId`/`Reference`, real shadowing/hoisting/TDZ-aware binding).
40	  This replaces regex/text-scanned local-usage resolution in `refs`/`definition` with genuine
41	  scope-aware resolution for within-file references — closing the exact class of technical debt
42	  codegraph's own maintainers flag as their worst (a 20+-resolver heuristic confidence cascade).
43	  `oxc_semantic` is file-scoped: it does not replace `oxc_resolver` for cross-file specifier
44	  resolution, it upgrades what feeds into that combination. Output must be converted to owned
45	  data before the arena drops, same discipline as the AST conversion already documented in §17.
46	- **Build an eval harness before further ranking/tuning decisions are made on faith.** BM25's
47	  `K1=1.5`/`B=0.5` and the token-budget defaults are carried over from Probe's prior tuning
48	  (§29) and are unvalidated for monokl specifically. Minimum viable harness: two layers, not
49	  one — (a) a deterministic retrieval eval (RepoBench-R- or CodeSearchNet-style recall@k/MRR)
50	  run on every commit, and (b) a properly-powered agent A/B (model/effort pinned and logged,
51	  ≥5 runs per condition reporting median + IQR, ≥10 repos with a task list frozen before either
52	  arm runs). Report token and dollar-cost deltas *separately*, broken out by cache-read vs.
53	  fresh-input token mix — codegraph's own published cost-savings claim reversed under
54	  independent replication specifically because token/call reductions and dollar cost decoupled
55	  when its context payload shifted from many cheap cached reads to fewer expensive fresh reads.

All four research threads plus the literature review are now written into `05-research-and-decisions.md` as §7 (prior-art survey: SCIP, stack-graphs, ast-grep, difftastic) and §8 (CHA/RTA/k-CFA literature grounding), with the concrete adopt/reject items folded into §2 and §5 respectively. Quick tally:

- **Adopted (§2)**: SCIP's `Relationship` shape for `TraitImplIndex` (not its wire format), an optional `.scip` reader as a precision upgrade, an RTA-style instantiation filter over `TraitImplIndex`, ast-grep's `MatchStrictness` spectrum + relational-rule vocabulary for the query/patterns pipeline, and a content-hash move detector for `diff` (something even difftastic still lacks).
- **Rejected (§5)**: stack-graphs (archived, no Rust/Go coverage), SCIP as an identity scheme or output format, difftastic's Dijkstra-graph algorithm as the `diff` command's core, and k-CFA for any resolution tier.
- **§8 verdict**: no new `CapabilityPrecision` tier needed — CHA and RTA map cleanly onto what `Structural` already does and could do, k-CFA is confirmed wrong-shaped and wrong-cost, and the one real gap is documentation: `Structural` should note it currently collapses two distinct literature-backed precision levels into one label.

That closes out every open research thread from this session — SCIP, stack-graphs, ast-grep, difftastic, and the call-graph/points-to literature are all now recorded. Remaining open items are the representative-codebases eval corpus (needs real scale verification before it goes in the spec) and, whenever you're ready, git-init plus starting actual implementation.

  "microsoft/typescript-go"

397	
398	**Rapid Type Analysis (RTA)** — Bacon & Sweeney, "Fast Static Analysis of C++ Virtual Function
399	Calls," OOPSLA 1996, pp. 324-341. RTA refines CHA with one extra static pass: track which classes
400	are actually instantiated (`new`) anywhere in the reachable program and prune CHA's target set to
401	those. On their benchmarks (7 C++ programs, 5-20 KLOC) this resolved 71% of virtual calls
402	statically, vs. CHA's much larger over-approximation. Critically, RTA is still single-pass,
403	non-iterative, and needs no aliasing or points-to information — it costs the same order as CHA,
404	not the order of a real type checker. That means RTA is not a stand-in for `Exact`; it is a
405	finer-grained rung *inside* what monokl currently collapses into one `Structural` tier. Concretely:
406	CHA-shaped = "declared hierarchy says `Type` could implement `Trait`"; RTA-shaped = "...and `Type`
407	is actually constructed somewhere in this corpus." An RTA-style filter over `TraitImplIndex` (§2)

content.text: Should we consider kotlin support? switft? what android uses?

payload.message:
**Android** has used Kotlin as Google's officially preferred language since 2019, but a large share of existing/legacy Android code is still Java — which is already on monokl's roadmap, so that's partial Android coverage today, not zero.

**Kotlin** is the stronger candidate of the two by the same "general market reach" logic that already promoted Go/Java over C#: it's not just Android anymore, it's picked up real server-side usage too (Ktor, Spring-with-Kotlin). My expectation, unverified, is it'd land in roughly the same spot as Java — no viable native Rust parser, `tree-sitter-kotlin` as the fallback, real semantic analysis (Kotlin's own compiler frontend) daemon-only.

**Swift** is real but narrower — it's essentially Apple's ecosystem (iOS/macOS/watchOS), without Kotlin's or Java's spread beyond mobile. `tree-sitter-swift` exists, but Apple's own semantic tooling (`swift-syntax`) is written in Swift itself, which would be the first language on this roadmap that isn't either native-Rust or a toolchain-free tree-sitter grammar — a real added-friction point worth weighing before committing to it.

Want me to run the same verification pass I did for Go/Java on both before touching the roadmap — real crates.io/tree-sitter-grammar maturity, semantic-tooling cost, and adoption data — rather than deciding this off general impressions?

TypeScript overtook Python and JavaScript as the most used programming language, marking a historic shift. ## Recommendation: adopt a generic tree-sitter fallback tier, but scope it tightly and reset expectations that per-language config stays "thin"

### Grammar maturity findings (per candidate)

- **C** (tree-sitter/tree-sitter-c): 53 open issues, mostly C23/C2y feature gaps and edge-case bugs (cast-vs-binary-expr, macro handling, enum parsing) — no fundamental ambiguity problem. Mature, widely embedded (difftastic, ast-grep, nvim-treesitter). Clean fallback-tier fit.
- **C++** (tree-sitter/tree-sitter-cpp): 62 open issues, and critically issue #74 documents a genuine unresolved grammar ambiguity — C++ statement parsing is expression-vs-declaration ambiguous without type info that may live in headers the parser never sees. Real bugs in typeid, casts, pointer-to-member, defaulted friend operators. Same tooling adoption as C, but real precision ceiling is lower.
- **Kotlin**: two competing grammars. fwcd/tree-sitter-kotlin (187 stars, active, systematically cross-validated against JetBrains' own PSI parser) is the real one — but its own validation suite reports only **61.2% structural match** against the official compiler AST. tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-kotlin is clearly the weaker alternative (8 stars, 14 commits, last commit Jan 2025). Even the "good" grammar has a hard, documented accuracy ceiling.
- **Swift** (alex-pinkus/tree-sitter-swift): mature — 4 years, 487 commits, 26+ contributors, zero open issues/PRs, used by difftastic and nvim-treesitter. Best-positioned "new" candidate technically, but mobile-concentrated reach per your existing framing.
- **Ruby**: official tree-sitter org grammar, 22 open issues/10 PRs, active (~Mar 2026), long production use (GitHub semantic highlighting, difftastic, ast-grep). Solid.
- **PHP**: official grammar, actively maintained (PHP 8.5 pipe operator recently added); split into `php`/`php_only` grammars in 2024 specifically to fix HTML-injection conflicts for Blade/Twig — real engineering investment, mature.
- **Scala**: official grammar but stale — latest published version is a year old and **explicitly does not support Scala 3 syntax**, now the mainstream dialect. Red flag for launch.
- **Bash**: official, mature, low-ambiguity. codegraph's own community explicitly flagged it launch-ready ("mature Bash tree-sitter grammar exists," issue #648). Cheap, low-risk win.
- **C#**: official grammar, healthy (315 stars, 29 open issues, active through Jun 2026), based on Roslyn's own grammar. Your earlier exclusion was about bespoke-investment ROI, not grammar quality — since the fallback tier explicitly skips that bespoke layer, the original reasoning doesn't transfer here. Legitimate fallback-tier candidate.

### Precedent for the architecture pattern

- **universal-ctags** already runs a two-tier model structurally similar to what you're considering: hand-written full parsers for complex languages, plus a genuinely generic, user-extensible regex-based "optlib" mechanism for everything else. optlib is real precedent that a thin/generic tier can work — but it's correspondingly low-precision (pattern/tag matching, no real tree), i.e. it validates Heuristic-only as the honest ceiling for a truly thin tier.
- **Sourcegraph** ships almost exactly your proposed shape at the product level: fast, always-available "search-based" nav (generically powered by ctags + tree-sitter) as a fallback alongside precise SCIP/LSIF nav for repos with real indexers. Credible evidence this two-tier shape is a legitimate, shipped product pattern, not a compromise nobody actually uses.
- **GitHub Linguist** is not real precedent here — it's heuristic pattern-matching + statistical classification for language ID, not AST-based analysis, so it doesn't validate a code-intelligence fallback tier specifically.
- **The strongest and most important finding**: codegraph — the tool this whole idea came from — does **not** actually keep its per-language config thin in practice. Its own architecture docs and issue tracker show real, substantial special-casing per language: Kotlin needs custom nested-property-declaration visiting, Java needs Lombok member synthesis (the *exact* problem monokl already solved bespoke), C# needs generic-unwrapping/nullable-stripping, C++ needs smart-pointer unwrapping, COBOL needs a fixed-to-free preprocessing pass before parsing even starts. Codegraph's maintainers describe this as ongoing, expected growth. This directly contradicts the "thin config" premise the idea was originally sold on — it's aspirational, not descriptive of what production quality actually requires.

### Architectural cost to monokl

Expect the same erosion codegraph experienced: any fallback-tier language that gets real usage will draw pressure for special-casing, and that pressure won't stop on its own — it has to be actively capped by policy (Heuristic-only ceiling, no `InspectEntry` classifier, no resolution beyond textual/structural reference-finding). The minimal-viable shape, following both ast-grep's precedent (no cross-language node-kind normalization) and codegraph's own `LanguageExtractor` interface shape (per-language string-keyed node-type buckets: functionTypes/classTypes/etc.), is a single generic analyzer keyed by extension, internally dispatching to a small per-language config table. That fits `AnalyzerRegistry`'s existing one-impl-per-language dispatch as one additional impl owning N languages — no dispatch restructuring needed. The one real twist: `CapabilityPrecision` needs to be reported per-language-instance inside that one analyzer, not per-analyzer-impl, since C's ceiling (Heuristic/Structural) genuinely differs from C++'s (Heuristic only, given the ambiguity) and Kotlin's (Heuristic only, given the 61% ceiling) — existing analyzers don't need this since each is already one language.

### Launch set (prioritized by real usage data)

1. **C** — clean fit, mature grammar, TIOBE #2.
2. **C++** — TIOBE #3, real gap, but declare Heuristic-only at launch (not Structural) given the unresolved ambiguity; expect it to generate the most special-case pressure.
3. **Bash** — cheap, low-risk, real demand.
4. **C#** — grammar-quality objection doesn't apply to fallback-tier scope; include.
5. **Ruby, PHP** — solid second-wave adds if usage data supports it.

**Hold back**: Kotlin (documented 61.2% ceiling, not a maturity-over-time problem — it's a hard fact about the grammar), Scala (stale, no Scala 3 support — don't ship a fallback that silently misparses the modern language). Swift is fine technically but low-priority per your existing mobile-reach framing — add opportunistically.

### Graduation threshold (fallback → bespoke Go/Java-style investment)

Two-part test, not usage rank alone: (a) sustained usage in the current Go/Java tier (top ~10-12 TIOBE/Octoverse) **and** (b) documented evidence of a structural-precision ceiling analogous to Java's Lombok problem — i.e., idioms common enough in real code that Heuristic/Structural-only output silently breaks call-chain/symbol resolution for a large fraction of real codebases. **C++ already meets both today** — it's the strongest near-term graduation candidate, and worth revisiting for a native-parser bespoke investment (mirroring the OXC/gosyn/ra_ap_syntax pattern) rather than assuming tree-sitter fallback is permanently sufficient for it.

Sources: github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-c(pp)/issues, tree-sitter-cpp#74, github.com/fwcd/tree-sitter-kotlin, github.com/tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-kotlin, github.com/alex-pinkus/tree-sitter-swift, tree-sitter/tree-sitter-{ruby,php,scala,bash,c-sharp}, Wilfred/difftastic languages_supported.html, docs.ctags.io/en/latest/optlib.html, sourcegraph.com/docs precise_code_navigation, github-linguist/linguist, colbymchenry/codegraph (DeepWiki §7.3 Adding Language Support) + issue #648.
</teammate-message>

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-parser-performance" color="pink" summary="Parser benchmark research findings and recommendations">
## Findings (with real citations)

**1. OXC's own numbers** (github.com/oxc-project/bench-javascript-parser-written-in-rust): parse-only, `iter_with_large_drop` to exclude AST-teardown cost, single-thread + parallel, tested on M3 Max/M2/i7. Concrete: `cal.com.tsx` — OXC 3.4ms vs swc 14.4ms (4.28x) vs Biome 18.3ms (5.42x); `typescript.js` — OXC 26.4ms vs swc 91.0ms (3.45x) vs Biome 139.3ms (5.28x). Biome comparison explicitly flagged non-apples-to-apples (CST vs AST). **Tree-sitter is not in OXC's own comparison set at all** — there is no OXC-vs-tree-sitter-typescript number anywhere I could find.

**2. tree-sitter's own performance framing**: no official MB/s or lines/sec figures exist. The closest thing is an offhand maintainer comment in tree-sitter/tree-sitter Discussion #3413: a custom grammar parsed a 6k-line file in ~80ms, Python's grammar parsed 20k lines in ~120ms — presented as "comparable," not a rigorous benchmark. More telling: tree-sitter/tree-sitter Issue #1277 reports a 1.6MB JSON file taking **~1.2s for a full cold parse and ~0.7s to "re-parse" with zero edits**, consuming ~300MB for two trees. That 0.7s no-op-reparse number is direct evidence that tree-sitter's headline incremental advantage has a real floor — it is not free even in its best case.

**3. Root cause of tree-sitter slowness, where documented**: tree-sitter-haskell's 50x speedup (owen.cafe, corroborated by tree-sitter-haskell issue #41 "terrible performance on medium/big files") traced to the grammar's **external scanner calling malloc per-token** — a C-side allocation-pattern bug in that specific grammar, not an inherent property of the Rust↔C FFI boundary. Separately, Symflower's reported 36x speedup migrating JavaParser→tree-sitter (Go host) was driven by eliminating **cross-process/cross-language calls**, which is a different failure mode than Rust-to-C FFI. Rust's `extern "C"` FFI itself is near-zero-cost (direct calls, no marshaling) — unlike Python ctypes or JNI, which do pay real marshaling tax. Net: no evidence tree-sitter-python/tree-sitter-java pay an FFI-crossing tax in monokl's Rust host; if they're slow, the more likely culprit (per the Haskell case) is grammar-specific allocation behavior, discoverable only by profiling those two grammars specifically.

**4. Head-to-head native-vs-tree-sitter, same language**: I could not find any published benchmark of `ra_ap_syntax` vs `tree-sitter-rust`, a native Go parser vs `tree-sitter-go`, or Ruff's parser/RustPython vs `tree-sitter-python`. Ruff's own writeup ("The Evolution of Ruff's Parser") only benchmarks its hand-written parser against its own predecessor (~2x faster, 20-40% overall linter speedup) — never against tree-sitter-python. This is a genuine gap in public data, not something I'm approximating around.

**5. `gosyn`** (chikaku/gosyn, the real pure-Rust Go parser): README has zero benchmark numbers published.

**6. Comparable tools**: ast-grep's own "Optimize ast-grep to get 10X faster" post (10.8s→0.975s on TypeScript's repo, six rules) attributes the win entirely to regex-cloning and `potential_kinds` matching-logic fixes — it says nothing about parse cost scaling with repo size or cross-language differences, despite specific searching. difftastic's "boost difftastic by 4x" (QuarticCat) confirms the bottleneck was `Vertex` construction/memory layout in the Dijkstra-based diff graph (millions of vertices), not tree-sitter parsing — but the post never gives a parse-time-vs-diff-time percentage split, so I can't cite a number for "tree-sitter's share." codegraph's README states ~60 files/sec end-to-end indexing (parse+extract+write, not parse-only), no per-language breakdown despite searching.

## Practical implications / verdict

- **No public evidence supports differentiated cache-tier treatment by parser type on FFI-crossing grounds alone** — Rust-to-C FFI isn't the tax; grammar-specific C allocation patterns are, and that's only provable per-grammar via monokl's own profiling of tree-sitter-python/tree-sitter-java specifically.
- **Tree-sitter's "incremental" selling point is close to irrelevant to monokl's architecture** — this is well-supported, not just inferred: monokl never holds a previous tree to diff against (fresh process, no daemon), so it always pays tree-sitter's cold-parse path, and issue #1277 shows even the best-case no-op reparse path isn't near-zero on larger files. Monokl should budget tree-sitter grammars at their cold-parse cost, full stop.
- **Memory**: the one real data point (1.6MB JSON → ~300MB for two trees) suggests tree-sitter's peak memory during parsing can be nontrivial for large files; no fleet-scale (10k-50k file) tree-sitter-vs-native memory comparison exists publicly. This is worth a targeted monokl-internal check given the "no arena-borrowed data escapes" rule — the transient peak during conversion to owned `FileAnalysis`, not steady-state, is the risk.
- **Target numbers**: I recommend NOT porting any of the above into `benches/pipeline.rs` as target thresholds — none of these numbers are apples-to-apples with monokl's own file mix, and I want to flag plainly that I found no defensible way to convert "OXC 3-5x faster than swc/Biome" or "tree-sitter Python ~120ms/20k lines" into a monokl-specific per-language budget without measuring monokl's actual fixtures. The one directionally useful data point is codegraph's ~60 files/sec real-world indexing throughput (parse+extract+write combined) — extrapolated naively that's ~167s for 10k files, which should make monokl treat its own 15s cold-build target as unvalidated and likely optimistic until `pipeline_cold` is actually run, not as a number to relax the OXC/ra_ap_syntax/gosyn tier by default. I'd recommend the research log state explicitly: **the only trustworthy fix is running `benches/pipeline.rs` per-language on monokl's own fixtures** — every public number surveyed here differs enough in methodology (file size, hardware, what's measured) that none should be treated as monokl's target.
</teammate-message>

content.text:
For the languages that are not well supported by tree sitter what should we consider? We care about data quality and performance greatly. We want good information for the agents.

For TS/JS we already use oxc, is clang appropriate? Are there better options? What about the Java based languages like kotlin and scala?

payload.message:
Good instinct — this is really asking "for the languages where §10's own research found a real quality ceiling (C++'s grammar ambiguity, Kotlin's 61.2% structural-match ceiling, Scala's no-Scala-3 grammar), is there a better answer than living with tree-sitter's limits?" Quick grounding before I verify it properly:

**C/C++ + Clang**: `libclang` via FFI bindings (`clang-sys`, the same foundation `bindgen` itself is built on — real, heavily-precedented Rust↔Clang integration) would give genuine compiler-grade parsing, not tree-sitter's heuristic approximation. But it's a different kind of dependency than anything else in this spec: OXC, `ra_ap_syntax`, `gosyn`, and every tree-sitter grammar are pure-Rust, `cargo install`-and-go. `libclang` means linking against an external LLVM/Clang installation on the host — the first non-Rust toolchain dependency anywhere in monokl. And real semantic resolution with Clang typically wants a compilation database (`compile_commands.json`) to know include paths and macros — the same fundamental shape as Java's classpath problem and Rust's `cargo metadata` cost, not a free win. There's also a pure-Rust option worth checking for C specifically (not C++): `lang_c`, a real pure-Rust C99/C11 parser with no FFI. C++ itself is a harder case regardless of tooling choice — its grammar is genuinely context-sensitive (disambiguating `a * b;` as multiplication vs. a pointer declaration requires a live symbol table during parsing), which is exactly why tree-sitter-cpp has an unresolved ambiguity bug rather than just an immaturity gap.

**Kotlin/Scala**: both are fundamentally "real compiler-as-a-library, JVM-hosted" stories — Kotlin's own compiler frontend (`kotlin-compiler-embeddable` or the newer K2 frontend) and Scala's Scalameta (the real production standard, used by Scalafmt/Scalafix). Both mean a JVM subprocess, which puts them in the same cost-model family already on record for Java's `jdtls` and (conceptually) `ra_ap_hir` — real, deep, but daemon/subprocess-oriented, not free per-invocation. That reframes the actual decision: rather than "stuck with tree-sitter's ceiling forever," Kotlin/Scala's real semantic tier probably belongs in the same deferred-daemon investigation track (§4) already on record for Rust, not treated as a dead end.

Launching verification on both threads now rather than asserting this from memory:

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-cpp-parsing" color="cyan" summary="C/C++ libclang vs tree-sitter research findings">
## Findings

**libclang FFI is real and production-precedented, but genuinely breaks the no-toolchain rule.** `clang-sys` (KyleMayes) is the real FFI layer — actively maintained (pushed 2026-02-25, 26 open issues, 160 stars) — and `bindgen` literally depends on it (confirmed via crates.io: bindgen 0.72.1's deps include `clang-sys` directly). But bindgen's own docs require Clang 9.0+ and document `LIBCLANG_PATH`/`llvm-config` discovery explicitly, and the friction is real, not hypothetical: rust-bindgen#1797, #2091, #1276, #1579, #2360, #1411 and clang-sys#74 are all live "could not find libclang" reports spanning Windows, Docker, and Alpine, plus actions/runner-images#3316 for GitHub Actions Windows runners. This is a well-worn pain point for exactly the "cargo install and just works" experience monokl wants.

There IS a better-fitting crate than bindgen for monokl's actual need ("parse and walk a tree," not "generate FFI bindings"): **`clang-ast`** by dtolnay — real and very actively maintained (pushed 2026-06-24, only 2 open issues, 575k downloads). It doesn't link libclang via FFI at all; instead you shell out to `clang -Xclang -ast-dump=json -fsyntax-only` yourself and clang-ast just deserializes the JSON into typed structs you define. That's a meaningfully lighter integration than clang-sys: no header/version-matching, no dlopen path-hunting — just "is `clang`/`clang++` on PATH." Still requires a real Clang install, but it's a strictly easier optional-dependency shape than libclang FFI.

**Compilation database: real degradation, not binary failure.** clangd's own docs and issues confirm: without `compile_commands.json` (or the simpler per-directory `compile_flags.txt`), it falls back to a generic command (default flags like `-std=c++20`) and drops into what its own docs call a degraded/basic-syntax-checking mode — no cross-compilation support, and a malformed fallback command yields diagnostics pinned to line 1 with most other features unavailable (clangd/clangd#784, clangd/vscode-clangd#547, clangd.llvm.org/design/compile-commands).

But there's a genuine, underappreciated Structural-tier win independent of full compile-command fidelity: **`-frecovery-ast`** (RecoveryExpr) has been on by default for C++ since Clang 11 (2020, LLVM D76696/D86602) — it preserves AST nodes across semantic errors (unresolved identifiers, overload failures, missing members) specifically because clangd needed navigation to keep working on broken code. This is Clang's own team already solving the "tolerate WIP/broken code" problem at the semantic layer — something tree-sitter structurally cannot do since it has no semantic layer at all. The real limit: RecoveryExpr only helps once a file is *found and parsed* — a missing `#include` is a preprocessor-level fatal "file not found" error with no equivalent recovery flag (clangd/clangd#695 and others confirm this is a constant real complaint). So the win is bounded: robust recovery over semantic gaps, no recovery over missing project headers. For header-heavy real-world C++ without real include paths, you're back near tree-sitter's ceiling; for self-contained or system-header-only files, Clang clears Heuristic easily.

**Pure-Rust C: `lang-c` (vickenty) is real but thin.** Crates.io shows a real gap worth flagging: last *published* 2023-09-04 (v0.15.1) but GitHub last *pushed* 2025-10-29 — two years of merged-but-unreleased work, a real single-maintainer bus-factor signal. C-only (no C++), claims "almost full C11" (not C17/C23). It's built on `rust-peg`, and rust-peg has no built-in error-recovery machinery — it's an open, unshipped feature discussion (kevinmehall/rust-peg#276) requiring hand-written skip-until recovery rules in the grammar, with no evidence lang-c's grammar does this. That's the same fail-fast risk that already ruled out `syn` for Rust. I found no other credible pure-Rust C parser on crates.io.

**C++'s ambiguity is real, documented, and structurally unsolvable except by real semantic analysis.** tree-sitter-cpp#74 (confirmed, still open) is exactly the `a * b;` expression-vs-pointer-declaration case: disambiguation requires knowing whether `a` names a type, which requires a live symbol table during parsing — not more lookahead, not better heuristics. Clang/GCC solve it by doing real Sema inline with parsing. Any "quick alternative" pure-Rust C++ parser hits the identical wall tree-sitter-cpp already hit; there is no known partial/heuristic escape from this specific class of ambiguity — only a real compiler frontend or an admittedly-approximate parse.

## Recommendation

- **C++**: Add an optional `libclang`-gated analyzer, feature-flagged and runtime-detected (prefer clang-sys's runtime/dlopen loading mode, or dtolnay's `clang-ast` subprocess approach for less integration friction), falling back automatically to the existing tree-sitter-cpp Heuristic tier when Clang isn't found. Cap it at Structural (not Exact) even with libclang unless a real compile database is present — RecoveryExpr buys real resilience to broken/WIP code but not to missing headers.
- **C**: Don't build a bespoke pure-Rust native analyzer around `lang-c` — its error-recovery gap mirrors the exact reason `syn` was rejected for Rust, and its release cadence is a real risk. Ride C along on the same optional libclang tier as C++ (C has none of C++'s context-sensitive ambiguity, so the same Clang integration gets C much closer to Exact for near-zero incremental engineering cost versus a second bespoke parser).

Sources: crates.io API (clang-sys, clang-ast, lang-c, bindgen metadata), GitHub API (repo activity), rust-bindgen requirements docs, rust-bindgen/clang-sys issue trackers, clangd design docs and issue tracker, LLVM RecoveryExpr design docs (D69330/D61722/D76696/D86602) and Clang 11 release notes, tree-sitter-cpp#74, kevinmehall/rust-peg#276.
</teammate-message>

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-kotlin-scala" color="red" summary="Kotlin/Scala semantic tooling research complete">
## Kotlin

**Compiler-as-library status:** `kotlin-compiler-embeddable` is what detekt/ktlint/IDE tooling historically used, but it's being abandoned — it's incompatible with the new Analysis API (relocated IntelliJ deps cause runtime failures), and detekt's own migration issue confirms this (github.com/detekt/detekt/issues/8027, closed 2026-05-10, moving to the plain `kotlin-compiler` artifact).

**K2 Analysis API has NOT solved the embeddable-frontend problem.** Its own docs state plainly: "the only officially supported use-case is IntelliJ IDEA plugin development... Standalone mode for command-line tool developers... is currently in development and subject to incompatible changes" (kotlin.github.io/analysis-api). So the hoped-for "lighter K2 frontend for external tools" doesn't exist yet as a stable thing — this is a real, current limitation, not FUD.

**But a real middle ground already exists and is production-proven**: ktlint and detekt's default (non-type-resolution) mode both run on the Kotlin compiler's **PSI** layer — the actual compiler AST — and explicitly need no classpath: "Parsing a Kotlin file does not require any knowledge about the project it belongs to" (blog.allegro.tech/2026/03/static-code-analysis-kotlin.html). detekt's opt-in "type resolution" tier requires `--classpath`/`--jvm-target` and only then unlocks rules annotated `@RequiresFullAnalysis` (detekt.dev/docs/gettingstarted/type-resolution) — this is the daemon-territory tier, same shape as jdtls. So: real compiler-grade parsing without classpath is possible for Kotlin (better than tree-sitter's 61.2% ceiling since it's the actual PSI tree, not an approximation), but it requires shelling out to a JVM — a new dependency class, not linked-in like tree-sitter. True semantic resolution stays classpath/daemon-only, and standalone Analysis API isn't a usable shortcut around that today.

## Scala

**Scalameta is mature, actively maintained, and Scala 3 is a solved, old problem, not an open gap.** Official docs state support for "Scala 2.12, 2.13, Scala 3, Scala.js, Scala Native." The Scala-3-parsing tracking issue (github.com/scalameta/scalameta/issues/2022, opened 2020) closed 2021 with the last edge case (infix type precedence) spun into #2315, closed 2022. Scalafmt has shipped `dialect = scala3` support since v3.0.0, in production use. Contrast with tree-sitter-scala, whose Scala 3 issue has sat open since 2021 with no maintainer response — this is a genuine, current, and structural gap for tree-sitter specifically, not just a maturity lag.

**Cost model is real and lightweight for the syntactic tier**: Scalameta's parser alone (no compilation) runs ~92k lines/sec, ~1.4MB memory per 100k LOC. Crucially, there's a **direct precedent for exactly monokl's use case**: `scalex` (github.com/nguyenyou/scalex, actively maintained, pushed June 2026) is explicitly "Scala code intelligence for coding agents. Zero Build Server. Zero Compilation." It uses Scalameta parse-only and documents the identical precision tradeoff monokl cares about verbatim: "No build, no classpath, no daemon... when two packages both define a class called `Config`, scalex can't tell which one `extends Config` refers to — that requires type resolution." Real numbers: 18.5k files/144k symbols in 2.7s cold / 349ms warm. Single maintainer, modest adoption (90 stars) — small but real and working.

**One more mitigation unique to Scala**: `scalafmt-native-image` (github.com/scala-cli/scalafmt-native-image) proves Scalameta-based tools can be GraalVM-native-image-compiled, meaning a Scalameta subprocess call could avoid the classic JVM cold-start tax entirely — a cost-model option with no confirmed Kotlin equivalent (no native-image build found for ktlint/detekt).

Real semantic Scala (SemanticDB) still requires actual compilation via a scalac/dotc plugin — that's the same daemon-territory tier as `ra_ap_hir`/jdtls, unchanged.

## Rust/WASM alternatives
Nothing usable on crates.io for either language, as expected: Kotlin has only `kotlin-parser` (WIP, v0.0.2) and the same tree-sitter grammars already evaluated; Scala has no real parser crate at all (`scala`/`serde_scala` are unrelated).

## Recommendation

Don't treat tree-sitter's ceiling as final for either language — a real **structural tier better than tree-sitter** exists for both, via each language's own compiler-grade parse-only mode (PSI for Kotlin, Scalameta for Scala), proven in production (ktlint; Scalafmt/Scalafix) and, for Scala, proven for this *exact* agent-facing use case by `scalex`. This is a distinct architectural shape from both tree-sitter (linked in-process) and a daemon (persistent warm state): a cold-per-invocation JVM subprocess, non-trivial but not daemon-scale. Scala's case is slightly stronger than Kotlin's — mature Scala 3 support since 2021-22, plus the native-image cost mitigation — where Kotlin's standalone Analysis API is explicitly unstable today per JetBrains' own docs. For both languages, true semantic/Exact-tier resolution genuinely requires classpath construction and belongs on the same deferred daemon/session-mode track as `ra_ap_hir` — that part of the original assumption holds. The new finding is that "Heuristic (tree-sitter) or bust" is not the full picture: a JVM-subprocess "Structural via real compiler parse" tier is a legitimate, evidence-backed option worth scoping as a near-term addition, separate from the daemon question.
</teammate-message>

**One more mitigation unique to Scala**: `scalafmt-native-image` (github.com/scala-cli/scalafmt-native-image) proves Scalameta-based tools can be GraalVM-native-image-compiled, meaning a Scalameta subprocess call could avoid the classic JVM cold-start tax entirely — a cost-model option with no confirmed Kotlin equivalent (no native-image build found for ktlint/detekt).

Real semantic Scala (SemanticDB) still requires actual compilation via a scalac/dotc plugin — that's the same daemon-territory tier as `ra_ap_hir`/jdtls, unchanged.

## Rust/WASM alternatives
Nothing usable on crates.io for either language, as expected: Kotlin has only `kotlin-parser` (WIP, v0.0.2) and the same tree-sitter grammars already evaluated; Scala has no real parser crate at all (`scala`/`serde_scala` are unrelated).

## Recommendation

Don't treat tree-sitter's ceiling as final for either language — a real **structural tier better than tree-sitter** exists for both, via each language's own compiler-grade parse-only mode (PSI for Kotlin, Scalameta for Scala), proven in production (ktlint; Scalafmt/Scalafix) and, for Scala, proven for this *exact* agent-facing use case by `scalex`. This is a distinct architectural shape from both tree-sitter (linked in-process) and a daemon (persistent warm state): a cold-per-invocation JVM subprocess, non-trivial but not daemon-scale. Scala's case is slightly stronger than Kotlin's — mature Scala 3 support since 2021-22, plus the native-image cost mitigation — where Kotlin's standalone Analysis API is explicitly unstable today per JetBrains' own docs. For both languages, true semantic/Exact-tier resolution genuinely requires classpath construction and belongs on the same deferred daemon/session-mode track as `ra_ap_hir` — that part of the original assumption holds. The new finding is that "Heuristic (tree-sitter) or bust" is not the full picture: a JVM-subprocess "Structural via real compiler parse" tier is a legitimate, evidence-backed option worth scoping as a near-term addition, separate from the daemon question.

Both threads are written into `05-research-and-decisions.md` as §12, with §10's stale "capped at Heuristic forever" / "held back" language for C++, Kotlin, and Scala updated in place to point forward to the real answer rather than reading as dead ends. Net effect on the language story:

- **C/C++**: an optional, runtime-detected Clang analyzer (via `clang-ast`'s subprocess approach, not `libclang` FFI) clears C++'s real, structurally-unsolvable parsing ambiguity and gets both languages to `Structural`, falling back to the tree-sitter tier only when Clang isn't on the host. This is also the concrete answer to §10's open "C++ graduation" question — a real-compiler-frontend tier, not a from-scratch native-Rust parser.
- **Kotlin/Scala**: both get an optional JVM-subprocess `Structural` tier (compiler PSI for Kotlin, Scalameta for Scala) — real production precedent in ktlint/detekt and Scalafmt/Scalafix, needing no classpath. Scala's case is stronger (Scala 3 solved since 2021-22, a native-image cold-start mitigation, and a direct precedent for monokl's own use case in `scalex`). True semantic resolution for either still sits on the same deferred daemon track as `ra_ap_hir` — this is a new middle rung, not a way around that.

The language roadmap now has four real tiers end to end: native-Rust (TS/Rust/Go), tree-sitter (Python/Java + the C/C++/Bash/C#/Ruby/PHP fallback tier), the new optional real-compiler-frontend tier (Clang for C/C++, JVM subprocess for Kotlin/Scala), and the deferred daemon tier (`ra_ap_hir`, `jdtls`, and now Kotlin/Scala's full semantic resolution) for whenever that track gets picked up.

Quick yes on the first part — the tiered model (native-Rust → tree-sitter → optional real-compiler-frontend → deferred daemon) is coherent now in a way it wasn't before §10-§12. Before I touch the spec files, let me lay out how I'd shape the architecture for both asks together, since they're actually the same problem: I checked the current trait code directly (`docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md`'s `LanguageAnalyzer` and `03-multi-language-platform.md`'s `AnalyzerRegistry`) rather than reasoning from memory.

**The core insight**: §12's Clang/JVM-subprocess tiers and the future daemon tier (`ra_ap_hir`, Salsa, `jdtls`, Kotlin/Scala full semantic resolution) are architecturally the *same mechanism* at different points on a warmth spectrum — "consult an external process that knows more than our in-process parser, and use it to upgrade specific results to a higher `CapabilityPrecision`, with graceful fallback when it's unavailable." The Clang tier spawns that process fresh per call; a daemon just reuses one across calls. If I design the boundary right now for §12's actual, immediate need, it should already be daemon-shaped — no speculative machinery required.

**Two real gaps I found while checking the current trait shape, independent of the daemon question:**
1. `LanguageId` (currently `TypeScript, Rust, Python, Go, Java`) has no variants for any of §10/§12's languages (C, C++, Bash, C#, Ruby, PHP, Kotlin, Scala) — needs adding regardless.
2. `LanguageAnalyzer::capabilities(&self) -> AnalyzerCapabilities` is fixed per analyzer *instance*, but §10 already requires per-language capability reporting (C's ceiling differs from C++'s within the same fallback-tier impl) — the trait signature itself needs to change, not just the fallback analyzer's internals. Same issue for `language_id(&self) -> LanguageId`, which returns one value but the fallback analyzer owns several languages.

**Proposed design** (leading with my recommendation, two alternatives considered below):

- **`LanguageAnalyzer` trait**: `language_id()` → `languages(&self) -> &[LanguageId]`; `capabilities()` → `capabilities(&self, language: LanguageId) -> AnalyzerCapabilities`. This is a small, mechanical change that fixes both gaps at once and is needed today for the fallback tier regardless of anything daemon-related.
- **New `PrecisionUpgrader` trait**, sitting alongside `AnalyzerRegistry` (not replacing it): takes an already-produced result and optionally promotes its `CapabilityPrecision`, given an external resource. One `lifetime` field distinguishes how that resource is held: `PerCall` (§12's Clang/JVM tiers today — spawn, use once, discard), `PerInvocation` (constructed once, reused across all files in one CLI run — a cheap near-term win even before any daemon exists), and `Session` (reserved now, unimplemented until daemon work starts — held warm across multiple calls within one long-lived host process). Kotlin gets the JVM-subprocess upgrader promoting `Heuristic`→`Structural`; Scala the same via Scalameta; C/C++ via the Clang subprocess. When daemon work eventually happens, it's "write a new `PrecisionUpgrader` impl with `lifetime: Session`," not a pipeline redesign.
- **Where `Session` actually lives**: I checked — the spec already mentions a "future MCP surface" in passing (`projection.rs`, Part 3) without having built it. I'd phrase `Session` as "held warm across calls within whatever process embeds monokl for a while" rather than assuming monokl itself becomes a server — that covers both "monokl ships its own MCP server binary" and "monokl is a library inside a longer-lived host process," without committing to one deployment shape prematurely.
- **Kotlin/Scala refinement to §10**: rather than fully excluding them from the fallback tier, give them baseline `Heuristic`-only tree-sitter presence in the same fallback analyzer's config table (a 61.2%-accurate tree is still better than no tree for text/coarse-symbol search) — then the JVM-subprocess `PrecisionUpgrader` promotes qualifying results to `Structural` when the JVM is available. Cleaner three-layer story than "excluded, then separately has its own tier."
- **Cache**: extend the existing two-tier cache (mtime/size → blake3) to also memoize upgrader outcomes keyed by `(content_hash, upgrader_id, target)` — same invalidation machinery, no new cache infrastructure. This matters even for `PerCall` today, since repeated Clang subprocess spawns are exactly the unmeasured cost §11 flagged.
- **DX**: unavailable toolchain (`is_available()` check) degrades via the existing `Diagnostic`/informational-skip pattern already established elsewhere in the spec — no new error class, no daemon start/stop commands, no socket-file management, since `Session` isn't implemented yet and, when it is, rides whatever session lifecycle the host process already has.

**Alternatives considered, not recommended**: (a) trait hooks only, no lifecycle concept — rejected, it doesn't actually give §12's Clang/JVM tiers a home today, so it under-delivers on work already decided; (b) a standalone `monokld` background service with its own IPC protocol, mirroring rust-analyzer/gopls exactly — real proven pattern, but a lot of new engineering surface (process supervision, staleness detection, its own protocol) monokl doesn't need yet given its likely-dominant use case is already inside a long-lived agent/MCP session; worth keeping as a fallback if usage data ever shows heavy pure-CLI/batch traffic with no long-lived host.

Want me to write this into the spec — `LanguageId`/`capabilities()` changes into Parts 1/3, and the `PrecisionUpgrader`/lifecycle design plus the Kotlin/Scala refinement into a new §13 of `05-research-and-decisions.md`?
