payload.message:
We should research the daemon work to make sure we won't run into issues with our architecture down the line and need to make radical changes. Can we deploy agent teams and/or workflows to do a very deep research into the daemon arch and the tools needed/best suited for each language an how we can ingest the data into our models. Combinining what is common but not wathering down the distinctions between the langauges?

The goal is not to provide the same exact data for all languages but to enable LLMs/agents to understand the code as it is. In high quality, without errors or omissions which can cause halucinations or other issues.

<result>## Research: How real semantic tools signal (or fail to signal) uncertainty, and what monokl's PrecisionUpgrader should do about it

**1. Neither LSP nor SCIP have a confidence field — verified directly.** Fetching the LSP 3.17 spec directly: `Location {uri, range}`, `LocationLink {originSelectionRange?, targetUri, targetRange, targetSelectionRange}`, and `ResponseError {code, message, data?}` — no field anywhere expresses confidence, ambiguity, or "multiple candidates considered." Fetching SCIP's actual `scip.proto`: `Relationship {symbol, is_reference, is_implementation, is_type_definition, is_definition}` and `Occurrence {range/typed_range, symbol, symbol_roles, syntax_kind, diagnostics, enclosing_range}` — same result, confirming the earlier SCIP finding and showing LSP is no better. The one structural signal LSP carries *incidentally* rather than by design: `textDocument/definition` and `textDocument/references` are typed to return `Location | Location[] | LocationLink[] | null`. A response with cardinality >1 for a query that implies a single binding is a real, always-present ambiguity signal — but nearly every client discards it by taking `result[0]`.

**2. The common pattern across failure modes: internal degradation signals exist but are deliberately smoothed away before reaching the answer surface.** clangd is the clearest case, confirmed against Clang source: `RecoveryExpr` is a real, grep-able AST marker (`<recovery-expr>(...)`, per `StmtPrinter::VisitRecoveryExpr` and Clang's own AST-dump tests) — but clangd's `FindTarget` logic *deliberately resolves through it* to keep hover/go-to-definition looking normal, per explicit test comments like "no overload matches, but we have recovery-expr with the correct type." The degradation is invisible at the LSP layer by design intent, not oversight. TypeScript shows the same pattern differently: unresolved types collapse into the same `any` as a deliberately-untyped value, with no marker distinguishing "genuinely any" from "inference gave up." jdtls's classpath problems surface on a separate build/project-diagnostics channel rather than tainting the specific hover/definition response that used the broken classpath — a consumer reading only per-symbol answers never sees it. Kotlin and Scala are the informative *exceptions*: both eventually gained real, stable, machine-detectable sentinels precisely because the underlying ambiguity was too dangerous to leave silent — Kotlin's `T!` platform-type notation (documented, kotlinlang.org) and internal `ErrorType`/`ErrorTypeKind` (JetBrains/kotlin source); Scala's `diverging implicit expansion` string (Scala 2) and Scala 3's numbered `E172` "Ambiguous given instances" diagnostic. The pattern: whether a signal survives to the surface is a language-community design choice, not a property monokl can assume — so it must go looking for these sentinels itself rather than trusting a "successful" response.

**3. CHA/RTA/points-to literature gives a real, citable precedent, with one caveat.** The precision ladder is real and graded by cost/soundness tradeoff (Dean, Grove & Chambers, CHA, ECOOP 1995; Bacon & Sweeney, RTA, OOPSLA 1996; Andersen 1994; Steensgaard, POPL 1996), and Bravenboer & Smaragdakis's Doop (OOPSLA 2009) proves this is operational, not just conceptual — it exposes context-sensitivity as a selectable, named parameter, i.e., analysis metadata about which tier produced a result. The closest citable principle for "make the tier explicit rather than pretend uniform confidence" is Livshits et al., "In Defense of Soundiness: A Manifesto" (CACM 58(2), 2015): document unsound design choices rather than hide them. Note this is about design-time disclosure, not literal per-fact provenance tagging — applying it to per-fact granularity is our extrapolation, not an existing paper's claim.

**Actionable rules for monokl's PrecisionUpgrader:**
1. Treat response cardinality as a signal: `definition`/`references` returning >1 location for an ostensibly-unambiguous query → downgrade to `Structural`, emit a `Diagnostic` listing all candidates instead of silently taking `[0]`.
2. Maintain a per-backend sentinel table checked against *raw* diagnostics/type-strings, not the polished LSP layer: `<recovery-expr>`/dependent-type markers for Clang; `T!`/`ErrorType`/`ErrorTypeKind` or smart-cast diagnostic IDs for Kotlin; `E172`/"diverging implicit expansion" for Scala; co-occurring unresolved-import diagnostics on an `any`-typed hover for TS.
3. Cross-check project/build-level diagnostics each call (classpath, missing deps) — don't trust a clean per-symbol answer if the file's classpath is known-incomplete.
4. Classify by question type, not tool: closed-world nominal resolution with a language-guaranteed unique answer (Rust trait dispatch post-coherence, Java overload resolution) can earn `Exact`; open-world/coincidental-match questions (Go interface-implementer search, Kotlin extension resolution, C++ ADL with multiple viable candidates) cap at `Structural` even on compiler success, with the full candidate set attached as a `Diagnostic` rather than the tie-broken pick presented alone.
5. Never infer trust from response *shape* alone — since no protocol here carries confidence, silence from LSP/SCIP is absence of evidence, not evidence of correctness.

Relevant files: none in monokl's repo yet (research-only task, no code changes made).</result>

<result>## Research Findings: Multi-Backend Semantic Data Unification — Precedent Analysis

I verified primary sources directly (SCIP's actual protobuf schema, its design doc, CodeQL's real repo structure, rust-analyzer's documented LSP extensions) rather than relying on recalled summaries. One caveat up front: the shared web-search budget for this session was exhausted before I could run search queries, so everything below comes from direct WebFetch of primary documents, plus one narrative point I flag explicitly as unverified this session.

**1. Sourcegraph (LSIF → SCIP): unifies the reference graph, not the semantics.**
SCIP's own `scip.proto` and `docs/DESIGN.md` (github.com/sourcegraph/scip) show a deliberately narrow common core: a `Relationship` message with four boolean flags (`is_reference`, `is_implementation`, `is_type_definition`, `is_definition`) and an `Occurrence`/`SymbolInformation` pair keyed by a human-readable symbol string. That core generalizes honestly across languages because "X references/implements/defines Y" means roughly the same thing everywhere. Critically, SCIP does *not* try to unify deeper semantics. Its two real extension points are (a) `SymbolInformation.kind`, an enum that keeps growing per-language (`AbstractMethod` for Java/Kotlin, `Accessor` for Ruby, `Contract`/`Modifier` for Solidity) rather than staying generic, and (b) `documentation`/`Signature.language`, which are markdown/text blobs — meaning anything genuinely rich (a Rust trait bound, a Java checked-exception spec) degrades to unstructured prose, not structured data. DESIGN.md is explicit that indexers themselves stay per-language ("tooling for a language tends to be implemented in the same language... impractical to expect indexers to settle on a common implementation"), i.e., unification happens only at the wire format, never in the analysis itself. The lesson: SCIP's unification succeeded *because* it scoped down to navigation (def/ref/impl), not because it found a clever way to preserve full semantic richness — which is exactly the scope monokl's stated goal exceeds. (Sourcegraph's earlier live-language-server era being abandoned for operational/scaling reasons is a plausible history I hold from training but could not re-verify with a primary source this session after repeated 404s — treat that specific claim as unconfirmed, not load-bearing.)

**2. LSP / multi-language IDEs: common baseline + explicit typed escape hatch — the strongest direct precedent.**
VS Code's `vscode.languages.*` API (code.visualstudio.com/api/language-extensions/programmatic-language-features) defines ~18 standardized capabilities (hover, go-to-def, completions, etc.), and any server can implement them via LSP. But the protocol also has a built-in, exercised-at-scale extension mechanism: `experimental` capabilities and vendor-namespaced custom request methods. rust-analyzer is the concrete, documented example (rust-analyzer.github.io/book/contributing/lsp-extensions.html): it ships real custom methods — `rust-analyzer/expandMacro`, `rust-analyzer/viewMemoryLayout`, structural-search-replace, runnables — specifically because generic LSP hover/completion cannot carry macro expansion or memory layout facts. The doc even notes plain brace-matching needs "a real parser" for Rust's angle-bracket ambiguity, i.e., even trivial-seeming operations need language-specific logic. This is a production-proven pattern of exactly the shape monokl is considering: a stable generic core, plus optional, strongly-typed, per-language payloads that are additive, not a replacement.

**3. CodeQL: two coexisting patterns, both real, doing different jobs.**
CodeQL's own docs (codeql.github.com/codeql-standard-libraries) confirm it is genuinely per-language: separate libraries/dbschemes for C/C++, C#, Go, Java+Kotlin, JS/TS, Python, Ruby, Rust, Swift, with no shared universal schema — this maps directly onto monokl's existing `FileAnalysis`/`LangData` envelope-plus-variant shape, which is already the right template for *base* per-file analysis. But CodeQL also has a second pattern for cross-cutting concerns: `github/codeql`'s `shared/` directory (confirmed via repo listing) contains a language-agnostic `dataflow` module whose README states it provides "shared, language-agnostic CodeQL libraries" where the *algorithm* is generic and parameterized, and each language plugs in by implementing that interface with its own `Node`/CFG types. This is a shared-interface-with-per-language-implementation pattern, structurally different from a shared-data-schema pattern.

**Recommendation for monokl's daemon tier:**
Keep `FileAnalysis`/`LangData` unchanged for base per-file output — it already matches CodeQL's per-language-schema precedent correctly. 51	        "findings": "# Research: Precedent for unifying multi-language semantic data without flattening

## 1. Sourcegraph: LSIF → SCIP was a wire-format fix, not a semantic-unification fix

The LSIF→SCIP rewrite is often assumed to be about reconciling different languages' semantics. It wasn't. Sourcegraph's own SCIP announcement lists the actual drivers: LSIF's "heavy usage of opaque ID numbers to encode the graph structure" made it hard to debug and hard to index incrementally, it has no machine-readable schema ("LSIF doesn't come with a machine-readable schema, and the dynamic graph structure makes it difficult to encode LSIF payloads as a simple set of structs or classes"), and it was slow to produce/consume at scale. SCIP fixed this with human-readable string symbol IDs over Protobuf, yielding measurable wins (e.g. a 10x CI speedup for TypeScript indexing). None of this is about Rust traits vs. Java classpaths — it's encoding engineering (docs.sourcegraph.com / lsif.dev / sourcegraph.com/blog/announcing-scip).

The actual answer to "how do they preserve per-language richness" lives one level down, in SCIP's schema itself (github.com/sourcegraph/scip, scip.proto): a single shared envelope (`Document`, `SymbolInformation`, `Occurrence`, `Relationship`) is used for every language, but the leaf fields are deliberately *not* flattened. `SymbolInformation.kind` is one enum, yet it explicitly enumerates dozens of language-tailored variants rather than one generic "callable": `AbstractMethod` ("for Java, Kotlin etc."), `PureVirtualMethod` ("analogous to AbstractMethod, for C++"), `Accessor`/`MethodAlias`/`SingletonClass` (Ruby-specific), `Contract`/`Modifier` (Solidity-specific). The spec's own rationale: "kind provides a fine-grained category of a symbol, suitable for presenting information about the symbol's meaning in the language... A Java method would have the kind `Method` while a Go function would have the kind `Function`, even if the symbols for these use the same syntax for the descriptor." That's a mature, production system explicitly rejecting lowest-common-denominator collapse in favor of typed per-language leaves inside a shared structural envelope. `Document.language` is likewise a free string, not a closed enum, so new languages don't require a schema break.

## 2. LSP / VS Code: shared baseline + namespaced, gracefully-ignorable extensions

The LSP spec's own extension mechanism is the cleanest precedent for daemon-tier "upgrade" data specifically. It defines a small generic baseline (hover, go-to-def, references, completions, diagnostics — ~18 features) via `vscode.languages.*`, but explicitly reserves a namespace for anything a specific server needs beyond that: methods starting with `$/` (or vendor-prefixed custom methods) are "protocol implementation dependent and might not be implementable in all clients or servers," and a client/server that doesn't support one must simply return `MethodNotFound`. More importantly, the spec's general compatibility rule is: "Clients should ignore server capabilities they don't understand," and enum values are versioned so "the using side of an enumeration shouldn't fail on a value it doesn't know — it should simply ignore it." This is exactly the shape needed when a capability (like a daemon backend) may or may not be present: absence degrades silently instead of breaking the contract.

Semantic tokens push this further with an explicit subtyping model: providers are "free to define new types and modifiers and create a subtype of the standard types," and by declaring the standard type as a supertype, "theme styling rules for `type` will also apply to `templateType`" — i.e., a language-specific extension gets automatic, safe fallback behavior from consumers that only understand the base concept. (code.visualstudio.com/api/language-extensions/semantic-highlight-guide; microsoft.github.io LSP...

payload.message:
All 16 agents landed with real, verified findings. Here's the shape of it:

**The core design survived, but its return type didn't.** Every backend researched (9 languages deep, plus C#/Ruby/PHP) maps cleanly onto `PerCall`/`PerInvocation`/`Session` as a real cost ceiling — no language forced a fourth lifetime tier, which is good news for the architecture you sketched. But five independent per-language studies (Kotlin, Go, Scala, Rust, C++) converged, unprompted, on the same structural problem: real backends don't hand back "a precision tier to promote," they hand back candidate sets (Kotlin's `KaErrorCallInfo`), unreconciled dual algorithms (Go's confirmed-vs-candidate interface satisfaction), two independently-scored axes (Scala's Metals can give you the resolved implicit value without reliably explaining *why* it won), or genuinely new structured facts (Rust trait predicates, C++'s `RecoveryExpr`). Collapsing any of that into one enum bump would manufacture confidence the upstream tool never claimed — exactly the failure mode you were worried about.

Some standout findings:
- **TypeScript**: TS 7.0 (the native Go port) went **GA on July 8, 2026** — this is no longer speculative, and it changes the calculus: it's LSP-based, ships no embeddable API until 7.1, and `PerCall` is a non-starter for it (whole-program load dominates cost). `Session` is TS's *native* mode — VS Code never runs it any other way.
- **Python**: Pyrefly and `ty` are real, fast, Rust-*implemented* — but neither ships an embeddable Rust library. "Written in Rust" turned out not to mean "linkable into monokl's process."
- **Java**: `jdtls`'s OOM past ~3000 files is a hard crash, not a graceful slowdown — monokl needs an explicit project-size gate before ever attempting promotion, not "try and let it degrade."
- **Go/gopls**: never unifies its local (real) and global (fingerprint-approximated) interface-satisfaction checks — monokl shouldn't either.
- **Confidence signaling**: neither LSP nor SCIP has a confidence field, confirmed by direct spec inspection. The compilers *do* often know internally (Clang's `RecoveryExpr`, JDT's `isRecovered()`) — the protocol just throws it away. This needs a per-backend sentinel denylist, not a generic check.
- **Ruby's Sorbet** was the one real surprise: a compiled-in stdlib blob gives it near-zero fixed cold-start cost, making it the one backend where `PerCall` is actually cheap.

I've written the full design into a new **`docs/spec/06-daemon-architecture.md`** — the amended `PrecisionUpgrader` trait, the lifetime model (now nesting sub-resources and distinguishing owned-vs-attached, per the adversarial critiques), the `DaemonExtension` ingestion model (additive per-language payloads, following the SCIP/LSP/CodeQL precedent the research found), the confidence-signaling rules, and the full per-language table — linked from `README.md` and cross-referenced from `05-research-and-decisions.md` §14.

One thing I deliberately did **not** fold in this pass: the `LanguageId`/`capabilities()` trait signature fix (making them per-language rather than per-analyzer-instance, needed for §10's fallback tier to actually compile) touches ~10 real call sites across Parts 1 and 3 with real logic implications, not just a signature change — I don't want to rush that in as a drive-by inside an already-large response. Want me to do that as a focused follow-up next?

869	## 14. Daemon/session-mode architecture — moved to Part 6
870	
871	The open daemon/session-mode question (§4) got a dedicated, research-backed design pass: a
872	16-agent workflow (9 per-language backend studies — TypeScript, Rust, Python, Go, Java, Kotlin,
873	Scala, C/C++, and a combined C#/Ruby/PHP pass — 3 cross-cutting architecture questions, 3
874	adversarial critiques of a draft design, and one synthesis) stress-tested a proposed
875	`PrecisionUpgrader` trait against how real semantic backends for every language on this roadmap
876	actually behave, rather than designing it in the abstract. The result is substantial enough to
877	need its own file rather than another entry here, per this log's own convention for
878	substantial changes: see **[06-daemon-architecture.md](./06-daemon-architecture.md)** for the full
879	design — the trait shape, the lifetime model (and why it needs to nest and distinguish
880	owned-vs-attached), the `DaemonExtension` ingestion model, confidence-signaling rules, and the
881	per-language lifetime table.
882	
883	Headline result, in brief: the core shape survived (every backend maps onto `PerCall`/
884	`PerInvocation`/`Session` as a real cost ceiling, no language demanded a fourth tier), but the
885	trait's *return type* did not — five independent per-language studies (Kotlin, Go, Scala, Rust,
886	C++) converged on the same finding that "promote a bare `CapabilityPrecision`" destroys real
887	candidate sets, dual precision axes, and structured facts the underlying tools actually hand back.
888	Also produced: real backend identification per language (`typescript-go`/TS 7.0's new LSP server
889	went GA July 8, 2026, superseding the plain-tsserver assumption; Python's `Pyrefly`/`ty` are
890	genuinely Rust-implemented but still subprocess/LSP-integrated, not embeddable libraries; Java's
891	`jdtls` import step hard-crashes via OOM past ~3000 files, a real gate requirement, not a graceful
892	degradation; Kotlin's `kotlin-lsp` is real but still built on the same unstable-per-JetBrains
893	foundation already flagged, just hidden behind a heavier IDE-embedding shell); and a confirmed,
894	structural gap in both LSP and SCIP — neither protocol carries a confidence field, so the
895	compilers' own internal degradation signals (Clang's `RecoveryExpr`, JDT's `isRecovered()`)
896	have to be recovered via a per-backend sentinel table, not trusted from protocol silence.
897	
898	---
[/external_agent_tool_result]

Both done. Summary:

**Confidence-after-the-fact / enrichment design**: added as new §5 in `06-daemon-architecture.md`, a `PrecisionLedger` keyed by `ContentHash`, storing small `PrecisionAnnotation` entries (target pointer + precision + provenance + optional sentinel) — decoupled entirely from `FileAnalysis`'s own cache lifecycle. This directly answers what you asked:
- **After the fact**: eager (at analysis time, as already designed), lazy (a query needs more precision than cached and a backend happens to be available *now*), or retroactive (a separate sweep over already-analyzed files) — all three write into the same ledger without touching or invalidating the base analysis.
- **Enrichment of AST data**: it's explicitly modeled on LSP diagnostics and SCIP's `Occurrence` — a thin annotation layer over already-existing data, addressed by span/symbol/occurrence, never a copy of the AST.
- **Minimize required context**: annotations stay small (a pointer + tag, never the subtree), and full reasoning (why a sentinel fired, which candidates existed) is deliberately *not* inlined into every response — it lives behind the `explain` command Part 2 already specifies, so the default output stays within the existing token-budget discipline and only pays the cost when an agent actually asks "why."

**`LanguageId`/`capabilities()`**: done. `language_id()` → `languages() -> &[LanguageId]` plus a new `language_for(&self, path) -> Option<LanguageId>`; `capabilities()` → `capabilities(&self, language: LanguageId)`. Updated every real call site — `TsAnalyzer`/`RustAnalyzer` impls, `AnalyzerRegistry::supports_language`, and `query_support.rs`'s three helper functions — plus added the missing `LanguageId` variants (`C`, `Cpp`, `Bash`, `CSharp`, `Ruby`, `Php`, `Kotlin`, `Scala`) that §10/§12 already referenced but the enum never actually declared. Logged in `05-research-and-decisions.md` §1 as a real compile-correctness fix, consistent with how the two earlier compile-breaking gaps were handled.

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-confidence-runtime-impl" color="yellow" summary="Runtime-confirmation precedent + Rust combinator crates findings">
## 1. MonkeyType — verified against Instagram/MonkeyType source, not memory

Mechanism: uses `sys.setprofile` (a profiling hook, not `sys.settrace`) to interpose on function calls, returns, and generator yields during real test execution, recording the concrete types observed (github.com/Instagram/MonkeyType README).

Multi-type handling: in `monkeytype/stubs.py`, `shrink_traced_types()` collects every observed type per argument/return/yield across *all* traces into a set, then calls `shrink_types()` to reduce that set to a minimal-equivalent type — effectively a full union (e.g. collapsing to `Optional[X]` when `None` appears), not a "most common type" heuristic.

Confidence: none, explicitly. There is no frequency count, no "seen 95% of calls" score. The docs state annotations are "an informative first draft, to be checked and corrected by a developer" — the confidence mechanism is human review, not an automated score. This is real precedent for confirming a static guess with a *fundamentally different* signal source (execution rather than parsing), but it stops at "recording observed reality," it does not model confidence.

## 2. JS/TS equivalent

**TypeWiz** (github.com/urish/typewiz) is real and did exactly this — runtime monitoring during execution auto-annotates TS with observed types. But it's dead: last release Apr 2019, repo explicitly archived Oct 2021 with an owner note "as of 2021 I'm no longer working on TypeWiz." No actively maintained equivalent found. Treat as historical precedent only, not a tool to integrate with or model implementation details on.

## 3. pytype `reveal_type`

Confirmed real by reading pytype's own source (not docs, which don't mention it): `pytype/overlays/typing_overlay.py` registers `reveal_type`, backed by `RevealType` in `pytype/overlays/special_builtins.py`. Its `call()` does exactly one thing: `self.ctx.errorlog.reveal_type(...)` — prints the inferred type, mirroring mypy's `reveal_type`. No confidence/certainty field attached. So: no precedent, anywhere I could verify, for a static checker exposing a *confidence score* distinct from the type itself via this mechanism — `reveal_type` conventions across the ecosystem (mypy, pyright, pytype) all just answer "what type," never "how sure." This actually strengthens the case that monokl's sentinel-based indirect degradation approach is already ahead of common practice, not behind it.

## 4. Rust crates for combining signals — direct crates.io API checks

- **Dempster-Shafer**: `furtif-core` is real and does implement belief-function fusion (`EnumRule::DempsterShafer` in its examples), part of the `silx-furtif` monorepo (LGPL-3.0). But it's essentially abandoned: 2 GitHub stars, 1 fork, 5 total commits, last updated March 2024, only 16 recent downloads against 5,573 lifetime (a one-time burst, not ongoing use). Not viable as a dependency.
- **Bayesian**: the `bayesian` crate is real but is a naive-Bayes *text classifier* (with TF-IDF), not a general evidence-combinator — wrong shape for merging independent confidence signals.
- **General combinator utility**: nothing suitable. Note: crates.io's search API backfills low-relevance queries with unrelated popular/trending crates (verified directly — a TUI library, FrankenTUI, appeared identically across unrelated queries like "evidence combination" and "bayesian"); I had to filter those out by checking real relevance per hit. Beyond the fillers, the only genuine hits were ultra-niche and off-target: `flux-perception` ("confidence-weighted sensor fusion for autonomous agents," 15 downloads, one month old, unproven) and `tracktor`/`multisensor-lmb-filters-rs` (Random Finite Set / Labeled Multi-Bernoulli filters — real techniques, but for radar/robotics multi-object tracking, a different problem shape entirely).
- **Bottom line**: no mature, general-purpose Rust crate exists for this. This part is genuinely "write it yourself."

## 5. Recommendation

Don't reach for Dempster-Shafer or Bayesian combination — both require inputs monokl doesn't have (mass assignments over a frame of discernment, or calibrated priors/likelihoods from training data). Given only categorical tier, candidate-set size, sentinel-degradation, and cross-tier agreement, the defensible approach is a small **deterministic ordinal downgrade lattice**, not a numeric probability:

- Start from the categorical tier as the baseline (already the primary signal).
- Each secondary signal can only *downgrade* confidence one step, never algorithmically upgrade it — this avoids manufacturing false precision from what are really just fewer red flags, not more positive evidence. `candidate_set_size > 1` → downgrade one level (ambiguous); sentinel-degradation detected → downgrade one level.
- The one signal allowed to counteract a downgrade is genuine cross-tier agreement (two independently-derived analyzers concurring) — that's authentic corroboration from a different source, structurally the same kind of "confirm with a different signal" precedent MonkeyType embodies, just applied deterministically instead of via observed-frequency.
- Implement as a small enum + explicit combination function (~50-100 lines, unit-testable), explainable directly in `michi`-formatted output (e.g. "high, downgraded: ambiguous candidate set"). No library needed for any part of this.
</teammate-message>

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-confidence-academic" color="blue" summary="Confidence-scoring research findings, all citations verified">
All citations below verified directly (arXiv/DBLP/ACM/PDF full-text), not recalled from memory alone.

## 1. ML-based type/fact inference — confidence signal & calibration

- **DeepTyper** (Hellendoorn, Bird, Barr, Allamanis, "Deep Learning Type Inference," ESEC/FSE 2018, DOI 10.1145/3236024.3236051) — REAL, verified via full-text PDF. Confidence = raw softmax probability of the top RNN prediction (Eq. 1 in paper: `P(τ) = softmax(...)`). Used directly as a precision/recall threshold: paper's own numbers show a 90% confidence threshold yields only ~80% precision, and a 99% threshold yields ~95% precision (Fig. 5). That gap (0.90 stated confidence → 0.80 actual correctness) is a textbook calibration gap — but the paper never uses the word "calibration" and does no reliability-diagram/ECE/Brier analysis. It's an unexamined side effect visible only in their raw results table.
- **TypeWriter** (Pradel, Gousios, Liu, Chandra, arXiv 1912.03768 / ESEC-FSE 2020) — REAL. Notably does NOT lean on model confidence at all — it validates predictions by round-tripping candidate types through a real gradual type checker and search, i.e. confidence is established by an independent symbolic oracle, not trusted from the model.
- **Type4Py** (Mir, Latoskinas, Proksch, Gousios, ICSE 2022) — REAL. Uses nearest-neighbor similarity ranking (MRR), not a calibrated probability at all.
- **HiTyper** (Peng, Gao, Li, Gao, Lo, Zhang, Lyu, ICSE 2022) — REAL. Hybrid: static "type rejection rules" filter/veto neural predictions rather than trusting a confidence score.
- **OptTyper** (Vlassi Pandi, Barr, Gordon, Sutton, arXiv 2004.00348) — REAL (note: 4th author is Charles Sutton, not Lahiri). Combines hard logical constraints from a real type system with a learned "natural" signal via continuous optimization — again, a symbolic check gates the statistical one.

**Pattern across all five:** none does formal calibration analysis, and every single one that ships a real system pairs the statistical signal with an independent symbolic validator rather than trusting raw model confidence. That validator-gates-model pattern is structurally identical to what monokl's sentinel/categorical design already does.

## 2. Naturalness of software (lightweight, non-ML)

**Hindle, Barr, Gabel, Su, Devanbu, "On the Naturalness of Software," ICSE 2012 (CACM 59(5) reprint 2016, DOI 10.1145/2902362)** — REAL, verified via full-text. Core method: plain n-gram MLE frequency counting over a code corpus (no neural net, no training pipeline — literally token co-occurrence counting), scored via cross-entropy/perplexity. This is genuinely lightweight — could run over monokl's own indexed corpus. Lineage confirmed: **Ray, Hellendoorn, Godhane, Tu, Bacchelli, Devanbu, "On the 'Naturalness' of Buggy Code," ICSE 2016** (DBLP-verified) empirically shows buggy lines score measurably less "natural" (higher entropy) than clean code — a real, direct precedent for using a statistical anomaly score as a confidence-adjacent signal, entirely apart from any ML type-inference model.

## 3. Ensemble/multi-tool agreement

**Habib & Pradel, "How Many of All Bugs Do We Find? A Study of Static Bug Detectors," ASE 2018** (DBLP-verified, DOI 10.1145/3238147.3238213) and **Lenarduzzi, Pecorelli, Saarimäki, Lujan, Palomba, "A Critical Comparison on Six Static Analysis Tools," JSS 2023** (DBLP-verified) — both REAL. Both found LOW agreement/overlap between independent static analyzers on real code — tools mostly find disjoint issue sets. This actually argues against naive "multi-tool agreement = confidence" reasoning: absence of agreement is the norm even among sound analyzers, so agreement can't be treated as a reliable confidence multiplier without a lot more calibration work of its own.

## 4. Bayesian/lightweight combination specifically for program analysis

Did NOT find real Dempster-Shafer work specifically applied to program analysis/verification — the DS papers I found were generic (not program-analysis-specific), so don't claim that citation. What IS real and directly on point:
- **Kremenek & Engler, "Z-Ranking: Using Statistical Analysis to Counter the Impact of Static Analysis Approximations," SAS 2003** — REAL. Simple frequency/z-score statistical model ranking static-analysis error reports by true-positive likelihood, no ML training required.
- **Kremenek, Ashcraft, Yang, Engler, "Correlation Exploitation in Error Ranking," FSE 2004** (DOI 10.1145/1029894.1029909) — REAL. Uses Bayesian factor graphs + belief propagation to combine multiple correlated static-analysis signals into one ranking/confidence value. This is the best real precedent for "combine several independent uncertain signals into one number, for program analysis specifically" — and it's 20+ years old, lightweight, no deep learning.

## 5. Honest verdict for monokl

The literature does not push toward a neural/ML confidence score — quite the opposite. Every real ML type-inference system either lacks calibration analysis or (when scrutinized, as with DeepTyper's own numbers) shows raw confidence overstating true accuracy, and every shipped system ends up gating the statistical signal with an independent symbolic check anyway — which is what monokl's categorical + sentinel design already is. Multi-tool agreement is empirically rare even among correct analyzers, so it's a weak standalone signal. The one genuinely defensible "beyond categorical" move, if you want one, is the Kremenek/Engler-style lightweight statistical combination: take signals monokl already computes per-span (PrecisionAnnotation tier, sentinel-denylist hit, optionally a cheap n-gram/naturalness anomaly score from its own corpus) and combine them with simple classical statistics (a z-score-style ranking or a small Bayesian/log-odds combinator) into a single ordering — not a trained/calibrated absolute probability. That requires no training pipeline, no ML infra, and has direct 20-year precedent in program-analysis literature specifically (not borrowed from an unrelated ML domain). Recommendation: keep `CapabilityPrecision`'s categorical tiers as the ground truth users see; if you want finer ranking for internal use (e.g. sorting query results by trustworthiness), add a Z-Ranking-style combinator over existing signals rather than a numeric confidence score presented to users as a probability — presenting an uncalibrated number as if it were a calibrated probability would be actively misleading given what the ML literature itself shows about calibration gaps.
</teammate-message>

- **DeepTyper** (Hellendoorn, Bird, Barr, Allamanis, "Deep Learning Type Inference," ESEC/FSE 2018, DOI 10.1145/3236024.3236051) — REAL, verified via full-text PDF. Confidence = raw softmax probability of the top RNN prediction (Eq. 1 in paper: `P(τ) = softmax(...)`). Used directly as a precision/recall threshold: paper's own numbers show a 90% confidence threshold yields only ~80% precision, and a 99% threshold yields ~95% precision (Fig. 5). That gap (0.90 stated confidence → 0.80 actual correctness) is a textbook calibration gap — but the paper never uses the word "calibration" and does no reliability-diagram/ECE/Brier analysis. It's an unexamined side effect visible only in their raw results table.
- **TypeWriter** (Pradel, Gousios, Liu, Chandra, arXiv 1912.03768 / ESEC-FSE 2020) — REAL. Notably does NOT lean on model confidence at all — it validates predictions by round-tripping candidate types through a real gradual type checker and search, i.e. confidence is established by an independent symbolic oracle, not trusted from the model.
- **Type4Py** (Mir, Latoskinas, Proksch, Gousios, ICSE 2022) — REAL. Uses nearest-neighbor similarity ranking (MRR), not a calibrated probability at all.
- **HiTyper** (Peng, Gao, Li, Gao, Lo, Zhang, Lyu, ICSE 2022) — REAL. Hybrid: static "type rejection rules" filter/veto neural predictions rather than trusting a confidence score.
- **OptTyper** (Vlassi Pandi, Barr, Gordon, Sutton, arXiv 2004.00348) — REAL (note: 4th author is Charles Sutton, not Lahiri). Combines hard logical constraints from a real type system with a learned "natural" signal via continuous optimization — again, a symbolic check gates the statistical one.

**Pattern across all five:** none does formal calibration analysis, and every single one that ships a real system pairs the statistical signal with an independent symbolic validator rather than trusting raw model confidence. That validator-gates-model pattern is structurally identical to what monokl's sentinel/categorical design already does.

## 2. Naturalness of software (lightweight, non-ML)

**Hindle, Barr, Gabel, Su, Devanbu, "On the Naturalness of Software," ICSE 2012 (CACM 59(5) reprint 2016, DOI 10.1145/2902362)** — REAL, verified via full-text. Core method: plain n-gram MLE frequency counting over a code corpus (no neural net, no training pipeline — literally token co-occurrence counting), scored via cross-entropy/perplexity. This is genuinely lightweight — could run over monokl's own indexed corpus. Lineage confirmed: **Ray, Hellendoorn, Godhane, Tu, Bacchelli, Devanbu, "On the 'Naturalness' of Buggy Code," ICSE 2016** (DBLP-verified) empirically shows buggy lines score measurably less "natural" (higher entropy) than clean code — a real, direct precedent for using a statistical anomaly score as a confidence-adjacent signal, entirely apart from any ML type-inference model.

## 3. Ensemble/multi-tool agreement

**Habib & Pradel, "How Many of All Bugs Do We Find? A Study of Static Bug Detectors," ASE 2018** (DBLP-verified, DOI 10.1145/3238147.3238213) and **Lenarduzzi, Pecorelli, Saarimäki, Lujan, Palomba, "A Critical Comparison on Six Static Analysis Tools," JSS 2023** (DBLP-verified) — both REAL. Both found LOW agreement/overlap between independent static analyzers on real code — tools mostly find disjoint issue sets. This actually argues against naive "multi-tool agreement = confidence" reasoning: absence of agreement is the norm even among sound analyzers, so agreement can't be treated as a reliable confidence multiplier without a lot more calibration work of its own.

## 4. Bayesian/lightweight combination specifically for program analysis

Did NOT find real Dempster-Shafer work specifically applied to program analysis/verification — the DS papers I found were generic (not program-analysis-specific), so don't claim that citation. What IS real and directly on point:
- **Kremenek & Engler, "Z-Ranking: Using Statistical Analysis to Counter the Impact of Static Analysis Approximations," SAS 2003** — REAL. Simple frequency/z-score statistical model ranking static-analysis error reports by true-positive likelihood, no ML training required.
- **Kremenek, Ashcraft, Yang, Engler, "Correlation Exploitation in Error Ranking," FSE 2004** (DOI 10.1145/1029894.1029909) — REAL. Uses Bayesian factor graphs + belief propagation to combine multiple correlated static-analysis signals into one ranking/confidence value. This is the best real precedent for "combine several independent uncertain signals into one number, for program analysis specifically" — and it's 20+ years old, lightweight, no deep learning.

## 5. Honest verdict for monokl

The literature does not push toward a neural/ML confidence score — quite the opposite. Every real ML type-inference system either lacks calibration analysis or (when scrutinized, as with DeepTyper's own numbers) shows raw confidence overstating true accuracy, and every shipped system ends up gating the statistical signal with an independent symbolic check anyway — which is what monokl's categorical + sentinel design already is. Multi-tool agreement is empirically rare even among correct analyzers, so it's a weak standalone signal. The one genuinely defensible "beyond categorical" move, if you want one, is the Kremenek/Engler-style lightweight statistical combination: take signals monokl already computes per-span (PrecisionAnnotation tier, sentinel-denylist hit, optionally a cheap n-gram/naturalness anomaly score from its own corpus) and combine them with simple classical statistics (a z-score-style ranking or a small Bayesian/log-odds combinator) into a single ordering — not a trained/calibrated absolute probability. That requires no training pipeline, no ML infra, and has direct 20-year precedent in program-analysis literature specifically (not borrowed from an unrelated ML domain). Recommendation: keep `CapabilityPrecision`'s categorical tiers as the ground truth users see; if you want finer ranking for internal use (e.g. sorting query results by trustworthiness), add a Z-Ranking-style combinator over existing signals rather than a numeric confidence score presented to users as a probability — presenting an uncalibrated number as if it were a calibrated probability would be actively misleading given what the ML literature itself shows about calibration gaps.
</teammate-message>

All four items verified against primary sources (not memory). Note: general WebSearch was exhausted early, so everything below came from direct WebFetch/curl against docs, real rule/query files, and PDFs.

**1. CodeQL `@precision` — real, per-query, categorical.**
Confirmed via codeql.github.com/docs/writing-codeql-queries/metadata-for-codeql-queries/: the tag takes exactly four values, `low`/`medium`/`high`/`very-high`, is set once by the query author in the `.ql` file header, and per the docs "indicates the percentage of query results that are true positives." Its only documented effect: "this, along with `@problem.severity`, determines how the results are displayed on GitHub." I explicitly checked whether `@precision` also gates query-suite membership (default vs. `security-extended` vs. `security-and-quality`) — the metadata page makes no such claim, so I'm not asserting it; what's verified is display-only, rule-author-declared, not computed per finding.

**2. Semgrep `confidence` — real, documented, but for security rules only, still rule-level.**
Not in the core rule-syntax reference, but confirmed real in Semgrep's own rule-contribution guide (docs.semgrep.dev/contributing/contributing-to-semgrep-rules-repository) and in actual shipped rules (fetched two directly from github.com/semgrep/semgrep-rules): e.g. `directly-returned-format-string.yaml` has `metadata: { likelihood: HIGH, impact: MEDIUM, confidence: MEDIUM }`; `detect-openai.yaml` has `confidence: LOW`. Values are HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW, each with explicit guidance — HIGH/MEDIUM are described as "useful in CI/CD pipelines," LOW is "audit style." So it's author-declared per rule, sits alongside separate `likelihood`/`impact` fields, and its real documented purpose is curating which rules go into CI-blocking vs. audit-only rulesets — not a live per-instance score.

**3. Facebook — partially verified, be aware of a gap.**
Distefano, Fähndrich, Logozzo, O'Hearn, "Scaling Static Analyses at Facebook," CACM 62(8):62-70, 2019, DOI 10.1145/3338112 — real, confirmed via Crossref/Unpaywall/DBLP and its abstract on research.facebook.com (Infer + Zoncolan run as bots on code-review diffs, "100 thousand reported issues fixed"). I could NOT get the actual body text — both dl.acm.org and cacm.acm.org are behind a Cloudflare challenge I couldn't clear. I also found a closely related earlier paper by overlapping authors, Calcagno/Distefano/O'Hearn et al., "Moving Fast with Software Verification" (NASA Formal Methods 2015, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-17524-9_1), which is almost certainly where the diff-time/feedback methodology is spelled out, but it's Springer-paywalled and its EPTCS companion listing is abstract-only. So: treat the specific "engineer accept/dismiss recalibrates warnings" mechanism as **plausible but unverified from primary text** for Facebook specifically — don't cite it as confirmed.

**4. Google Tricorder — fully verified, and this is your strongest citation.**
Sadowski, Aftandilian, Eagle, Miller-Cushon, Jaspan, "Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google," CACM 61(4):58-66, 2018 (PDF: storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/pubtools/4365.pdf — I read the full text). This is exactly the real, shipped, production mechanism the design question is after: every finding shown in code review has a "Please fix" and a "Not useful" button; the team computes the ratio of not-useful to please-fix clicks per analyzer, and "if the ratio for an analyzer goes above 10%, the Tricorder team disables the analyzer until the author(s) improve it." Separately, they set fixed a priori thresholds by workflow stage, not by finding: compiler-level checks require 0% effective false positives, code-review-level checks are allowed up to 10%. This is categorical + rule/analyzer-level, tuned by a slow human-feedback loop — never a per-instance number.

**Synthesis for monokl.** The dominant, actually-shipped pattern across all three tools that I could fully verify is: **categorical, author-declared, rule-level precision/confidence tags** (CodeQL's 4-value `@precision`, Semgrep's HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW `confidence`) **plus a separate, slow-moving, human-feedback loop that retunes at the rule/analyzer level, not per finding** (Google's disable-if->10%-not-useful mechanism is the one I could fully confirm with quotes; Facebook's Infer/Zoncolan almost certainly does something analogous but I couldn't verify the specifics). I found zero evidence in any of these three tools of a live, per-instance, numeric confidence score attached to individual findings — every real mechanism operates at the rule/checker level. That directly supports monokl's existing design: keep the categorical `Unsupported/Heuristic/Structural/Exact` tag as the per-result label (closest real analogue: CodeQL's `@precision`, but monokl's is backend/operation-tagged rather than purely query-author-declared, which is arguably better since it's grounded in what actually ran). If you want to add a Google/CodeQL-style refinement later, the defensible move is a slow-moving suppression/re-tag loop keyed on backend+operation combination (not per-finding) — e.g., "Structural via clangd without a compilation database" gets systematically down-weighted if users repeatedly reject/ignore its results — rather than inventing a numeric per-finding score that no verified production tool actually ships.
</teammate-message>

All three threads converge on the same answer, which is itself a strong signal — three independent research angles (academic ML literature, industry-shipped tools, runtime/implementation options) all arrived at the same conclusion without coordinating. Let me synthesize directly against your questions.

**How would we compute/gather it — some from the AST, some after the fact?** Yes, cleanly split:
- **From the AST/parse, at analysis time**: the base categorical tier (`Heuristic`/`Structural`/`Exact` — already what `CapabilityPrecision` is) and candidate-set size (1 resolution vs. N ambiguous candidates — a structural fact straight out of the symbol table).
- **After the fact**: sentinel-detected degradation (consulting an external tool's raw output for known fallback markers — already designed), and, if ever added, a slow-moving reliability signal per backend+operation gathered over many runs (see Tricorder below) — genuinely decoupled from any single file's analysis, which is exactly why the `PrecisionLedger` from last time is the right shape for it.

**What tools/libraries — checked, and the honest answer is "none, write it yourself."** No viable Rust crate exists for combining uncertain signals (Dempster-Shafer crate is essentially abandoned; the "bayesian" crate is a text classifier, wrong shape). That's fine — the right technique is small and deterministic, not something a library would help with anyway.

**What does the state of the art actually say — this is the important part.** It says *don't* build a numeric confidence score shown to agents as a probability:
- Every real ML type-inference system checked (DeepTyper, TypeWriter, Type4Py, HiTyper, OptTyper) either skips calibration entirely or — when you look at its own published numbers — shows a real gap between stated confidence and actual accuracy. And every one of them, without exception, still gates the statistical signal with an independent symbolic check rather than trusting it — which is structurally what monokl's sentinel design already does.
- Multi-tool agreement is empirically *rare even among correct analyzers* (two separate verified studies) — so cross-tier agreement is real corroboration when it happens, but its absence isn't a red flag and shouldn't be over-weighted.
- Every real shipped tool checked (CodeQL's `@precision`, Semgrep's `confidence`) uses **categorical, rule-author-declared tags** — exactly what `CapabilityPrecision` already is — never a live per-finding score.
- Google's Tricorder (fully verified, full paper read) has the one real, production-proven feedback mechanism: a "Please fix" / "Not useful" button per finding, with the *ratio* tracked **per analyzer**, and an analyzer auto-disabled once its not-useful rate crosses 10%. Categorical, slow-moving, tuned at the rule/backend level — never per-instance.

**Concrete recommendation, converging all three threads**: keep `CapabilityPrecision` categorical (already right). Compute per-result precision via a small deterministic **ordinal downgrade lattice** — start from the categorical tier, let ambiguous candidate sets and sentinel hits each downgrade one step, let genuine cross-tier agreement counteract one downgrade (real signal, just not a strong one) — no numeric score, ~50-100 lines, unit-testable. Separately, add a Tricorder-style slow feedback loop: track a reliability ratio per `(backend, operation)` pair over time (not per-finding), and let a chronically-unreliable combination get systematically down-weighted — the one long-term-learning mechanism with genuine production precedent. And one optional, real, lightweight extra signal worth keeping in your pocket: n-gram "naturalness" scoring (Hindle et al., real, no ML training needed, just corpus frequency counting) — statistically anomalous code measurably correlates with bugs, so it's a legitimate additional downgrade signal if you ever want one, without committing to it now.

Writing this into Part 6 now.

- Every real shipped tool checked (CodeQL's `@precision`, Semgrep's `confidence`) uses **categorical, rule-author-declared tags** — exactly what `CapabilityPrecision` already is — never a live per-finding score.
- Google's Tricorder (fully verified, full paper read) has the one real, production-proven feedback mechanism: a "Please fix" / "Not useful" button per finding, with the *ratio* tracked **per analyzer**, and an analyzer auto-disabled once its not-useful rate crosses 10%. Categorical, slow-moving, tuned at the rule/backend level — never per-instance.

**Concrete recommendation, converging all three threads**: keep `CapabilityPrecision` categorical (already right). Compute per-result precision via a small deterministic **ordinal downgrade lattice** — start from the categorical tier, let ambiguous candidate sets and sentinel hits each downgrade one step, let genuine cross-tier agreement counteract one downgrade (real signal, just not a strong one) — no numeric score, ~50-100 lines, unit-testable. Separately, add a Tricorder-style slow feedback loop: track a reliability ratio per `(backend, operation)` pair over time (not per-finding), and let a chronically-unreliable combination get systematically down-weighted — the one long-term-learning mechanism with genuine production precedent. And one optional, real, lightweight extra signal worth keeping in your pocket: n-gram "naturalness" scoring (Hindle et al., real, no ML training needed, just corpus frequency counting) — statistically anomalous code measurably correlates with bugs, so it's a legitimate additional downgrade signal if you ever want one, without committing to it now.

Writing this into Part 6 now.

883	## 14. Daemon/session-mode architecture — moved to Part 6
884	
885	The open daemon/session-mode question (§4) got a dedicated, research-backed design pass: a
886	16-agent workflow (9 per-language backend studies — TypeScript, Rust, Python, Go, Java, Kotlin,
887	Scala, C/C++, and a combined C#/Ruby/PHP pass — 3 cross-cutting architecture questions, 3
888	adversarial critiques of a draft design, and one synthesis) stress-tested a proposed
889	`PrecisionUpgrader` trait against how real semantic backends for every language on this roadmap
890	actually behave, rather than designing it in the abstract. The result is substantial enough to
891	need its own file rather than another entry here, per this log's own convention for
892	substantial changes: see **[06-daemon-architecture.md](./06-daemon-architecture.md)** for the full
893	design — the trait shape, the lifetime model (and why it needs to nest and distinguish
894	owned-vs-attached), the `DaemonExtension` ingestion model, a `PrecisionLedger` for attaching
895	confidence after the fact (eagerly, lazily, or retroactively, decoupled from `FileAnalysis`'s own
896	cache lifecycle), confidence-signaling rules, and the per-language lifetime table.
897	
898	Headline result, in brief: the core shape survived (every backend maps onto `PerCall`/
899	`PerInvocation`/`Session` as a real cost ceiling, no language demanded a fourth tier), but the
900	trait's *return type* did not — five independent per-language studies (Kotlin, Go, Scala, Rust,
901	C++) converged on the same finding that "promote a bare `CapabilityPrecision`" destroys real
902	candidate sets, dual precision axes, and structured facts the underlying tools actually hand back.
903	Also produced: real backend identification per language (`typescript-go`/TS 7.0's new LSP server
904	went GA July 8, 2026, superseding the plain-tsserver assumption; Python's `Pyrefly`/`ty` are
905	genuinely Rust-implemented but still subprocess/LSP-integrated, not embeddable libraries; Java's
906	`jdtls` import step hard-crashes via OOM past ~3000 files, a real gate requirement, not a graceful
907	degradation; Kotlin's `kotlin-lsp` is real but still built on the same unstable-per-JetBrains
908	foundation already flagged, just hidden behind a heavier IDE-embedding shell); and a confirmed,
909	structural gap in both LSP and SCIP — neither protocol carries a confidence field, so the
910	compilers' own internal degradation signals (Clang's `RecoveryExpr`, JDT's `isRecovered()`)
911	have to be recovered via a per-backend sentinel table, not trusted from protocol silence.
912	
913	---
914

# Research & Decisions Log (pre-implementation)

Findings from a competitive deep-dive (colbymchenry/codegraph), follow-on research into ranking,
eval methodology, scale targets, and language support (Rust/Python/Go/Java), and a Rust-idiom
audit of the verbatim code in Parts 1-4 — run before any of this spec gets built, so assumptions
get stress-tested on paper instead of in a PR review. Two compile-breaking gaps this audit found
(a `LanguageAnalyzer` trait missing methods it's called with, and four `MonoklError` variants
that were constructed but never declared) are fixed directly in
[01-core-architecture.md](./01-core-architecture.md) and
[03-multi-language-platform.md](./03-multi-language-platform.md) — this log records why.

Part of the [monokl spec](./README.md).

---

# Part 5: Pre-implementation research amendments

> Added before any of Parts 1-4 have been built. A competitive deep-dive against
> colbymchenry/codegraph (a mature, production multi-language code-intelligence tool) plus
> targeted follow-on research were used to stress-test this spec's assumptions before they
> calcify into code. Two categories below: fixes already applied directly to the sections
> above, and decisions/open tracks that change what future PRs should do.

## 1. Fixes applied in this document

- **§Python fidelity, problem 5** (type annotation resolution): `CapabilityPrecision::Approximate`
  was not a real variant of the enum defined in §11 (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural <
  Exact`). Corrected to `CapabilityPrecision::Heuristic`.
- **§Section 6, `STOP_WORDS`**: added `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe`
  — near-universal Rust tokens the original TS/Rust-tuned list omitted, found by tracing the
  tokenizer's actual splitting rules against real Rust source rather than assuming coverage.
- **`LanguageAnalyzer` trait, §11**: `language_id(&self) -> LanguageId` and
  `capabilities(&self) -> AnalyzerCapabilities` were both fixed at one value per analyzer
  *instance* — a real gap once §10's generic fallback-tier analyzer owns several languages with
  genuinely different ceilings in one instance (C reaches `Structural`, C++ is capped at
  `Heuristic`). Without this fix, §10's own design doesn't actually compile against the trait it's
  specified to implement. Fixed to `languages(&self) -> &[LanguageId]`, a new
  `language_for(&self, path: &Utf8Path) -> Option<LanguageId>` resolving which specific language a
  path maps to, and `capabilities(&self, language: LanguageId) -> AnalyzerCapabilities`. Every call
  site in `03-multi-language-platform.md` updated to match: `TsAnalyzer`/`RustAnalyzer`'s impls,
  `AnalyzerRegistry::supports_language`, and `query_support.rs`'s `resolve_canonical_source`/
  `add_precision_diagnostic`/`require_precision_capability`. `LanguageId` itself gained the §10
  fallback-tier variants (`C`, `Cpp`, `Bash`, `CSharp`, `Ruby`, `Php`) and the §10-refined
  `Heuristic`-only Kotlin/Scala variants, none of which existed on the enum before this pass despite
  being referenced throughout §10/§12.

## 2. Adopted, not yet implemented

- **Add `oxc_semantic` to the `lang-ts` feature's dependency set**, versioned in lockstep with
  `oxc_parser`/`oxc_ast`/`oxc_span`/`oxc_allocator` (same version string — no separate
  compatibility matrix). `SemanticBuilder::build(&program)` runs against the same per-file
  `Allocator` arena the parser already uses and produces a `Semantic` result (scope tree +
  symbol table: `SymbolId`/`ScopeId`/`Reference`, real shadowing/hoisting/TDZ-aware binding).
  This replaces regex/text-scanned local-usage resolution in `refs`/`definition` with genuine
  scope-aware resolution for within-file references — closing the exact class of technical debt
  codegraph's own maintainers flag as their worst (a 20+-resolver heuristic confidence cascade).
  `oxc_semantic` is file-scoped: it does not replace `oxc_resolver` for cross-file specifier
  resolution, it upgrades what feeds into ...
[/external_agent_tool_result]

This replaces regex/text-scanned local-usage resolution in `refs`/`definition` with genuine scope-aware resolution for within-file references — closing the exact class of technical debt codegraph's own maintainers flag as their worst (a 20+-resolver heuristic confidence cascade). `oxc_semantic` is file-scoped: it does not replace `oxc_resolver` for cross-file specifier resolution, it upgrades what feeds into that combination. Output must be converted to owned data before the arena drops, same discipline as the AST conversion already documented in §17.
- **Build an eval harness before further ranking/tuning decisions are made on faith.** BM25's `K1=1.5`/`B=0.5` and the token-budget defaults are carried over from Probe's prior tuning (§29) and are unvalidated for monokl specifically. Minimum viable harness: two layers, not one — (a) a deterministic retrieval eval (RepoBench-R- or CodeSearchNet-style recall@k/MRR) run on every commit, and (b) a properly-powered agent A/B (model/effort pinned and logged, ≥5 runs per condition reporting median + IQR, ≥10 repos with a task list frozen before either arm runs). - **Add worked query examples and a tolerant natural-language fallback** to the `search` command's tool-facing description. Embeddings find *vibes*. monokl parses your code with a real compiler-grade parser ([OXC](https://oxc.rs) for TS/JS, [`ra_ap_syntax`](https://crates.io/crates/ra_ap_syntax) for Rust) and answers structural questions: ``` mnkl search "validatePrice" --path src/ mnkl refs Button --root . --include-tests mnkl definition useCart --root . mnkl dependents src/utils/format.ts --root . mnkl explain src/components/Button.tsx ``` Text search ranks by BM25 and node-type relevance, not string distance. `refs`/`definition` resolve real bindings, not name matches. `dependents` walks an actual import graph. Everything returns structured JSON by default, with a JSON Schema per result type — built to be a tool an agent calls, not a report a human scrolls through. ## Why Existing code-search-for-agents tools mostly fall into two camps: fast-but-fuzzy (grep, embeddings) or precise-but-heavyweight (a full language server, a persistent daemon). monokl aims at the middle — real AST parsing without the cost of running a language server, no persistent index to keep warm, cache-friendly enough that repeat queries in one session don't re-pay the parse cost. Embeddings find *vibes*. monokl parses your code with a real compiler-grade parser ([OXC](https://oxc.rs) for TS/JS, [`ra_ap_syntax`](https://crates.io/crates/ra_ap_syntax) for Rust) and answers structural questions: ``` mnkl search "validatePrice" --path src/ mnkl refs Button --root . --include-tests mnkl definition useCart --root . mnkl dependents src/utils/format.ts --root . mnkl explain src/components/Button.tsx ``` Text search ranks by BM25 and node-type relevance, not string distance. `refs`/`definition` resolve real bindings, not name matches. `dependents` walks an actual import graph. Everything returns structured JSON by default, with a JSON Schema per result type — built to be a tool an agent calls, not a report a human scrolls through. ## Why Existing code-search-for-agents tools mostly fall into two camps: fast-but-fuzzy (grep, embeddings) or precise-but-heavyweight (a full language server, a persistent daemon). monokl aims at the middle — real AST parsing without the cost of running a language server, no persistent index to keep warm, cache-friendly enough that repeat queries in one session don't re-pay the parse cost. The spec is about as hardened as pre-implementation research can reasonably make it — Parts 1-4 are reconstruction-grade, Part 5 has fourteen-plus research threads closing every open design question that surfaced, Part 6 has a validated future-daemon shape waiting in the wings. Continuing to research now would hit diminishing returns; the next real signal comes from writing code and finding out where the spec is wrong in practice, not from more analysis on paper.

Concretely, that means: initialize git (still pending from earlier in this session, and nothing past this point should happen without version control), scaffold the actual Cargo workspace per Part 1, then implement in the order the spec itself implies — core types/error handling/cache first, since everything else depends on them, via TDD against the fixtures `docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md` already specifies, per CLAUDE.md's own mandated skill order (`writing-plans` for the implementation plan, `test-driven-development` per module). Scope it to Parts 1-4 as literally specified; Part 5's still-unbuilt "adopted" items (the tree-sitter fallback tier, the real-compiler-frontend tier, the eval harness) and all of Part 6 stay deferred — they're designed, not blocking, and pulling them forward now would be scope creep against a v0.1.0 that hasn't been built yet at all.

The main tradeoff worth naming: this is a genuinely large spec (six parts, thousands of lines), so "start implementing" is itself a multi-week undertaking, not a single sitting — worth using `writing-plans` to break it into a real sequence rather than diving into code cold.

Want me to kick off git init and the Cargo workspace scaffold, or start with the implementation plan first?

1. Primary Request and Intent:
   This is a continuation of an extremely long spec-development session for "monokl," a Rust crate providing AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents (part of the "orin-axi" suite alongside Firkin/Lumen/Pulse, all meant to depend on shared crate `michi`). Within the portion of the conversation covered here, the user's explicit requests, in order, were:
   - Confirm/approve proceeding with four research threads flagged earlier (stack-graphs/tree-sitter-graph, ast-grep, difftastic, CHA/RTA/k-CFA literature) to further ground monokl's spec.
   - "Verify the representative-codebases list, then write it into 05" — demanding real verification (not just names) of a proposed eval-harness corpus.
   - "Should we consider kotlin support? swift? what android uses?" — exploratory language-roadmap question.
   - "What are the top languages for usage that we should consider? What corpus is a good sample of that language's features in production use?" then, mid-turn: "We should consider performance and how we can best optimize it for all of the languages. Other tree-sitter supported languages?"
   - "This looks much better right? What should we adjust in our spec to account for these changes? How can we prepare the architecture for the future daemon work? Think deeply about the architecture, performance and DX are huge parts of this right?"
   - "We should research the daemon work to make sure we won't run into issues with our architecture down the line and need to make radical changes. Can we deploy agent teams and/or workflows to do a very deep research into the daemon arch and the tools needed/best suited for each language an how we can ingest the data into our models. Combinining what is common but not wathering down the distinctions between the langauges? The goal is not to provide the same exact data for all languages but to enable LLMs/agents to understand the code as it is. In high quality, without errors or omissions which can cause halucinations or other issues." — explicit opt-in to multi-agent Workflow orchestration.
   - "How do we leverage this enrichment, anootation and confidence score? How would we compute or gather such information? Would some of it come from the AST? Some added after the fact? What tools/utilities/libraries and techniques should we use? What does the state of the art say? What does research say?"
   - "Shall we tackle the langID + capabilities now?" (asked alongside the above) — confirming a previously-deferred mechanical trait fix should be done now.
   - "Don't forget that MD files should not be artificially wrapped, also note that we want the languge to be devoid of AI word salad, slop and filler words. We want to document the spec not the historical account of how that has changed as we've done more research. Historical account is not necessary here is it?" — a durable style/process rule for all spec writing going forward: never hard-wrap markdown, avoid AI slop/filler, and write new spec sections (especially Part 6) as direct specification rather than a narrative of the research process — while `05-research-and-decisions.md` intentionally keeps its historical/decision-log nature, since that is its established, by-design purpose.

No numeric/ML confidence score.

payload.message:
Mise + just is the better call here. Mise has a much larger plugin registry and more battle-tested Rust/Node version pinning; proto (moonrepo's tool) is newer and really shines when paired with `moon` for full monorepo orchestration, which monokl doesn't need — it's a single Rust crate with a TS/JS fixture-testing dependency, not a polyglot monorepo. `just` gives you a plain, dependency-free task runner for the common verbs (`just test`, `just bench`, `just fixtures`) without inventing shell-script sprawl.

Concrete setup sequence I'd recommend:

1. `git init` — nothing has been versioned yet; this project has nine markdown files and a research history worth protecting.
2. `.mise.toml` pinning `rust` (stable, or whatever MSRV Part 1 settled on if it did) and `node`/`pnpm` (for the TS/JS fixtures under `tests/fixtures/small-ts/`).
3. `Cargo.toml` workspace scaffold matching Part 1's crate layout.
4. `justfile` with the obvious verbs: `build`, `test`, `bench`, `fixtures`, `fmt`.
5. `pnpm` only inside the fixtures directory (it's test data, not a package monokl ships) — `pnpm init` there if it isn't already set up.

2	
3	The `AnalyzerRegistry`, the real Rust analyzer (`ra_ap_syntax`), pipeline modularization, PR-aware git scopes, the capability/precision model that lets unsupported languages degrade gracefully instead of erroring, and the human-readable presentation layer.
4	
5	Part of the [monokl spec](./README.md). Builds on [01-core-architecture.md](./01-core-architecture.md) and [02-inspection-and-analysis.md](./02-inspection-and-analysis.md).
6

8	
9	# Part 3: Phase 2+ Additions (0.4.0 → 0.7.0)
10	
11	> Added since Part 2. Multi-language architecture, analyzer registry, Rust parity via ra-ap-syntax, pipeline modularization, PR-aware scopes, capability-driven query, agent tool contracts.
12	
13	## 1. Overview of Phase 2+ changes
14	
15	Monokl Phase 2+ spans versions 0.4.0 → 0.7.0 of the `monokl` crate. It is approximately 8 PRs of work that transforms monokl from a single-language (TypeScript/JavaScript) AST search tool into a multi-language, capability-driven, mixed-workspace code intelligence platform.
16	
17	Major themes:
18	
19	1. **Multi-language architecture** (0.5.0). A new `AnalyzerRegistry` dispatches per-file to language-specific `LanguageAnalyzer` implementations. First-class Rust support via `ra-ap-syntax` (rust-analyzer's syntax library). The CLI/library can now ship `--no-default-features --features lang-rs,cli` (Rust-only) as well as the full TS+Rust default.
20	2. **Library contract & focused agent commands** (0.4.0). New `deps`, `deps-from`, `classify`, `migration-surface` commands. Field projection (`--only`/`--fields`) across `inspect`, `search`, `patterns`, `refs`, with `--format json|minimal|schema`. Inspect kind-filtering moved into the `InspectOptions` library contract.
21	3. **Pipeline modularization**. `pipeline.rs` split into `pipeline/{search, symbols, deps, graph, inspecting, session}.rs`. Workspace `WorkspaceSession` cached across calls for analyzer registry + standard index reuse.
22	4. **PR-aware review scopes** (0.6.0). New `git_scope` module backed by `gix`. `QueryScope::{FullRepo, ChangedFiles, ChangedLines, ImpactedNeighbors}` for `search`/`symbols`/`refs`/`definition`/`dependents`. PR semantics use `merge-base(base, head)..head`; `diff` keeps explicit snapshot semantics. Changed-line filtering and one-hop import-graph neighbor expansion.
23	5. **Human presentation layer** (0.6.0). `--format`, `--profile`, `--detail`, `--color` global flags. Text renderers for `search`, `symbols`, `refs`, `definition`, `dependents`, `inspect`, `deps`, `deps-from`, `classify`, `migration-surface`, `diff`, `explain`, `coverage`. Mermaid rendering for small `dependents` graphs. JSON remains the canonical agent contract.
24	6. **Capability-driven query behavior** (0.7.0). `search`, `inspect`, `dependents`, `refs`, `definition` now use shared analyzer capability policy. Unsupported surfaces emit explicit `Skipped` diagnostics; approximate-precision analyzers emit consistent warnings. `symbols`' classified-imports omission is keyed off `AnalyzerCapabilities::classified_imports` rather than a TS check.
25	7. **Cache architecture rework**. `DashMap`-only hot path in `analysis/cache.rs` (no more `Mutex<CacheMeta>`/`fs2` advisory locks at the in-memory layer). Disk persistence keys on content hash + mtime + size in `analysis/persist.rs` (consumed by `RustAnalyzer`).
26	8. **Read-safety floor** (`io_safety.rs`). Symlink rejection and 50 MB file size cap on user-facing entry points to prevent path-traversal and allocator-bomb surprises.

Two things surfaced while checking this against the spec that change the shape of the answer.

**The Rust crate list is fully spec'd — no guessing needed.** From `01-core-architecture.md` (v0.1.0 baseline) and `03-multi-language-platform.md` (v0.7.0 additions):

Core runtime: `blake3`, `camino`, `dashmap`, `grep-regex`, `grep-searcher`, `ignore`, `rayon`, `regex`, `rustc-hash`, `serde`, `serde_json`, `thiserror`, `tiktoken-rs`, `tracing`, `gix`, `fs2`, `tempfile`
Feature-gated (`lang-ts`): `oxc_parser`, `oxc_ast`, `oxc_span`, `oxc_allocator`, `oxc_resolver` (OXC 0.128 suite, `oxc_resolver` versioned independently on its own 11.x line)
Feature-gated (`lang-rs`): `ra_ap_syntax`
Feature-gated (`cli`): `clap`, `miette`, `owo-colors`
Dev-dependencies: `insta`, `pretty_assertions`, `proptest`, `tempfile`, `criterion` (benches use `harness = false`)
Workspace lints already spec'd in `[lints]`: `unwrap_used`/`expect_used`/`panic`/`unreachable`/`unimplemented`/`dbg_macro`/`todo` all deny, `print_stdout`/`print_stderr` warn — so `clippy::pedantic` at warn priority plus that deny-list is what the workspace `Cargo.toml` needs, and it's a straight port, not a decision.

**Real gap #1 — the spec assumes an `orin-axi` monorepo that doesn't exist yet here.** The verbatim `Cargo.toml` has `io-errors = { path = "../io-errors", ... registry = "orin-cargo" }` and a `moon.yml` (moonrepo project file). That's a private-registry path dependency on a sibling crate and a monorepo task-runner file — neither of which exists in this standalone `/Users/gabe/Projects/monokl` checkout. Nothing in `AGENTS.md`/`ARCHITECTURE.md`/`README.md` mentions where that monorepo lives. I need you to tell me: is there an actual `orin-axi` monorepo checkout elsewhere I should nest this into (or symlink `io-errors` from), or do we stub `io-errors` locally for now and swap to the real path/registry dep later? This also reopens the mise+just vs proto question, since `moon.yml` implies moonrepo's own toolchain (`proto`) was the intended pairing, not mise.

**Real gap #2 — tsdown/vitest/oxlint/oxfmt aren't in the spec at all**, and checking why: every `tsconfig`/`vitest`/`napi` reference in the docs is monokl *detecting* those tools in codebases it analyzes (e.g. `is_test_utility` classifying a target repo's `vitest` usage), not monokl's own build tooling. The only place your question is genuinely open is the `@orin-axi/monokl` npm wrapper package (thin binary-dispatch shim) and the `tsconfig.json` fixtures under `tests/fixtures/small-ts/` (which need a real `tsconfig.json` file to exercise `TsconfigDiscovery`, not a build pipeline). For the wrapper, I'd recommend `tsdown` (esbuild-based, fast, fine for a shim this thin) + `vitest` for its handful of tests + `oxlint` for linting (thematically consistent — monokl itself is OXC-built). I'd hold off on `oxfmt` specifically: it's still quite new/early relative to Prettier or Biome's formatter, and formatting a tiny wrapper package isn't worth taking on an immature tool's edge cases — Prettier (already in use for markdown here) is the lower-risk default unless you want to standardize on the OXC toolchain end-to-end.

Can you confirm the monorepo situation first — that decides whether `git init` targets this directory alone or a parent `orin-axi/` root?

1	# michi (道)
2	
3	AXI response primitives for agent-ergonomic tools — TOON lists, key-value blocks,
4	truncation, structured errors, status, and `help[]` hints, in one small, pure-computation
5	crate.
6	
7	`michi` is the primitive layer of the **orin-axi** suite. It doesn't know about your
8	protocol, your CLI framework, or your async runtime — it takes structured data in and
9	returns token-efficient, agent-readable strings out. Four tools in the suite (Monokl,
10	Firkin, Lumen, Pulse) build on it instead of re-implementing this formatting themselves.
11	
12	Available from Rust directly, or from TypeScript via the `@orin-axi/michi` npm package.
13	
14	## Why
15	
16	Agents pay for every token they read. A JSON list of even modest size burns tokens on
17	repeated field names and punctuation that a human reader would never notice and an LLM
18	doesn't need restated per row. TOON (Token-Optimized Object Notation) states field names
19	once, in the header:
20	
21	```json
22	[
23	  { "number": 51815, "title": "[Bug]: Telegram plugin", "state": "open" },
24	  { "number": 51812, "title": "dark mode request", "state": "open" }
25	]
26	```
27	
28	```text
29	issues[2]{number,title,state}:
30	  51815,[Bug]: Telegram plugin,open
31	  51812,dark mode request,open
32	```
33	
34	Same information, fewer tokens. Values only get quoted when they actually contain a
35	comma, quote, or newline — no wasted punctuation on the common case.
36	
37	## Quick start
38	
39	```rust
40	use michi::toon::{self, ToonOptions, Value};
41	
42	let opts = ToonOptions {
43	    type_name: "issues".to_string(),
44	    fields: vec!["number".to_string(), "title".to_string(), "state".to_string()],
45	    rows: vec![
46	        vec![Value::Int(51815), Value::Str("[Bug]: Telegram plugin".to_string()), Value::Str("open".to_string())],
47	        vec![Value::Int(51812), Value::Str("dark mode request".to_string()), Value::Str("open".to_string())],
48	    ],
49	    total_count: Some(8771),
50	    hints: vec!["Run `gh-axi issue view <number>` to view an issue".to_string()],
51	};
52	
53	print!("{}", toon::render_toon(&opts));
54	```
55	
56	```typescript
57	import { renderToon } from "@orin-axi/michi";
58	
59	const out = renderToon({
60	  typeName: "issues",
61	  fields: ["number", "title", "state"],
62	  rows: [
63	    [{ type: "int", intVal: 51815 }, { type: "str", strVal: "[Bug]: Telegram plugin" }, { type: "str", strVal: "open" }],
64	    [{ type: "int", intVal: 51812 }, { type: "str", strVal: "dark mode request" }, { type: "str", strVal: "open" }],
65	  ],
66	  totalCount: 8771,
67	  hints: ["Run `gh-axi issue view <number>` to view an issue"],
68	});
69	
70	process.stdout.write(out);
71	```
72	
73	Both produce (verbatim, checked against the actual renderer):
74	
75	```text
76	issues[2]{number,title,state}:
77	  51815,[Bug]: Telegram plugin,open
78	  51812,dark mode request,open
79	totalCount: 8771
80	help[1]:
81	  Run `gh-axi issue view <number>` to view an issue
82	```
83	
84	The Rust struct-literal shape is deliberately explicit rather than a fluent builder —
85	`ToonOptions` is one struct, easy to construct from whatever data you already have. A
86	higher-level `toon::list(type_name, items)` convenience API is also available (behind the
87	`serde` feature) for building `ToonOptions` directly from a slice of `Serialize`-able
88	structs, inferring `fields` and `rows` from the serialized shape.
89	
90	## Install
91	
92	```toml
93	[dependencies]
94	michi = "0.1"
95	```
96	
97	```bash
98	pnpm add @orin-axi/michi     # or npm install / yarn add
99	```
100	
101	Default features add zero runtime dependencies — no tokio, no async runtime, nothing
102	beyond `thiserror`. You opt into more as you need it (see below).
103

105	
106	| Module | Purpose |
107	|---|---|
108	| `toon` | TOON list rendering — the token-optimized agent list format |
109	| `kv` | Key-value single-item rendering |
110	| `hints` | `help[]` contextual next-step blocks |
111	| `tru...
